objects.title: Ayam-ayam bernaga
objects.period: Late eighteenth century and nineteenth century
objects.caption:
The ayam-ayam bernaga (literally "roosters and dragons") is a traditional accessory worn by brides in the Brunei Malay community. Placed on the bride's head, it is worn during the powdering night, a ceremony in which the bride and groom are blessed with colourful powders separately at their respective homes. It originated among the Malays of Kampong Ayer (the water village), before becoming widely used among Malay communities throughout Brunei Darussalam.

Positioned at the crown of the bride during a moment of transition, the rooster and dragon on this bridal headpiece serve as auspicious guardians for the beginning of married life. The rooster is associated with courage, vigilance and the arrival of a new day through its dawn call, while the dragon carries associations of power, protection and authority. Together, they express qualities desired for the bride’s new household: vitality, strength and prosperity.

The ayam-ayam bernaga reflects the layered symbolic world of Brunei Malay ceremonial culture, where local customs incorporated animal imagery shaped by centuries of interaction across maritime Southeast Asia. Worn at the threshold between maidenhood and marriage, the headpiece demonstrates how communities across the region incorporated both familiar animals and mythical creatures into ceremonies and rituals as protectors, blessings and markers of social identity.

objects.title: Bronze rooster
objects.place_of_production: Ban Ta Phed, Phanom Thuan District, Kanchanaburi Province
objects.caption:
This bronze sculpture, discovered at the Ban Don Ta Phet archaeological site in Kanchanaburi Province, Thailand, dates to the late prehistoric period. The rooster is carefully rendered to include its characteristic features, including a prominent comb, long tail feathers, hackles and sharp spurs. It stands on a bronze post that fits precisely into a bronze enclosure that was discovered nearby during archaeological excavations, suggesting that the two objects originally formed part of a single composition.

The object demonstrates the advanced metalworking skills of the Ban Don Ta Phet community. Analysis of the bronze found that it contains between around 23 per cent and 28 per cent tin, which gives the metal a distinctive golden-silver appearance. The production of the sculpture required specialized knowledge of alloy composition, mould-making and metal casting, placing it among the community’s more technically accomplished objects.

The bronze rooster and enclosure were found alongside burial assemblages containing glass beads, carnelian, agate ornaments and silk fragments. Traces of hemp textile were found adhered to the rooster’s tail feathers, possibly originating from a burial wrapping or garments placed with the deceased. The presence of woven hemp textiles demonstrates the sophisticated use of natural fibres alongside metal technology during this period, while the variety of products in the assemblages indicates that the community had contact with other communities across long-distance exchange networks.

The form of the sculpture, the rooster, is evidence of the widespread presence of chickens in prehistoric Thailand. Chicken remains have been found at several Neolithic and Bronze Age sites, including Ban Chiang and Ban Non Wat, indicating that domesticated chickens were part of community life at the time. This bronze representation portrays that familiar animal in a carefully crafted object associated with burial and remembrance.

Together, the rooster sculpture and its burial context reveal how the chicken, an animal embedded in everyday life, also held an important place in rituals and spirituality and was part of a larger expression of identity and artisanship among prehistoric communities of mainland Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Domestic Chicken
objects.caption:
The chicken (Gallus gallus domesticus) that many of us are familiar with is a domesticated form of the red junglefowl (Gallus gallus), which is native to Southeast Asia and parts of South Asia. While  domestic chickens can have a variety of plumage colours and forms, the red junglefowl has several distinct physical characteristics. The adult male junglefowl has a red comb, facial skin and lappets, white ear patches, golden-yellow neck feathers, maroon scapulars and an arched dark green tail. The female has brown plumage and golden neck feathers.

Archaeological evidence supports the presence of domestic chickens in Southeast Asia before 6000 BC, and research suggests that it was introduced in China and India over the following 3000 to 4000 years. As a result of its long presence as part of human societies, the chicken has become deeply embedded in cultures of the region. Besides becoming a culinary staple in Southeast Asia, the animal has become a significant part of the region’s belief systems and sport.

The rooster is associated with various qualities, including with courage and perseverance in East Timor and with diligence and fertility in Thailand. In several religions of the region, the rooster is considered a sacred creature and is part of rituals.

In Bali, Indonesia, ceremonial cockfighting (known as tabuh rah, the 'spilling of blood') is a temple practice intended to provide an offering to the spirits. The rooster is also used in the sport of cockfighting, particularly in Indonesia and the Philippines.

objects.title: Lawi ayam
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies, Thailand
objects.material: Hardwood (mai nuea khaeng), composite pattern-welded iron (lek nuea phrasom) and brass alloy (lo-ha thong luang)
objects.dimensions: Hilt – length 10.3 cm; width 5.5 cm – made of orange jessamine wood (mai kaeo dee pli), hand-carved into the form of a rooster's head, fitted with a brass ferrule collar (pluok rat) and brass hand-guard (krong); Blade – length 19 cm; base width 2.5 cm – forged from composite pattern-welded iron (lek phrasom), creating a Mai Phok pattern, with a curved profile and a tapered, sharp point; Sheath – length 20.5 cm; width 4 cm – made of hill neem wood (mai sadao chang); the throat (pak fak) is inlaid with the dense heartwood of East Indian ebony (mai sao dam)
objects.object_biography: Hand-forged by master bladesmith Pichai Kaewkhao. Exhibited in the Knife and Weaponry Room (Hong Mit Lae Satthrawut), Folklore Museum, Institute of Southern Thai Studies.
objects.caption:
A lawi ayam (translated as the tail feather of a mature rooster) is a traditional close-quarters dagger. The weapon was named for the blade's curved, slender profile, which resembles the sweep of a rooster's tail feather. This example comes from the Patani School of Bladesmithing (Sakon Chang Pattani), one of the most historically significant centres for weapon production in southern Thailand.

The rooster shape gave the weapon meanings beyond its practical function. Across Malay and southern Thai communities, the rooster was associated with courage, vigilance and fighting spirit. As the bird that announces dawn and drives away darkness, it was understood as a symbol of alertness and protection. By shaping the weapon in the form of the rooster’s tail feather, the qualities of the animal were connected with those expected of the bearer: bravery, agility and resilience.

The weapon demonstrates the high level of artisanship associated with Patani bladesmithing. Its hilt is carved from mai kaeo dee pli (orange jessamine), a prized local hardwood, and is fitted with a brass ferrule and protective finger guard. The blade was forged through pattern-welding, layering iron and carbon steel through repeated folding and hammering to create the patterned surface known as lai mai phok, a regional expression of the Pamor tradition found across Malay and Indonesian blades. Its sheath is made from hill neem wood with an ebony inlay, both with auspicious associations.

The lawi ayam was once worn widely across Pattani, Songkhla, Phatthalung and Trang in Thailand and in the northern Malay sultanates. Its compact size allowed it to be worn discreetly within a sarong or waist belt, ready for immediate use. According to Malay martial texts such as the Kitab Silat, the dagger’s inward-curving blade was well suited for hooking and controlling an opponent’s movements, reflecting a close-combat fighting style built around speed, precision and adaptability.

The lawi ayam reflects a shared martial and symbolic tradition that developed across southern Thailand and the Malay Peninsula. Its form preserves both the technical knowledge of Patani bladesmiths and a wider regional understanding of the rooster as a symbol of strength and protection.

objects.title: Rooster-headed brass charcoal iron
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies, Thailand
objects.material: Cast heavy-gauge brass alloy and indigenous hardwood
objects.dimensions: Width 10 cm, length 19.5 cm, height 19.8 cm (Note: companion registry variants from Nakhon Si Thammarat record dimensions of 10 cm × 18 cm × 17.5 cm – preserved as given in source)
objects.object_biography: Sourced from the collection of Mrs Chong Kaeotui, Ban Thale Noi, Pha Nang Thong Sub-district, Khuan Khanun District, Phatthalung Province. Data recorded on 9 January 1996. Exhibited in the Metalwork and Metallurgy Culture Room (Hong Watthanatham Khruang Lo-ha lae Lo-hat), Folklore Museum, Institute of Southern Thai Studies.
objects.caption:
This rooster-headed brass charcoal iron was cast from thick, high-density brass alloy. Resembling a pointed hull or a sailing galleon, it was engineered to provide substantial weight, allowing the user to smooth heavy fabric with minimal physical exertion. The hollow interior houses a chamber for charcoal, with an internal baffle plate distributing thermal energy uniformly.

The defining mechanical feature of this iron is the sculpted rooster head (hua kai) at the front apex. This component securely locks the hinged lid during use, preventing red-hot embers or fine ash from spilling out and scorching the textile. This unique feature gave rise to its colloquial name, the rooster-headed iron (tao rit hua kai). Along the lateral walls, air vents allow oxygen to circulate and keep the embers burning evenly. Larger models featuring nine vents are known locally as nine-hole irons (tao rit kao ru).

Operating the iron requires filling the core with burning charcoal and fanning it to draw air through the vents, then rubbing the hot brass soleplate over a fresh green banana leaf to release natural wax from the heated leaf. The latter process creates a smooth, non-stick surface that protects delicate fabrics while leaving a faint fragrance on the cloth.

The rooster form on the iron reflects the cultural beliefs of Chinese communities that settled in trading hubs along the Malay Peninsula, in Nakhon Si Thammarat, Songkhla and Phuket. Within Chinese cosmology, the rooster represents the virtues of early rising, tireless diligence and spiritual alertness. The iron's exterior is engraved with low-relief depictions of the dragon (mangkon) and phoenix (hong). The combination of these creatures on a domestic iron is an auspicious pairing: the dragon representing supreme authority and the masculine forces of heaven, while the phoenix represents virtue, grace and feminine power. Together they signify marital harmony and domestic abundance, qualities fitting for an object used to press clothing for weddings, festivals and ceremonies. Objects such as this iron were either imported from southern China or produced locally by Chinese-diaspora metalsmiths. This iron is a demonstration of how communities across maritime Southeast Asia adopted imported technologies and the cultural meanings associated with them.

objects.title: Sulang
objects.period: Late eighteenth century and throughout the nineteenth century
objects.dimensions: Height 33.5 cm, width 30 cm; Top Cover 13.5 cm
objects.caption:
A sulang is a traditional storage box made of copper or brass. It is designed to hold water or store rice and other dry food, and it was historically used at gatherings such as weddings and thanksgiving events. Today containers of this type tend to serve as decorative objects in Bruneian homes.

The handles of this sulang invite close attention. At first glance they may suggest a buffalo, but overall, taking into account the legs and the flowing tail, the overall form can be viewed as a bird. Most likely, it depicts either a Rhinoceros Hornbill (Buceros rhinoceros) or a rooster (Gallus gallus).

The hornbill, native to Borneo and deeply embedded in the spiritual life of the island's communities, carries associations of protection, vitality and sacred guardianship that make it a natural presence on a vessel holding water and food staples for important occasions.

The rooster also carries distinct cultural weight. Prized for its strength and used in traditional cockfighting (sabung ayam), the rooster is associated with good fortune, energy and domestic abundance, which gave it a prominent place in the material culture of everyday life.

The uncertainty surrounding the type of bird depicted in this vessel’s form reflects the flexibility of Brunei’s folk craft traditions, where animal forms were not always fixed representations but were amalgams of various creatures, carrying overlapping associations. Whether intended as a hornbill or a rooster or a mix of the two, the motif reveals a wider Southeast Asian tradition of embedding the qualities of animals and their associated strengths, including protection, vitality and prosperity, within objects of everyday and ceremonial use.

objects.title: Tempayan
objects.period: Late eighteenth to early twentieth century
objects.place_of_production: Likely southern China or Southeast Asia
objects.caption:
These large earthenware storage jars (tempayan), likely produced in southern China or Southeast Asia between the late eighteenth century and early twentieth century, were once common household items in Peranakan Chinese homes across maritime Southeast Asia.

Crafted from high-fired clay, tempayan reflect shared domestic practices across the region. Larger jars were commonly used for water storage, while smaller ones held pickles, rice and other dry ingredients.

Everyday objects such as the tempayan featured hand-painted motifs, including birds, floral scrolls and bamboo, expressing cultural identity and aspirations. These motifs were chosen for their auspicious meanings, drawing from Chinese visual traditions in which certain plants and animals convey wishes for harmony, prosperity, longevity and abundance.

The birds painted on this jar, including chickens, belong to this tradition. The rooster, associated across Chinese and Southeast Asian communities with diligence, vitality and the arrival of dawn, brought these qualities into the sphere of everyday provisions and family life.

Placing such imagery on a vessel used for preserving the household’s necessities connected ordinary acts of storage and sustenance with broader hopes for prosperity and continuity. This tradition reflects how animal symbolism was woven into the material culture of everyday life across maritime Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Tin ingots
objects.dimensions: Height 6.1 cm, width 8.5 cm, weight 0.070 grams
objects.caption:
These tin ingots in animal forms, including some shaped as roosters, represent the tradition of zoomorphic currency used across the Malay Peninsula and beyond. The state of Perak was the primary producer of such ingots, which were created in the forms of roosters, crabs, crocodiles, elephants, fish, goats, grasshoppers and tortoises from at least the sixteenth century onwards.

Although the original purpose of such ingots has been debated – with suggestions that some may have served as talismans, weights or even objects of display – historical records confirm that they served as standard weights used to measure the accuracy of other tin blocks and traded goods, and, at times, as a direct medium of exchange. In the Kinta Valley of Perak during the mid-nineteenth century, for example, a cast tin cockerel (gambar ayam) was valued at 10 Pitis or 100 Duit Ayam (copper tokens bearing the image of a fighting cock issued by certain Singapore merchants).

Records indicate that animal-shaped tin ingots were used in Perak, Sumatra southern Thailand and the Philippines, reflecting the circulation of tin, trade practices and monetary systems across maritime Southeast Asia. Their recurring animal forms reveal how economic exchange operated through familiar animals, linking commerce with the shared visual languages of communities connected by trade.

objects.title: Wooden Cold-Press Cake Molds with Elephant, Horse, and Fowl Motifs
objects.title_raw:
Wooden Cold-Press Cake Molds with

title_variants: Wooden Cold-Press Cake Molds with Elephant, Horse, and Fowl Motifs
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies, Thailand
objects.caption:
This phim yen (literally "cold mold") is a wooden pastry mold used to make Khanom Putu, a traditional pastry. Such molds are carved from durable local hardwoods such as jackfruit or velvet tamarind wood, with hollow cavities roughly 1 to 2 inches deep chiselled into detailed, recessed designs. This collection contains motifs of elephants, horses, and poultry, traditionally popular for Khanom Putu. The "cold-press" method gives the mold its name: the dough is shaped entirely inside the wooden matrix without baking or heat, then extracted with a sharp tap against a wooden table, releasing the pastry with sharp, embossed reliefs.

This heritage pastry has held an essential position within the daily life, rites of passage, and religious rituals of both Chinese and Malay-Javanese communities in Southern Thailand for centuries. It is used at births, cradle ceremonies, engagements, weddings, and circumcision rituals. During Songkran, younger generations arrange these pastries inside fine betel nut caddies or lacquerware to offer to elders in exchange for ancestral blessings. Within the Sathing Phra Peninsula, this pastry holds a profound allegorical connection to matrimony: its name sounds identical to the Thai word meaning "to hold fast" or "to intertwine," making the cake an edible prayer for marital fidelity.

Carving specific fauna onto the phim yen allowed families to embed unspoken blessings directly into the food served to guests. The Elephant (Chang) denotes absolute authority, spiritual merit, and structural prosperity — pastries stamped with this form are reserved for grand auspicious celebrations or offered to high-ranking Buddhist monks and Muslim leaders. The Horse (Ma) represents rapid progress and career advancement, standardly served at housewarmings or gifted to young adults. The Chicken (Kai), which awakens at dawn to forage, signifies industriousness, material abundance, and financial luck and is served more widely.

The phim yen tradition illustrates trans-regional interactions. Diasporic Chinese Hokkien and Baba-Peranakan communities introduced the technology of hand-carved wooden blocks for compressed pastries. They substituted Chinese mythological creatures with animals familiar to local agrarian life and folk belief: the elephant, the horse, and the chicken. Meanwhile, Malay-Javanese and Islamic traditions contributed to the pastry’s recipe.

This mold, encoding Chinese technological knowledge, Malay culinary tradition, and the symbolic vocabularies of the elephant, the horse, and the chicken, speaks to a layered process of exchange, adaptation, and sharing that shaped the Southern Thai-Malay Peninsula over centuries.

Across Chinese, Malay-Javanese and southern Thai communities, traditional pastries made this way are served at key milestones and rites of passage, including births, cradle ceremonies, engagements, weddings and circumcision rituals, and are given as offerings in religious rituals. During Songkran (Thai New Year), younger family members arrange these pastries on fine betel nut trays or in lacquerware and offer them to their elders, receiving blessings in return. On the Sathing Phra Peninsula, this type of pastry holds a profound allegorical connection to matrimony: its name sounds identical to the Thai word meaning ‘to hold fast’ or ‘to intertwine’, making the pastry an edible prayer for marital fidelity.

Carving motifs of auspicious animals into the moulds embedded blessings directly into the pastries. The elephant (chang) denotes authority, spiritual merit and prosperity, so pastries stamped with this form are reserved for grand auspicious celebrations or are offered to high-ranking Buddhist monks and Muslim leaders. The horse (ma) represents rapid progress and career advancement, so pastries with this form are served at housewarmings or are gifted to young adults. The chicken (kai), which awakens at dawn to forage, signifies industriousness, material abundance and financial luck, so pastries with this form are served more widely.

This type of traditional mould demonstrates the trans-regional transfer of technology and beliefs. Diasporic Hokkien and Baba-Peranakan communities introduced the Chinese technology of hand-carved wooden blocks for such pastries to South-East Asia but substituted Chinese mythological creatures with animals familiar to local agrarian life and folk belief: the elephant, the horse and the chicken. Meanwhile, Malay-Javanese and Islamic traditions contributed to adapting the pastry’s recipe.

Such moulds, encompassing Chinese technological knowledge, Malay culinary tradition and the symbolic vocabularies of the elephant, the horse and the chicken, speak to a layered process of exchange, sharing and adaptation that shaped cultural life in the southern Thai-Malay Peninsula over centuries.

objects.title: Koffo cloth
objects.caption:
Koffo, also known as hote, is a woven textile made from the fibres of the abaca banana (Musa textilis), a plant native to the Philippines that also thrives in North Sulawesi, Indonesia, an area that has historical connections with the southern Philippines.

Woven primarily by women in the Sangihe and Talaud Islands, koffo cloth is valued for its strength, buoyancy and resistance to salt water – qualities that made it well suited to use in maritime communities. In addition to being used to make wall hangings and room dividers, such fibres were also used to make ropes for boats and other objects related to seafaring activities.

objects.title: Dragon-head tortoise and crane ornaments
objects.dimensions: Height 78 cm, width 20 cm, depth 38 cm
objects.object_biography: Probably purchased in the early 1900s by the late Mr Chan Cheng Siew for his house, which is now the Baba & Nyonya Heritage Museum. Currently only one set is on display, on the first floor.
objects.caption:
This set of three brass statues features a large crane standing atop a tortoise, which has a dragon's head and dragon-like paws, flanked by two smaller cranes perched on tortoises that have ordinary heads. The smaller pieces serve as candle holders. Together, the three statues form a composition that was likely designed to be displayed at an entryway, as their size made a desk arrangement impractical.

Across Chinese, Japanese and Korean traditions, the tortoise represents endurance, stability and protection, while the crane signifies peace, harmony and purity. In these traditions, the tortoise and crane are paired as symbols of longevity, based on the knowledge that both creatures possessed extraordinarily long lifespans. Together, they express the wish for a long and prosperous life. Within Baba & Nyonya households, the pairing of cranes and tortoises appeared widely on embroidered textiles, porcelain, jewellery, furniture and other objects.

Crafted in brass, these statues were intended to endure. The dragon-headed tortoise adds another layer of auspicious meaning. The dragon and tortoise are two of the four celestial animals in Chinese cosmology, associated respectively with power and stability. Their pairing combines multiple forms of protection and good fortune.

In this set, animals drawn from land, water and the mythical realm were brought together to create an auspicious guardian at the threshold of the household, as a talisman for long life and stability. This set reflects how Peranakan communities adapted Chinese symbolic traditions within the material culture of maritime Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Turtle-shaped maritime box
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies, Thailand
objects.dimensions: Width 8 cm, length 15 cm, height 6 cm
objects.object_biography: Sourced from the personal collection of Mr Hem Sando Sen, House No. 22, Village No. 8, Koh Taeo Sub-district, Mueang Songkhla District, Songkhla Province (ritual donation). Exhibited in the Recreation Exhibition Room (Hong Nanthanakon), Folklore Museum, Institute of Southern Thai Studies.
objects.caption:
Historically, compact wooden storage chests were used by communities along the Southern Thai coast for safeguarding vital provisions during deep-sea voyages. To construct such boxes, local woodworkers selected high-density, resinous hardwoods such as kiam (Cotylelobium lanceolatum) and lumpho (Intsia palembanica) for their natural resistance to rot, humidity and brine. The box's low-set rectangular silhouette was engineered for equilibrium on the deck of a rolling vessel, minimizing sliding or inversion during heavy swells. Its lid was crafted to ensure a hermetic friction fit, and many such boxes featured tongue-and-groove slide locks or rattan tie-down cords to block sea spray. This impeccable design kept the contents of the box – including, tobacco, nipa palm wrapper leaves, fire-striking apparatus, currency and family documents – dry across multi-day expeditions.

The box’s turtle-form lid, carved with stepped relief patterning mirroring the natural scutes of a marine turtle's carapace, invokes a creature that navigates thousands of miles of open ocean yet unerringly returns to shore, a talisman for the safe return that fishermen sought. Furthermore, the smooth, rounded edges of the turtle box served a practical purpose, preventing the container from snagging or tearing fragile fishing nets within the cramped spaces of the boat.

The object's presence across southern Thai and Malay coastal communities, whose lives were shaped by the same maritime networks, reflects a shared material culture. Here practical engineering, animal symbolism and the logic of survival at sea were inseparable.

objects.title: Zoomorphic lime container
objects.object_biography: Donated by Mr. Yothin and Mrs. Wiwan Tharahirunchot in 2021.
objects.caption:
This glazed ceramic container is in the form of a turtle, with a small head, rounded body and four small legs, and has a circular opening at the centre of the back. Produced at the Phnom Dongrek kilns in Buriram Province in the twelfth century, it was crafted to hold slaked lime, an essential ingredient in betel chewing. Slaked lime was mixed with betel leaf, areca nut and other additions before consumption. Introduced to Southeast Asia through long-standing cultural connections with India, betel chewing became deeply embedded in daily life across the region, serving as both a gesture of hospitality and a shared social practice.

The Phnom Dongrek kilns, located within the cultural sphere of the Khmer Empire, were known for producing sophisticated stoneware vessels in various forms. These forms drew simultaneously from the natural world and from wider religious and symbolic traditions. Animal forms included elephants, crocodiles, fish and turtles. They were also crafted in the forms of figures drawn from Hindu-Buddhist traditions, such as Ganesha.

The hard shell of the turtle was associated in local traditions with safeguarding against harm, while its longevity made it an auspicious form for an object used repeatedly in daily life. Within Hindu traditions, the turtle is associated with Vishnu’s Kurma avatar, in which the divine tortoise supports Mount Mandara during the Churning of the Ocean of Milk, sustaining the balance of the cosmos upon its back.

Lime containers were produced in a variety of materials, from humble everyday forms to finely crafted vessels such as this glazed ceramic example. The turtle form of this container connected the practice of betel chewing with ideas associated with the turtle, including protection, endurance and cosmic stability.

By shaping the container in the form of this creature, the artisan transformed it from a routine household object into one carrying layers of meaning. The turtle that symbolically supports the universe was brought into the everyday act of preparing and consuming betel, transferring the meanings associated with the turtle to the practice.

objects.title: The greater mouse-deer
objects.collection: Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum, Singapore
objects.caption:
The greater mouse-deer (Tragulus napu), a forest-dwelling creature that feeds on vegetation and fallen fruit, is one of the world’s smallest hoofed mammals. Mouse-deer resemble true deer but are much smaller. Adults measure only around 50 cm to 60 cm in length. They have distinctive triangular white markings extending from the chin down the throat.

Their historical range encompassed mainland and maritime Southeast Asia, extending from Myanmar and Thailand through to Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia. Although the species was thought to have disappeared from Singapore, a population was confirmed on Pulau Ubin in 2009.

The mouse-deer occupies an outsized place in the cultural imagination of communities that share its forests across the Malay-speaking world. Known as Sang Kancil, the mouse-deer is the protagonist of some of the region’s most beloved folktales. These stories depict the mouse-deer as a symbol of wit, adaptability and resilience. Rather than relying on strength, the Sang Kancil survives through intelligence and quick thinking, most famously in a tale in which it tricks crocodiles into forming a bridge by pretending to count them as it crosses.

The mouse-deer was historically a source of food, hunted across parts of Southeast Asia before wildlife protection measures were introduced from the mid-twentieth century onwards. The remaining fragmented populations of greater mouse-deer continue to face pressure from habitat loss and illegal hunting.

The story of the mouse-deer reflects a long-standing relationship between humans in Southeast Asia and the forests they inhabit: a creature celebrated in folklore and once hunted for food is now also recognized as an essential part of the fragile ecosystems that sustain the region’s shared natural heritage.

objects.title: Kijang gold coins
objects.period: between the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries (undated)
objects.caption:
Kijang gold coins from Kelantan were once used as currency across the region. This gold coin (kupang) weighs around 0.64 grams. It features a red barking deer (kijang) on one side and is inscribed on the other side with ‘Al Adil’ in Arabic script.

The kijang motif on these coins is associated with Che Siti Wan Kembang, the legendary queen said to have ruled the east coast of the Malay Peninsula in the sixteenth century. In Kelantanese Malay culture, the kijang represents qualities admired in rulers and leaders: grace, swiftness, vigilance and strength. Its elegance and rarity made it a fitting emblem of royal identity, economic trust and protection, while also distinguishing Kelantan’s coinage and state symbols from those of neighbouring regions. This motif remains present today in the Kelantan State Emblem (Jata Negeri). The kijang also carries broader cultural and symbolic meanings.

Kelantan and Pattani were historically connected through overlapping sultanates, dynastic ties and trading networks, which led to symbols such as the kijang crossing political boundaries. The motif on these coins therefore reflects not only Kelantan’s royal heritage, but also the shared cultural connections that linked communities across the eastern Malay Peninsula.

objects.title: Nang Talung Puppetry Deer
objects.object_biography: Donated by Khun Nartnikorn (Tai Na Pombejra) on 25 March 1954.
objects.caption:
This shadow puppet in the form of a deer was crafted for Nang Talung, the shadow-theatre tradition of southern Thailand. Made from hide that has been intricately carved, it is mounted on a single bamboo control stick. During a performance, the nai nang (puppet master) manipulates the figure before a lit screen, casting its shadow onto a white cloth, while providing narration and vocalization. The performance is accompanied by a musical ensemble featuring drums, thap (goblet drums), mong (gongs), ching (cymbals) and the pi chawa (Javanese oboe).

Nang Talung belongs to a family of shadow-theatre traditions across Southeast Asia including Sbek Thom in Cambodia, Nang Yai in the Chao Phraya River Basin, Wayang Kulit in Malaysia and Wayang Purwa and other regional forms in Indonesia. Shadow theatre draws on Indian epics, namely the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, as well as local legends. Many of the shadow-theatre traditions feature animal-shaped puppets based both on fauna from the natural environment familiar to the community and on creatures in the community’s literary repertoire.

When the deer moves across the shadow screen, it brings something of its accumulated natural and symbolic meanings. The deer has a deep presence in the Southeast Asian region’s landscape and its stories. The kijang is embedded in Malay and Iban folklore as a figure of quickness, cunning and spiritual power. The mouse-deer, known as Sang Kancil, features in the Malay oral tradition as the most beloved trickster figure, and the barking deer appears in Iban mythology as a powerful spirit.

Shadow plays in Southeast Asia are not only sources of entertainment but are integral to rituals of ancestral invocation, healing and the exorcism of malevolent spirits. In Thailand, Nang Talung is traditionally performed between April and July, prior to the Buddhist Lent. The sacred context of the performance invests each animal figure, including the deer, with meaning. Animal-shaped shadow puppets are a form through which shared beliefs about the natural and imagined world are given shape and set in motion.

objects.title: Cannon with dragon motif
objects.dimensions: Length 101.7 cm, height 17 cm, weight: 23.36 kg
objects.caption:
This dragon-shaped cannon merges mythological symbolism with functional military technology. Across East and Southeast Asia, the dragon has long symbolized power, prosperity and command over cosmic forces. In Borneo, the water-dragon, associated with rivers and the sea, was especially revered as a protective entity, and for that reason the dragon motif was often incorporated into local material culture.

Between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries, firearms became an integral part of military, socio-economic and ceremonial life in the Sultanate of Brunei. Their presence was documented as early as 1521 by Antonio Pigafetta, who noted bedil (portable firearms) and bronze cannons surrounding the sultan’s palace. At the time, cannons served primarily to defend national sovereignty, acting as vital strategic weapons during internal civil wars – such as the conflict between Sultan Abdul Hakkul Mubin and Pengiran Bendahara Muhyiddin – and against expanding foreign empires, including repelling two Spanish invasions.

Beyond the battlefield, these weapons occupied a central role in civilian life before the adoption of standardized currency. Cannons circulated as a primary medium of trade, where their value was calculated by both weight – measured in units of picul (equivalent to 133.3 pounds) – and the artistic quality of their carvings. They also functioned as instruments of customary law among the Dusun and Belait to pay fines, served as required bridal gifts to secure marriage and were fired from embankments as long-range communication tools to announce major events. Because cannon ownership signalled immense status, production was strictly controlled by the sultan, who maintained a massive collection as a display of royal authority.

Bruneian cannons were crafted by pouring a molten alloy of copper and tin into clay moulds. After being left to cool for several hours, the cannons were removed from the moulds and were sculpted. While many cannons were decorated with flora and fauna motifs, this particular piece  was crafted in the form of the creature itself: the gaping mouth forms the muzzle, a curled snout serves as the sight, the rear handle coils into a tail and intricate metalwork details a spine ridge and scales throughout its body (now set on a modern mount).

By casting a cannon in the form of a dragon, local artisans incorporated Chinese design elements into Malay decorative art, charging the weapon with the dragon's protective and destructive power and situating it within the local cosmological order – a choice of form that carried deep resonance when defending the Sultanate against aggressors.

This artistic fusion was not isolated to Brunei; carved guns and portable cannons bearing similar mythological motifs are found across Southeast Asia, including in modern-day Indonesia, Thailand and Myanmar. The widespread prevalence of weapons embellished with dragons suggests that the dragon was a shared regional motif that communities across Southeast Asia drew upon as they integrated firearms into their military, social and ceremonial systems.

objects.title: Holy water vessel
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies, Thailand
objects.material: Blackened cast brass alloy (Lo-ha thong luang rom dam)
objects.dimensions: Width (from left handle to right handle) 10.35 cm, Height (from base to rim) 9.8 cm, Base diameter 7 cm, Inner rim diameter 3.8 cm, outer rim diameter 5 cm
objects.object_biography: Donated by Phra Athikan Prathom Pathamo, originally from Wat Thai, Village No. 8, Koh Yo Sub-district, Mueang Songkhla District, Songkhla Province. Exhibited in the Metalwork and Metallurgy Culture Room (Hong Watthanatham Phra Khruang Loha lae Lohat), Folklore Museum, Institute of Southern Thai Studies.
objects.caption:
Within Theravada Buddhist practice, urns such as this vessel are used to hold Nam Phra Phutthamon (holy water), which is consecrated through monastic chanting and protective blessings. This sanctified water is sprinkled during ceremonies such as longevity rites, the consecration of new buildings and housewarmings. The act of sprinkling holy water serves as a physical channel to convey blessings, spiritual safety and peace to the participants.

The vessel’s most prominent features are its dragon handles, cast on opposite sides of the body with their heads turned inwards towards the rim. In Chinese tradition, dragons (long) were associated with imperial authority, prosperity and control over water and rainfall. These auspicious associations resonated strongly in Southeast Asia, where Naga – powerful serpent-like beings of Hindu-Buddhist traditions – similarly guarded rivers, lakes and sources of fertility. In the water-dependent societies of the Songkhla Lake basin, dragons and Naga shared a common symbolic role: as protectors of the waters that sustained human life. The presence of dragons on the holy water vessel indicated protection for the sacred waters it contained, connecting human communities with spiritual forces.

The vessel’s other decorative elements reinforce this connection between spiritual protection and worldly well-being. Its base is in the form of overlapping lotus petals, a Buddhist symbol of purity and enlightenment. Six low-relief panels around the vessel’s body depict auspicious imagery, including birds among blossoms, guardian lions, ducks among rice stalks, cranes beside bamboo, deer near plum blossoms and egrets among aquatic plants. Together, these motifs express aspirations for longevity, prosperity, agricultural abundance and harmony between humans and the natural world.

The vessel’s hybrid style reflects the cosmopolitan character of the place it was forged, the Songkhla Lake basin, where Chinese migrant communities, local Thai populations and Buddhist institutions interacted over centuries through maritime trade networks. From the late Ayutthaya to early Rattanakosin periods, Chinese artisans and merchants contributed metalworking skills and decorative traditions that were incorporated into local religious objects. Wealthy merchants and community leaders often commissioned elaborate ritual vessels as temple offerings – acts of communal devotion.

Produced in a region shaped by centuries of trade and migration, the vessel combines Chinese decorative traditions with Theravada-Buddhist ritual function, demonstrating how communities around the Southern Thai Peninsula adapted artistic and spiritual traditions into local forms. Whether expressed as the Chinese dragon or the Naga of Buddhist and Hindu traditions, these creatures embodied the protection and renewal of the life-giving waters upon which communities depended.

objects.title: Canang
objects.period: Late eighteenth century and nineteenth century CE
objects.dimensions: Width 18 cm, height 10 cm, chain length 36 cm
objects.caption:
A canang is a gong-like percussion instrument traditionally used in Brunei’s royal court as both a time marker and a means of announcing royal decrees or summons from the sultan. It also played a role in ceremonial occasions, where its sound marked important moments in court life.

This canang is decorated with the image of the dragon. Across East and Southeast Asia, the dragon was associated with sovereignty, power and protection, making it an appropriate symbol for an object connected with royal authority. By placing the dragon on an instrument whose sound carried the presence of the ruler, artisans transformed this canang from a functional object into a symbol of royalty.

The dragon became prominent in Bruneian decorative arts as a result of centuries of exchange with China. The imagery on the instrument therefore reflects the movement of artistic motifs with traders and communities as they travelled across maritime networks and how the motifs were adapted and incorporated into local traditions in Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Dragon-shaped incense tray
objects.object_biography: Exhibited at Phra Thinang Phrommetthada (Lower Floor), Phra Wiman Complex, National Museum Bangkok.
objects.caption:
This decorative incense tray features a dragon with its head held high, gazing upward with wide, bulging eyes, a short snout and an open mouth. The body is straight, featuring a central rectangular compartment coated in red cinnabar lacquer (chat). The piece is supported by a rectangular base carved in the form of dragon legs and claws, tapering off into a dragon's tail at the end.

It is believed that this dragon-shaped tray was either a component of, or inspired by, the ‘incense clock’ (xiangpan), a traditional timekeeping device. In such devices, incense was laid along a track – often referred to as a ‘dragon boat’ – with metal weights suspended from threads at specific intervals. A metal tray was placed underneath. As the incense burned steadily to a thread, the weight would drop into the tray below, creating an audible chime to mark the time. These served as early alarm clocks. Records from the nineteenth century (the twenty-fourth Buddhist century) indicate that Cantonese communities also used these dragon incense trays as lighting stations for tobacco after evening meals.

Across East and Southeast Asia, dragons were associated with authority, prosperity and command over cosmic forces, making the dragon a powerful symbol of rulership and auspicious power. In this incense tray, the depiction of the dragon’s raised head, powerful claws and commanding posture made this everyday object a statement of prestige.

This prestige was further reinforced through its mother-of-pearl inlay, a decorative technique that involved highly skilled artisanship. Developed in China over centuries, skills in mother-of-pearl inlay moved with artisans along trade networks, and the technique was adapted into local artistic traditions across mainland Southeast Asia. The pairing of the dragon motif with this craft technique reflects the movement of both material knowledge and symbolic language across interconnected societies.

The significance of the dragon on this incense tray lies precisely in its ability to remain recognizable across borders. Whether appearing in Chinese courts or Southeast Asian households, the dragon communicated power, prosperity and auspicious protection. This object therefore represents the circulation of a shared visual language through which communities across and beyond Southeast Asia expressed status, aspiration and connection to forces beyond the human world.

objects.title: Flintlock firearm
objects.period: Ca. eighteenth and nineteenth century CE
objects.object_biography: Received from the Royal Ceremonial Section, Royal Palace.
objects.caption:
This flintlock firearm is distinguished by its flared muzzle in the form of the head of a Naga or a dragon, with bulging eyes, fangs and serrated edges lining the circumference of the mouth. As part of the Royal Ceremonial Section of the Royal Palace, this firearm likely had ceremonial as well as military significance. Weapons in the Siamese court featured in rituals of allegiance, present at occasions where officials swore oaths to the king by drinking consecrated water prepared by monks. The Naga's dominion over water would have made such weapons a natural presence in rituals where consecrated water was the medium of sacred oath. The decision to adorn a firearm with the head of a mythical serpent was, in that setting, also an assertion of royal power and legitimacy.

At first glance, the pairing of a water-dwelling serpent with a weapon that produces fire and smoke may seem paradoxical. Yet, along the Mekong River, communities have long attributed the mysterious phenomenon of fireballs rising from the river’s surface to Naga, calling them ‘Naga fireballs’.  Thus, the serpent was already considered to be a creature of fire as much as water.

In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the Dutch East India Company conducted diplomatic and trade relations with the Ayutthaya kingdom, exchanges that included the gifting of firearms. The Siamese court, which held a monopoly on the weapons trade and maintained gun control policies within Ayutthaya, received such objects into a very specific political context.

Similar firearms were produced for the Chinese market, pointing to a broader practice of adapting the form of weapons to the symbolic vocabularies of their intended recipients. The specificity of the design suggests this was very likely a piece custom-made for local or regional tastes. That the design of this firearm finds parallels across Southeast Asia and China speaks to the depth of the serpent's hold on the regional imagination – powerful enough and revered enough to be mobilised by communities across the region to communicate both martial and royal strength.

objects.title: Large tile with dragons
objects.dimensions: Length 71 cm, height 74 cm, width 13 cm
objects.object_biography: Accession No. 2014-00577.
objects.caption:
This large earthenware tile from the Ly dynasty (1009–1225) reflects the powerful role of the dragon in Vietnamese traditions. The tile portrays sinuous dragons in vigorous movement amidst scrolling clouds – imagery typical of Ly dynasty art. During the Ly dynasty, the dragons adorned temples and palaces frequented by the king. Similar elements in this style have been found at the ancient royal capital in Hanoi, formerly known as Thang Long (rising dragon).

Dragons have long had important symbolic and ritual meaning in Viet Nam and elsewhere in Southeast Asia. According to Vietnamese origin stories, the Vietnamese people are descended from the union of Lạc Long Quân, the Dragon Lord of Lạc, and Âu Cơ, the Mountain Fairy. Their children inherited both the qualities of the sea and the mountains, reflecting a worldview in which dragons connected different realms of nature. As beings associated with rivers, clouds and subterranean waterways, dragons were believed to shape the landscape itself, with their presence sustaining the flow of life-giving energy (khí) through the earth.

This connection between dragons and the land is also reflected in the legend of Hạ Long Bay (the bay of the descending dragon). According to this legend, when a young Vietnamese nation faced invasion from the sea, a mother dragon and her offspring descended to protect the people. They cast jewels that became islands and barriers that defended the coast. This story presents the dragon not only as a creature of power, but as a guardian whose presence protects both the people and the territory they inhabit.

The dragon’s prominence in Ly dynasty architecture reflects a wider Southeast Asian pattern in which mythical beings were closely tied to stories of origins, protection and the order of the world. Across the region, dragon and serpent traditions once connected communities to the landscapes around them, reflecting the belief that human societies were sustained through relationships with powerful forces of nature.

objects.title: Sunda Pangolin
objects.collection: Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum, Singapore
objects.caption:
The Sunda pangolin (Manis javanica) is a shy, nocturnal mammal native to the tropical forests of Southeast Asia. Enclosed in overlapping keratin scales, it resembles a living suit of armor and curls into an impenetrable ball when threatened. Preserved specimens at the Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum—mostly salvaged from accidental roadkill—offer visitors a rare, up-close look at this creature's unique anatomy. To combat local threats, the Singapore Pangolin Working Group was established in 2014, uniting government agencies, researchers, and community organizations to coordinate rescue efforts, habitat conservation, and public education.

Beyond modern ecology, the pangolin holds a fascinating place in traditional folklore due to its resemblance to mythical creatures—most notably the dragon. In classical East Asian texts, such as Li Shizhen’s Bencao Gangmu, the pangolin was referred to as lingli (“scaly carp”) and colloquially dubbed the “Earth Dragon” (Di Long). Because traditional dragons were portrayed as composite beasts covered in carp scales with power over subterranean realms, the pangolin—the world's only scale-covered mammal—was viewed as a living, terrestrial relative of the mythical beast. Its powerful claws and burrowing habits gave rise to legends that it navigated through a vast network of underground tunnels, cementing its image as a creature of protection, quiet resilience, and subterranean mastery.

Today, the Sunda pangolin is critically endangered. Driven by illegal wildlife trafficking for its meat and scales—falsely valued in traditional medicine—alongside rapid habitat fragmentation, wild populations face severe decline. High-profile transit seizures in Singapore highlight the global scale of wildlife crime, while climate change threatens the ant and termite populations vital to the pangolin's survival.

Bridging past and present, natural history and cultural heritage, the Sunda pangolin shows that animals in material culture are not just decorative motifs but storytellers carrying meaning across time. Through this remarkable creature, we can reflect on how cultural heritage can inspire conservation and care for endangered species. Protecting pangolins safeguards not only their lives but also the stories, creativity, and traditions they represent, preserving both natural and cultural heritage for future generations.

objects.title: Jar decorated with fish and a beast
objects.title_raw: Jar decorated with fish and a beast
objects.object_biography: Accession No. 2014-00949.
objects.caption:
This large blue-and-white jar features the makara – a mythical aquatic beast – and two fish, one of which is devouring the other. The makara, a mythical guardian of aquatic realms shaped by Hindu-Buddhist and regional traditions, has a hybrid form, with an elephant-like trunk and a fish body, representing its place between the worlds of animals, spirits and the divine, as well as between land and water. The fish are familiar creatures associated with water, fertility and abundance.

The painted decoration on this jar was likely inspired by Yuan-dynasty Chinese porcelain exported to the Southeast Asian region. The fish and the lotus-petal borders are typical of Yuan wares but seem to be rendered by artists in an entirely free and distinct manner here.

Vietnamese jars like these were often used for storing valuable household goods such as wine, tea, spices, medicines and salted food. Finely crafted ceramic jars such as this were in high demand among Southeast Asia’s wealthier communities. Similar jars discovered on the island of Sulawesi in Indonesia reflect the movement of such ceramics via the maritime trade networks that connected Viet Nam with island Southeast Asia. The decorative forms and symbolic ideas expressed via the creatures on the ceramics travelled together along these routes.

Inspired by Chinese artistic vocabulary but produced in Viet Nam and exported to other parts of Southeast Asia, jars such as this one, featuring both mythical and real-life creatures that express shared ideas, reflect the interconnected world of maritime Southeast Asia. The jar shows how communities across the region understood and exchanged ideas and motifs across the waters that connected them.

objects.title: Rostrum of the largetooth sawfish
objects.place_of_production: Jao Pho Khao Tok Shrine, Ratchakhrue Worawihan Temple, Talat Phlu, Thon Buri District, Bangkok
objects.caption:
The largetooth sawfish (Pristis pristis) is a relative of rays and is distinguished by its elongated, flattened snout known as a rostrum, which is lined with bilateral transverse teeth, resembling a double-sided saw. Sawfish possess the physiological capacity to transition between marine, brackish and freshwater environments, allowing them to inhabit both estuaries and rivers.

Historically, sawfish were prevalent across tropical Indo-Pacific waters, including Thailand, Viet Nam, Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines. In Southeast Asian folk belief, the formidable appearance of the sawfish gave it the status of a guardian spirit.

This association with protection led to the rostrum of the largetooth sawfish being used as a protective charm. In the Kinabatangan River basin of Sabah, Malaysia, the rostrum is nailed above doorways as a talisman to ward off evil. When wrapped in cloth and hung over a cradle, it is believed to pacify restless infants.

Elsewhere in the region, the animal’s totemic status has given the species some protection. In Dondai village at Lake Sentani in Papua, Indonesia, it is taboo to consume the flesh of the sawfish. Traditional architecture features house posts carved with sawfish motifs to commemorate maritime ancestors, and the animal also appears in bark paintings as a visual record of natural and spiritual heritage. Today, the cultural significance of the sawfish as a guardian spirit and talisman endures as part of the region’s shared beliefs and practices.

The sawfish population in Southeast Asia faces numerous threats, and the species has declined dramatically in recent decades. A unique issue experienced by this species is that its physical shape makes it highly vulnerable to entanglement in fishing nets. In addition, despite its revered status, it is harvested for its meat, for its skin, which is processed into leather, and for its rostrum, which is used in traditional medicine. Since 2006, sawfish in Southeast Asian waters have been classified as Critically Endangered on the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List.

objects.title: Skeleton of Singapore’s first recorded sperm whale
objects.title_raw: Skeleton of Singapore’s first recorded sperm whale
objects.collection: Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum, Singapore
objects.caption:
Discovered drifting off the coast of Jurong Island in July 2015, this 10.6-metre adult female sperm whale – named Jubi Lee in honour of the year Singapore celebrated its golden jubilee – offers rare insight into the marine ecosystems of Southeast Asia and the perceptions of whales among communities in the region.

Staff from the Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum secured the specimen and, with assistance from the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore, towed it carefully across the West Johor Strait to the Tuas Marine Transfer Station. Here museum scientists began the process of examination, dissection and recovery. The whale was first displayed to the general public on 15 March 2016.

The remains of the whale tell a powerful story: ship-strike injuries and a stomach containing, tragically, pieces of plastic. This serves as a reminder of the profound impact of human activity. The remnants of deep-sea creatures, such as squid, in Jubi Lee’s gut suggest that she had been hunting in waters well beyond Singapore and its surrounding seas before her death. An analysis of her stomach contents and DNA revealed that she may have originated from a population in the Indian Ocean, near the Cocos (Keeling) Islands or Indonesia.

Southeast Asia’s waters support several species of whales. Sperm whales have been observed around Malaysia, Indonesia and Brunei, where they feed and reproduce. Humpback whales have been sighted – as they migrate to warmer waters for breeding – off the coast of the Philippines. Bryde’s whales – often called tropical whales due to their preference for waters above 15°C – have been recorded in the waters off Thailand, Indonesia and Brunei. Together, these species reflect the importance of Southeast Asia’s seas as part of ecological and migratory networks.

That this sperm whale skeleton should find a place of prominence in a museum, preserving its significance for a community, is, in the context of Southeast Asia, a continuation of past practices. On the island of Lembata in eastern Indonesia, for example, whale skulls were once displayed in temples and were venerated much like the bones of ancestors. Jubi Lee's place in the museum, though shaped by science rather than ritual, is a similar kind of honour.

The impulse to recognize the whale as significant is one the region has long known and shared. Along the coast of Viet Nam, hunting whales was taboo because they were regarded as protectors. A major temple dated to 1762 was even dedicated to the whale deity known as Lord Fish. Indeed, emperors of the Nguyen dynasty conferred titles upon whales in the nineteenth century. Through research, preservation and education, the Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum in Singapore continues to turn such discoveries into lessons for future generations.

objects.title: Spotted white eagle ray spines
objects.dimensions: (1) Width 18.5 cm, length 1.1 cm; (2) width 18 cm, length 1 cm; (3) width 15.8 cm, length 1 cm; (4) width 14 cm, length 0.6 cm
objects.caption:
The spotted white eagle ray (Aetobatus ocellatus) is a marine animal recognized by its smooth skin, white spots scattered across its back and white underside. It can reach a width of 1.5 metres, with a maximum recorded width of 3 metres and weight of 200 kilograms. Its body is shaped like a rhombus, allowing it to swim as if it were a bird in flight. It features one to six venomous spines located near the base of its long, slender tail. These spines are used strictly for self-defence.

Its habitat spans the Pacific and Indian Oceans. It enters brackish water near river mouths to feed and uses its mouth to dig into the sandy seabed in search of shellfish, shrimp and crabs.

Historically, parts of the stingray were used for various purposes across Southeast Asia. The stingray tail, equipped with natural barbs, was once used as a whip for punishment and was later adapted into short, knife-like defensive tools in southern Thailand and other parts of the region. Stingray skin, valued for its naturally rough texture, was used as a material for sword hilts, providing grip and durability. Eagle rays were also eaten, prepared as shredded grilled stingray for Khao Chae, a dish created by the Thai-Mon community. The ray also served as an ingredient in Chinese medicine.

Today, the spotted eagle ray is under threat as a result of being hunted for these uses. Overfishing of the species, combined with it being part of bycatch from fishing methods that indiscriminately capture non-targeted marine species, has contributed to declining populations. Environmental pressures are also a threat. The degradation of coral reefs and altered marine ecosystems have reduced its food sources and habitats, leading to further population declines. As a result of these combined pressures, the species is classified as Endangered on the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List.

objects.title: Stingray barb dagger
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies, Thailand
objects.material: Stingray caudal spine (barb) and animal horn
objects.dimensions: Blade (Stingray Spine/Barb) – length 16.3 cm, blade width 1.3 cm; base width 1.8 cm; Hilt (Handle) – made of animal horn, length 8 cm
objects.object_biography: Contributed by Mr Pichai Kaewkhao. Exhibited in the Knives and Weaponry Room (Hong Mit lae Sattrawut), Folklore Museum, Institute of Southern Thai Studies.
objects.caption:
Mounted on a handle fashioned from animal horn, hand-polished to ensure a secure, ergonomic grip, the blade of this dagger is made from the caudal spine of a stingray, the serrated defensive barb, known in Thai as the ngiang. Deliberately minimalist yet structurally robust, the dagger reflects how southern Thai folk artisans created items that were both useful and durable.

Seafarers, fishermen and maritime nomads (chao lay) carried such compact daggers as weapons for self-defence on long-distance maritime voyages. Naturally rigid, exceptionally sharp and flanked by retroverted, saw-like serrations, the barb blade functions as a devastating weapon. Its overall architecture allows it to pierce soft tissue effortlessly upon thrusting, while its backward-facing barbs cause extensive, jagged lacerations upon extraction.

While classical treatises on military strategy (Tamra Pichai Songkhram) focused on standard iron and steel weaponry, regional folk traditions recognized the importance of weapons crafted from raw organic matter such as bone, antler and horn.

The use of the stingray barb to form a dagger stems from the perceptions of stingrays by seafaring and fishing communities. Due to the highly painful venom delivered by live stingray barbs, folk belief attributed an inherent spiritual potency to the barb itself. Consequently, it was carried as an active talisman, believed to be capable of neutralizing hazards and warding off malevolent spirits. According to regional esoteric lore, because the barb formed a blade without being melted, smelted or altered by human fire, it retained a state of primordial purity, which elevated it from a tactical weapon into a spiritual amulet.

This dagger’s discovery in Pattani, a historical maritime trading hub on the eastern coast of the Malay Peninsula, places it within a trade-port culture. Complex commercial environments such as this, where piracy and trade disputes were common, required that coastal communities arm and protect themselves. The fact that communities across the Malay Peninsula drew on the same animal for the same purpose reflects a shared martial and spiritual vocabulary, rooted in the creatures of the water with which they shared enduring connections.

objects.title: Sukhothai celadon bowl fragment with fish design
objects.title_raw: Sukhothai celadon bowl fragment with fish design
objects.period: Between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries CE
objects.object_biography: Donated by Pol Gen Monchai Phankhongchuen on 11 August 1976. Provenance unknown.
objects.caption:
This fragment of a glazed stoneware bowl features a fish design positioned within two concentric circles. It was painted with a black underglaze beneath a transparent glaze and is accompanied by an inscription in Sukhothai Thai script reading “mae pla ka”. The rim carries simple black painted lines. At the interior base, spur marks appear at the centre: these traces are left by supports used during the kiln-firing process to prevent the vessels from sticking together.

The fish depicted on the bowl is a freshwater fish similar to the common carp. It has a stout, bulging body with small scales and a deeply-forked caudal fin (tail). Fish of this type can be found in rivers and freshwater sources throughout Thailand and typically graze on algae and aquatic plants. The fish motif is associated with fertility and abundance, and it first became popular among Sukhothai potters in the fourteenth century.

This glazed vessel exhibits the technique of applying black patterns under the clear glaze, a style prevalent in the mid-Sukhothai pottery production period to which it belongs. The black pattern was created using iron rust. This technique has been found at the Koh Noi kiln sites in Si Satchanalai and the Sukhothai city site, alongside vessels using other techniques such as brown-black and bluish-green glazes.

The marks left by the kiln-firing process are an important part of the vessel’s appearance. The supports used to separate vessels during firing left impressions on the base, which are partially hidden by the mottled surface of the fish. The fish image therefore presents not only the artistic intention but also the craft methods that brought it into being.

Although the history of this particular fragment remains unknown, vessels like this were widely circulated through Southeast Asia’s maritime trade networks. During the Ming dynasty, restrictions on private Chinese ceramic exports between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries reduced the availability of Chinese wares in some markets. This led to increased demand for ceramics from production centres in Southeast Asia. Thai ceramics, particularly high-quality glazed wares from Sukhothai, were transported across the region. Many examples have been recovered from shipwrecks including the Turiang and Longquan wrecks (c. 1370–1400), as well as the Ko Khram wreck (c. 1400). These ships and trade networks reveal how local ceramic technologies and riverine fish imagery became part of a shared material culture that travelled across and even beyond Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Vessel in the form of a fish
objects.title_raw: Vessel in the form of a fish
objects.caption:
This stoneware vessel is in the form of a fish, with the body glazed green and the fins and tail finished in brown. The vessel was carefully modelled with defined eyes and scales and a mouth formed as a circular opening for pouring. It may have been used as a sprinkler vessel, possibly for pouring lustral water in ritual settings.

The shape of the vessel reflects the long association across Southeast Asia of fish with fertility, abundance and the life-giving qualities of water. By shaping a practical pouring vessel in the form of a fish, the artisan brought these associations into tangible use. Each act of pouring transformed the vessel from a simple container into an auspicious one.

The auspicious symbolism of fish carried practical weight. According to the Royal Chronicles of Ayutthaya, when King U-Thong, the first monarch of Ayutthaya, was seeking a site for his capital, he encountered plentiful fish in the waters around Nong Sano and chose the location as an auspicious sign. Vessels such as this are a reminder of the region’s shared cultural connections with water and its creatures.

objects.title: Wooden chalk-line reels
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies, Thailand
objects.place_of_production: Tha Khuen Sub-district, Tha Sala District, Nakhon Si Thammarat Province
objects.dimensions: Fish form – width 10 cm, length 25 cm; Serpent form – width 12 cm, length 20 cm, height 10.5 cm
objects.object_biography: Exhibited in the Arts and Crafts Room (Hong Silpa Hattakam), Folklore Museum, Institute of Southern Thai Studies.
objects.caption:
These fish- and snake-shaped objects are examples of rang that (also known as phrok that) – a traditional woodworking marking tool used by master carpenters to snap straight, highly accurate reference lines onto raw timber before sawing, hewing or joinery. This tool was once a foundational implement for builders across the southern Thai peninsula. It was used in the construction of vernacular stilt houses, traditional seafaring boats, domestic furniture and everyday woodenware.

Using hardwood, cotton thread and carbon soot produced from everyday domestic resources, artisans created a reliable precision instrument adapted to local building practices. While rang that often had minimalist rectangular geometry, artisans across Southeast Asia frequently sculpted these wooden tools into zoomorphic forms. The two specimens displayed here – one in the form of a fish and the other like a snake – balance artistry with everyday industrial utility and reflect the prevalent cultural associations with fish and snakes in the region.

The southern dialect preserves the presence of this tool in its idiom: dam muean rang that (as black as a carpenter's chalk-line reel), which became a common metaphor for an exceptionally sun-darkened complexion, a phrase that could only have currency in a society where this tool was present in every workshop.

The rang that reflects a sophisticated understanding of materials and mechanics. Internally, the tool is divided into two chambers: a reeling chamber housing a spool of fine cotton thread attached to a manual turning crank (mue muan) and a pigment well packed with raw cotton saturated in carbon lampblack (khamau dam) mixed with water. To use it, the carpenter draws the thread out across the timber, passing it through the lampblack-soaked well. Once the black-coated thread is pulled taut against the wood, the craftsman pinches the midpoint, pulls it vertically upward and snaps it back down. He thus transfers a razor-sharp, uniform straight line onto the surface. The crank can then be rotated to retract the cord back into the wooden body.

The fish-shaped rang that is a demonstration of how technological knowledge and familiarity with local natural resources were intertwined in traditional Southeast Asian artisanship. By adapting a precision tool to the form of a creature from their coastal surroundings, artisans connected the practical demands of construction with the landscapes and livelihoods that sustained them.

objects.title: Badau
objects.caption:
The badau is a traditional tool and weapon of the Murut people of Brunei Darussalam. Similar in form to a machete, its handle is in the form of the head of the Rhinoceros Hornbill (Buceros rhinoceros), complete with the animal’s distinctive large beak.

Among the Murut, hornbills are regarded as sacred birds. Traditionally, strict taboos surrounded the hunting of the hornbill. It was believed that harming these birds would bring misfortune, including blindness or cholera. By shaping the badau in the form of the hornbill rather than using materials from the bird itself, the badau therefore embodies a relationship of respect and protection: the animal’s spiritual power is invoked through representation, while the creature remains unharmed.

Reverence for the hornbill extends across Borneo’s communities. Among the Dayak peoples of Kalimantan and the Iban of Sarawak, the hornbill occupies an important place in ceremonial objects and spiritual traditions. As a native species of the island, the hornbill transcends ethnic and political boundaries, linking communities through shared understandings of the bird’s power and protective associations.

objects.title: Calapa with bird motif
objects.period: Late eighteenth century and nineteenth century
objects.dimensions: Length 24 cm, height 12 cm, width 16.5 cm
objects.caption:
This container, a calapa, serves to store betel leaves, areca nuts (pinang) and tobacco (sigup), and it was historically used when guests came to visit and during gatherings such as weddings and thanksgiving ceremonies. In the form of a bird, featuring large wings and a spread tail, the calapa is an object whose form invites interpretation.

The design may have been inspired by the Rhinoceros Hornbill, a species native to Borneo and once common in Brunei Darussalam. The long, curved beak on this container and the prominent structure rising above the bird’s head closely resemble those of the hornbill, suggesting that the artisan may have drawn inspiration from the most familiar and culturally significant bird of the local landscape. At the same time, the design of the calapa also resembles the peacock, a bird whose elaborate plumage and regal bearing have inspired art across much of Southeast Asia. Peacocks are not native to Brunei Darussalam, however, so the resemblance here likely speaks to the influence of artistic traditions carried along the trade networks that long connected Brunei to the wider region.

Whether a peacock, hornbill or an imaginative synthesis of both, the bird form chosen for this vessel of hospitality speaks to the way Southeast Asian decorative traditions have long drawn on the natural world. The vessel also reflects the movement of ideas across the Southeast Asian region. In the context of Brunei traditions, a container associated with generosity and ceremony is a fitting vehicle for the image of the hornbill as the bird’s associations with protection and vitality run deep across the communities of Borneo.

objects.title: Copper pot
objects.caption:
This traditional copper pot is decorated with fine circular engravings encircling the body and lid, a raised line at the centre of the body and motifs of birds alongside Islamic calligraphy. Such pots are used in daily life for cooking rice and preparing traditional medicine.

The bird motifs on this vessel, which include the hornbill, carry associations of protection and vitality deeply rooted in communities’ beliefs. In Brunei and across Borneo as a whole, the hornbill has long been understood as a guardian figure, a messenger of the upper world and a symbol of life force. As such, this pot for preparing food and medicine, decorated with hornbill motifs, is imbued with the hornbill’s protective qualities, and can transfer it to meals and remedies.

The Islamic calligraphy engraved alongside the bird motifs reflects the layered spiritual world of Brunei's material culture, where indigenous animist beliefs and Islamic faith have coexisted and inflected one another across centuries. In this vessel, the protective associations of the hornbill and the blessing invoked through sacred script reinforce each other in a single object designed for everyday cooking and healing.

This copper pot reflects a wider Southeast Asian tradition in which everyday objects bring together traditional knowledge, spiritual beliefs and relationships with the natural world. Through the hornbill motif and Islamic inscriptions, a domestic vessel becomes a bearer of protection and healing.

objects.title: Iban’s Hornbill
objects.dimensions: Length 100 cm, width 20 cm, height 80 cm
objects.caption:
Of the wood carvings produced by the Iban of Sarawak, those of the hornbill (kenyalang) are among the most spectacular. This carving is one such example. Made from wood and pigments, this hornbill holds a fig in its beak – a detail whose shape deliberately resembles a trophy head, calling to mind the headhunting traditions of Iban society. Hornbill figures like this were carved for the sacred ceremony of Gawai Kenyalang, originally associated with fighting, raiding and headhunting, but which today has evolved into a thanksgiving celebration.

For the Iban, the hornbill is considered the chief of birds and a messenger of the deities in the upper world, representing the vital life force present in all living beings. Communities believed they could invoke the hornbill’s assistance in warfare, calling upon its power to carry their intentions into the divine realm. The kenyalang reflects an Iban worldview in which animals are active participants in relationships between humans, ancestors and the divine.

Among the Dayak peoples of Borneo, the hornbill holds a place of highest reverence as a sacred intermediary and a bearer of good omens. Dayak tradition further holds that the intricate designs on hornbill carvings are not created solely through human skill but are guided by divine inspiration.

Central to the cosmology of this carving is the figure of Sengalang Burong, the Brahminy Kite who is venerated in Iban belief as their ancestor, and whose messages are carried by the hornbill. During Gawai Kenyalang, which is held after the harvest in Sengalang’s honour, a carving such as this would be mounted on a tall pole, surrounded by offerings of food and sacred incantations. Positioned at the centre of the ceremony, the kenyalang gave physical form to the community’s relationship with the upper world and the spiritual forces believed to sustain it. Such reverence of the hornbill echoes wider Southeast Asian understandings of animals as sources of spiritual power, protection and connection.

objects.title: Kalimantan war helmet
objects.material: Hornbill head, rattan, beads, cotton, bird feathers, glass
objects.caption:
The base of this war commander's helmet (katapu) is crafted from tightly woven Bornean rattan, strong enough to deflect enemy arrows and mandau sword slashes. Set above this practical shell of armour is the skull of a rhinoceros hornbill (burung enggang), symbolizing protection by spirits.

This helmet represents the Dayak people's ingenuity in merging earthly and celestial powers for protection on the battlefield. In Dayak belief, the hornbill embodies Panglima Burung (Bird Commander), a mystical figure who emerges during warfare to instil battlefield confidence. By fixing the hornbill's skull to the crown of the helmet, the wearer brought this protective spirit into direct physical contact with his own person. Thus, the wearer is situated simultaneously within the practical and the cosmic dimensions of battle.

The embellishments such as hornbill skulls, feathers, intricate beadwork and mirrors on this katapu indicate that it was reserved exclusively for high-ranking figures such as tribal chiefs or war commanders. At the time that the helmet was constructed, the beads and mirrors that adorn it were rare items that served as distinct markers of high social status. In parallel, the spiritual protection and association with upper-world spirits afforded by the hornbill was commensurate with that status.

The hornbill, whose home is the forest canopy – the threshold between the earthly world and the sky – was an ideal symbol for the connection between humans and spirits. Through the hornbill’s presence on the katapu, the warrior was not only connected to the protection of ancestral and spiritual forces, but also to the living landscape and the region that sustained Dayak communities over millennia.
