objects.title: Oriental Pied Hornbill and Rhinoceros Hornbill
objects.title_raw: Oriental Pied Hornbill and Rhinoceros Hornbill
objects.collection: Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum, Singapore
objects.scientific_name: Anthracoceros albirostris (Oriental Pied Hornbill); Buceros rhinoceros (Rhinoceros Hornbill)
objects.caption:
The Oriental Pied Hornbill (Anthracoceros albirostris) and the Rhinoceros Hornbill (Buceros rhinoceros) – belong to a family of birds known for their large, curved bills and prominent casques, the hollow structures rising above their beaks. Of the 59 extant hornbill species worldwide, thirty-one are found in Asia, where they inhabit tropical forests. Through eating fruit they serve to disperse seeds, which helps to regenerate plants and trees and sustain the diversity of forest ecosystems.

Beyond their ecological importance, hornbills have generated rich symbolic and ceremonial traditions among communities in Borneo. The Rhinoceros Hornbill holds the most prominent cultural role. Known as the kenyalang among the Iban of Sarawak and as burung enggang among the Dayak peoples of Kalimantan, it is regarded as the chief of birds and a messenger of the deities in the upper world. The bird is believed to embody the vital life force present in all living beings, serving as an intermediary between the human and spiritual realms by carrying prayers, and granting protection to those who honour it.

In Dayak traditions, the hornbill is also associated with Panglima Burung (Bird Commander), a mystical guardian figure invoked during warfare to inspire courage and protection. The bird’s skull and feathers are part of the ceremonial attire and weapons of chiefs and warriors, and its image appears on both domestic and ritual objects such as copper pots, storage vessels and ceremonial containers.

Despite their cultural and ecosystem importance, populations of hornbills have declined sharply in recent decades. They are threatened by hunting and trade and by habitat loss brought about by deforestation, agricultural expansion, unsustainable mining and fires. The decline of hornbills represents not only a loss of biodiversity, but also the erosion of cultural traditions that have connected communities with these remarkable birds for generations.

Conservation efforts demonstrate that these connections can be renewed. In Singapore, for example, where the Oriental Pied Hornbill was once considered extinct, populations were successfully re-established through initiatives such as the installation of artificial nesting boxes.

objects.title: Horse-shaped lighter
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies, Thailand
objects.dimensions: Width 3.2 cm, length 10 cm, height 10 cm
objects.object_biography: Sourced from the private collection of Mrs Tueanjai Isarapruk, Pak Thong Village, Kho Hong Sub-district, Hat Yai District, Songkhla Province. Official museum documentation recorded on 25 October 2010. Exhibited in the History and Ethnology Room (Hong Prawattisat lae Chattiphan), Folklore Museum, Institute of Southern Thai Studies.
objects.caption:
This horse-shaped lighter integrates twentieth-century ignition technology with decorative metal sculpture, demonstrating a skilled blending of everyday function and artistic form. The horse is cast entirely from solid brass (thong luang), a material well suited to this object as it allowed artisans to capture fine sculptural detail, including the mane, tail, saddle and bridle, while retaining the durability required of a functional device. Built directly into the sculpture is a mechanical ignition assembly consisting of a thumb lever, a flint housing and a burner cap. This type of spring-loaded mechanism became popular globally during the mid-twentieth century.

As mechanical lighters replaced earlier methods of lighting, such as using hearth embers or flint-and-steel tools, they became part of hospitality, social exchange and business interactions. Designed to ignite cigarettes, cigars and candles, this lighter would have occupied a prominent place in reception rooms, offices and household spaces, where it functioned as both a convenience and an object of display.

The horse form of the object shows that modern technology was not adopted in isolation from older systems of meaning. Across Chinese and Southeast Asian traditions, the horse symbolised vitality, endurance, speed and success. By using this auspicious animal form to contain an industrial device, the object also expressed the associations represented by the horse.

This object is representative of a wider trend in southern Thai society during the post-war era: a period of rapid modernisation and expanding global trade, when household items increasingly served not only practical purposes but also expressed wealth, cosmopolitan identity and a modern lifestyle. This was especially significant in Hat Yai, Songkhla Province, where post-war growth driven by railway connections, rubber production and trade transformed the area into a major commercial centre linking southern Thailand with Penang, Singapore and wider maritime markets.

Donated by a merchant family from Hat Yai, this lighter preserves a moment when imported technologies entered southern Thai households and were given new local meanings. The horse-shaped form reveals how communities across maritime Southeast Asia interpreted modern technologies through familiar symbols of local identity, progress and ambition.

objects.title: Dastar with horse motif
objects.caption:
A dastar is a head adornment traditionally worn by Bajau and Kadazandusun men during customary ceremonies and festive celebrations in Sabah. This piece originates from Kota Belud, Sabah, and dates to around the 1940s.

Made from cotton, it was woven using a supplementary weft technique and features a horse rider motif alongside geometric patterns. In Bajau and Kadazandusun textiles, the horse rider motif is rich in meaning. Horses are markers of social status and also convey physical strength, vitality, movement, leadership and nobility.

The Bajau of Kota Belud are well known for their horse-riding culture and have been referred to as the ‘cowboys of the East’. In contexts such as marriage celebrations, riding a horse is a display of skill, bravery and prestige. According to Bajau cultural records, when a groom rides a horse to the bride's home, it is a symbol of his strength and status. The horse-rider motif thus symbolizes strength, masculinity and social prestige, as well as the identity of horse-riding communities.

In weaving and textile arts, such motifs preserve this heritage in fabric. Worn on the head, which is the most visible and honoured part of the body, the dastar carries the horse rider motif into the ceremonial space during formal occasions. A community's relationship with the horse, lived on horseback and expressed in ceremony, is here encoded in thread.

objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies, Thailand
objects.material: Supplementary-weft (yok dok) handwoven cotton, embellished with antique glass beads
objects.local_name: Pha hum thammasan / ผ้าหุ้มธรรมมาสน (ผ้าทอเกาะยอ)
objects.object_biography: Original heirloom piece: Transferred via ritual donation by Phra Athikan Prathom Pathamo, the late Abbot of Wat Thai Yo, from Village No. 8, Koh Yo Sub-district, Mueang Songkhla District, Songkhla Province. Accessioned into the permanent collection vaults of the Folklore Museum on 9 October 2014. Modern replica piece: Hand-loomed and donated by Ms Ubolsri Attaphan, sourced from Mueang Songkhla District, Songkhla Province. Exhibited in the Local Textile Exhibition Room (Hong Pha Tho Pheurm Mueang), Folklore Museum, Institute of Southern Thai Studies.
objects.caption:
This is a liturgical pulpit cover (pha hum thammasan) from the temple of Wat Thai Yo in Songkhla Province, Thailand. Hung around the pulpit (thammasan), the cloth transforms the space of the sermon into a sacred setting for the transmission of the Dhamma.

Creating and donating such textiles are considered acts of merit-making (bun), with laywomen dedicating their labour, skill and devotion to supporting the Buddhist community. Originally made in 1934 as an offering to the temple, it was woven in saffron yellow, emerald green and charcoal black against a deep red background using the intricate yok dok (supplementary weft) technique, creating raised patterns.

Among the designs depicted on the cloth are two powerful animal forms: the Garuda (krut) and sacred steeds (ma). Both are depicted as celestial vehicles associated with movement between earthly and higher realms. The Garuda, which in Hindu-Buddhist traditions is the divine mount of Vishnu, carries associations of power, protection and heavenly authority. The horse, long associated across Southeast Asia with nobility, strength and martial ability, similarly represents a vehicle of elevation and prestige. Together, these animals frame Buddhist devotion through images of ascent, guardianship and spiritual aspiration.

The colours of the textile highlight the community's use of local natural resources. The dyes include red from the iron-rich earthen clays of Koh Yo's hillsides, yellow from jackfruit heartwood and black from fermented ebony berries. These colours were traditionally reserved for ritual objects across the region, symbolizing spiritual protection, dynastic prosperity and cosmic blessing.

This textile not only serves spiritual purposes but is also a record of collective devotion. Using the yok dok technique, weavers incorporated the names of the women who sponsored and produced the cloth directly into its structure.

This pha hum thammasan demonstrates how animal imagery travelled across South and Southeast Asian religious traditions while acquiring local meanings through community actions. In this textile, the Garuda and horse represent sacred vehicles woven into an offering through which the community expressed faith, identity and its relationship with the Buddhist cosmos.

objects.title: Nang Talung puppetry horse
objects.object_biography: Given by Khun Nartnikorn (Tai Na Pombejra) on 25 March 1954.
objects.caption:
This shadow puppet in the form of a horse was crafted for Nang Talung, the shadow-theatre tradition of southern Thailand. Made from bovine or buffalo hide that has been scraped thin, sketched and intricately carved, it is mounted on a bamboo stick. During a performance, the nai nang (puppet master) manipulates the figure before a lit screen, casting its shadow onto a white cloth, while providing narration and vocalisation.

The performance is accompanied by a musical ensemble featuring drums, thap (goblet drums), mong (gongs), ching (cymbals) and the pi chawa (Javanese oboe). The repertoire draws on Indian epics, namely the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, as well as local legends.

Nang Talung belongs to the family of shadow-theatre traditions found across Southeast Asia that includes Sbek Thom in Cambodia, Nang Yai in the Chao Phraya River Basin, Wayang Kulit in Malaysia and Wayang Purwa and other regional forms in Indonesia. Many of these traditions feature animal-shaped puppets representing fauna from the natural environments familiar to each community and creatures from their literary repertoire.

The horse is one of many such animals. Horses were not native to Southeast Asia but were imported from the Middle East, India, China and Mongolia via overland and maritime routes. Horses have been in Thailand since at least the Dvaravati period (sixth to eleventh centuries CE), as evidenced by archaeological finds and their frequent depiction in works of art. Horse imagery was employed in the decoration of utilitarian objects, personal ornaments, architectural stucco reliefs and narrative scenes associated with Buddhism. This tradition continued into the Lopburi period (eleventh to thirteenth centuries CE).

Animal-shaped shadow puppets were a way in which shared beliefs about the natural and imagined world were given shape and set in motion. When this puppet moved across the screen in shadow-play performances, it carried with it a long association between horses, sovereignty and the sacred. Closely associated with rulers and kingship, the horse likely accompanied royal characters.

Beyond being a source of entertainment, shadow-play performances in Southeast Asia were traditionally integral to rituals of ancestral invocation, healing and the exorcism of malevolent spirits. In Thailand, Nang Talung is traditionally performed between April and July, prior to the Buddhist Lent. The sacred context of the performance invests each animal figure — including the horse — with meaning that exceeds the narrative.

objects.title: Oracle Bone
objects.place_of_production: Probably Karo Batak (acquired in Aceh province, Kutacane)
objects.object_biography: This object exists on online inventory, Accession No. XXXX-11755.
objects.caption:
This buffalo bone is most likely an amulet made by magician-priests to be worn by the Batak people for protection, granting powers during hunting and battles and warding off evil spirits and illnesses. Such amulets were often made of animal bones – usually a rib or long bone cut into small cylindrical forms.

This bone is inscribed on both sides. The concave face is inscribed with symbols of fish, seven-pointed stars, stylized lizards and human motifs, while the convex face features Batak script. The inscriptions are highlighted with a black, ink-like substance to reveal magic formulae, motifs and astrological signs.

Batak heritage is thought to be rooted in ancient Austronesian culture, influenced by Indian communities who settled in the Barus area as early as the seventh century, as well as Hindu-Buddhist traditions emanating from ritual centres such as Padang Lawas in north Sumatra.

objects.title: Traditional maritime boxes in horse design
objects.title_raw: Traditional maritime boxes in horse design
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies, Thailand
objects.dimensions: Length 45 cm, height 23 cm, width 11.5 cm
objects.object_biography: Sourced from the personal collection of Mr Hem Sando Sen, House No. 22, Village No. 8, Koh Taeo Sub-district, Mueang Songkhla District, Songkhla Province (ritual donation). Exhibited in the Recreation Exhibition Room (Hong Nanthanakon), Folklore Museum, Institute of Southern Thai Studies.
objects.caption:
This is a wooden storage chest (ko-ta) that was used by communities from along the southern Thai coast for safeguarding vital provisions during voyages and as a charm to ensure stable sailing and good fortune. Strict taboos governed the ko-ta onboard. Under no circumstances could it be stored upside down; it had to be placed completely upright with its lid facing the heavens.

Such chests were made with high-density, resinous hardwoods such as Kiam (Cotylelobium lanceolatum) and Lumpho (Intsia palembanica), selected for their natural resistance to rot, humidity and brine. The low-set elongated rectangular shape was engineered for equilibrium on the deck of a rolling vessel, minimizing sliding or inversion during heavy swells. Lids were structured to ensure a hermetic friction fit, and many specimens featured tongue-and-groove slide locks or rattan tie-down cords. This design kept the contents of the box, such as tobacco, nipa palm wrapper leaves, fire-striking apparatus, currency and family documents, dry across multi-day expeditions.

What elevates this ko-ta into a work of folk art is its zoomorphic carving in the form of a horse, which symbolizes endurance, bravery and safe passage. Fisherfolk, despite spending much of their lives on water rather than on land, chose the horse as a spiritual companion, as it represented the courage needed to survive long voyages and could allow a vessel to gallop across cresting ocean waves. Here animal symbolism, practical engineering and the logic of survival at sea were inseparable.

The Malay-Thai linguistic root of the box’s name and the object’s presence across southern Thai coastal communities, whose lives were shaped by trade networks, reflect the shared material culture across maritime Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Sandstone lintel depicting Vishnu Anantashayana
objects.period: Lopburi art, twelfth century CE (seventeenth century in the Buddhist calendar)
objects.place_of_production: Prasat Ku Suan Taeng, Ban Mai Chai Phot District, Buriram Province
objects.caption:
This sandstone lintel depicts Vishnu Anantasayin: the reclining of Vishnu upon the serpent Ananta. Unusually, the carving gives prominence to the makara, a mythical aquatic creature that represents the cosmic waters surrounding Vishnu. The makara has features drawn from multiple animals, including the serpent or Naga.

According to Hindu belief, as expressed in the Puranas, before creation began, the Hindu god Vishnu reclined in meditation upon the endless serpent Ananta in the cosmic Ocean of Milk (Kshira Sagara), from which the universe is renewed. This cosmic ocean is the setting of the great churning myth, when gods and demons used the serpent Vasuki as a rope to churn the waters in search of amrita, the nectar of immortality. Through these stories, serpents and aquatic beings became associated with the forces that sustain creation: water, fertility, cosmic balance and renewal.

The serpent and makara reveal a shared regional imagination in which animals from rivers, oceans and mythical realms became symbols of the forces that shaped life itself, connecting landscapes, cosmology and communities across Asia. Such imagery reflects the movement of Hindu-Buddhist ideas across Southeast Asia, where creatures of water and serpent forms were adapted into local artistic traditions.

objects.title: Balinese Naga-shaped corbels
objects.caption:
These elaborate Naga-shaped corbels at the Ada Guna Museum in Bali feature alongside figures of Garuda and singha (lion), serving as striking structural and decorative elements that reflect the museum’s dedication to preserving architectural collections and traditional artisanship.

In Balinese culture, the mythical serpent known as the Naga marks the threshold between the profane outer world and the sacred inner sanctuary and is a vital guardian. While rooted in Indian and Southeast Asian traditions, the Balinese Naga is uniquely localized and has been woven into the island’s architectural, spiritual and artistic identity. Balinese mythology perceives the serpent as a emblem of balance and community guardianship. This reflects a synthesis with pre-Hindu animism – a heritage preserved in villages where offerings continue to be given to sacred trees and rivers today.

Guided by traditional master builders (undagi), artisans create structures in the form of serpents to anchor temple staircases, foundations and royal baths. At water temples like Tirta Empul and Goa Gajah, serpentine sculptures guard waterspouts and gates, channelling tirtha (holy water) to safeguard both the physical purity of water and to serve in the metaphysical purification of the soul.

During religious observances such as Odalan (temple anniversaries) and Melasti (ocean purification), Naga effigies are paraded to the sea to cleanse the community and bridge the seen world (sekala) with the unseen spiritual realm (niskala).

Today, the Naga remains a central symbol across shadow puppetry (Wayang Kulit), performing arts and ceremonial regalia. Even amidst modern tourism, the watchful Naga stands as a timeless sentinel of Bali’s living spiritual foundations.

objects.title: Bencha
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies, Thailand
objects.caption:
A bencha is a small, tiered pavilion – a form of temporary architecture – used during the Songkran festival for bathing Buddha images and pouring water over the elderly. Songkran marks the end of the dry season, a period of new beginnings. The bencha is distinguished by its stacked roof, intricate kanok patterns (a flame-like or stylised leaf design) and gold-leaf lacquer.

A key feature is the Naga-shaped water flume, which symbolises the Great Serpent spouting water as an offering to the Buddha and a prayer for abundance. Pouring water through this flume allows devotees to show respect without direct physical contact.

The Naga's image here is significant: as a creature whose nature is bound to water, it is a fitting vessel through which blessing flows – linking the mythological power of the serpent to the communal act of renewal.

This tradition functions as a social glue, fostering unity through the collective construction of the pavilion, while reflecting gratitude toward elders and the belief that the power of water brings prosperity to the community.

objects.title: Embossed Brass Basin with Mythical Animal Motifs
objects.title_raw: Embossed Brass Basin with Mythical Animal Motifs
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies, Thailand
objects.caption:
This repoussé and chased brass holy water basin (khan nam mon) is a prime specimen of Southern Thai metal artistry, produced historically in the major coastal principalities (hua mueang) of Southern Thailand — most notably Nakhon Si Thammarat and Songkhla — which served as metallurgical hubs intertwined with maritime trading networks, fostering cultural exchanges between the Thai, Malay, and Chinese worlds.

The artistic composition of the basin is anchored by a structured layout of auspicious animals embossed around its body, featuring the Elephant (Chang), the Tiger (Suea), the Naga (Phaya Nak), the Rajasiha (Ratchasiha, the mythical lion), the Garuda (Khrut), and the Bear (Mee). Each carries symbolic weight rooted in regional folklore and cosmological thought: the Elephant represents physical strength, institutional stability, and agricultural fertility; the Naga, the element of water, rainmaking, and subterranean abundance; the Rajasiha, sovereign command and divine protection; and the Garuda, supreme authority and power over evil spirits. Consolidating this specific pantheon of beasts onto a single vessel reflects an ancient ideological pursuit: channelling the balancing forces of nature to manifest comprehensive good fortune. In folk theology, these animal motifs are linked to the concept of Guardian Spirits (Sat Phu Phitak); arranging such a diverse assembly around the basin acts as a metaphor for summoning spiritual energies from all directional axes into the ritual space.

The vessel was hand-shaped from a single piece of brass and embellished using the repoussé technique (dun lai noon tam): the metalsmith works from the reverse side, hammering the metal outward to create raised, three-dimensional designs, before flipping the vessel over to execute precision chasing from the front — a craft demanding intimate mastery of metallurgy and intense concentration. Due to the highly intricate, labour-intensive and costly production process, such basins were exclusively commissioned for prominent temples or held by wealthy merchants, community leaders, and the elite.

The holy water basin is used to contain consecrated holy water (nam phra phuttha mon) for protective chanting assemblies, ordinations, weddings, monastic bathing rites, and housewarming blessings.Within these settings, the water serves as a conductor of collective faith and divine blessings, and, in the context of Southern Thai society historically shaped by riverine ecosystems, as a sanctified symbol of purity, seasonal abundance, and communal nourishment.

Beyond ornament, the animals depicted on this basin — the elephant, naga, garuda, and mythical lion — represent a shared symbolic vocabulary that circulated across maritime Southeast Asia. Through the metalworking techniques that transformed these regional beliefs into a single crafted object, the basin reveals how knowledge, materials, and animal-inspired meanings travelled alongside the communities that shaped the region’s shared heritage.

objects.title: Langguai
objects.period: Late eighteenth century and nineteenth century CE
objects.caption:
A langguai is a traditional Malay container designed to store the ingredients required for betel chewing. The main compartment held betel leaves, while smaller compartments (anak-anak langguai) placed on the lid stored lime, gambir and areca nut.

Produced in various sizes, langguai served multiple functions: while smaller examples were used for everyday betel preparation, larger forms could also be used to store garments, valuables and, at times, food such as meat. In domestic contexts, elaborately crafted langguai were objects of importance, presented when receiving honoured guests or during important occasions.

The motifs adorning such containers could include floral patterns, geometric designs and animal imagery such as lizards, dragons and snakes, reflecting a wider regional tradition in which skilled metalwork and auspicious symbols elevated functional objects into expressions of spiritual meaning, identity and standing. This example is distinguished by its engraved decoration, including a coiling snake and frogs that encircle the body of the container alongside floral motifs. The snake on this langguai connected domestic hospitality with a wider world of symbolic meaning.

Brunei became particularly known for its brass langguai, with artisans producing elaborate forms decorated according to the preferences of their buyers. Brass and copper artisanship became well established during this period, particularly in Kampong Ayer, which was renowned for its metalworking tradition.

As betel culture was transferred across maritime Southeast Asia, so too were the visual languages attached to the vessels that carried betel. The snake’s presence on a Bruneian betel container demonstrates how a shared symbol was locally reinterpreted. It linked households to the broader cultural networks of Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Kolek
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies, Thailand
objects.caption:
A kolek is a traditional fishing vessel of the lower south of Thailand. Known as a buatan barat across the border in northern Malaysia, its hulls are carved and painted with motifs of the Naga, Hanuman and Burong Singo (lion-bird) amidst waves and floral vines that draw together Thai, Malay and Javanese traditions. The kolek's builders work without lofting or drafting techniques; the design emerges instead from the builder's imagination and experience, shaped by the owner's requirements for size and the materials provided. Each boat is, in this sense, a unique object.

The Naga, featured on this boat, represents authority, abundance and protection from the sea. Depicted in bright colours, its presence is intended to project bravery and fierceness – qualities a vessel and its crew would need on open water. These designs are therefore not just artistic; they are spiritual anchors for fishermen, reflecting a worldview that sees the ocean as both a source of life and a sacred space.

The kolek and its imagery belong to a region whose cultural connections long preceded the borders that now divide it. As far back as the second century CE, ancient settlements here linked the markets of India and China across a shared trans-Peninsular route. Though the arrival of Islam and Theravada Buddhism drew this area into two distinct cultural orbits, they continued to share natural resources, agricultural and trading life and a common material culture. The region was also situated between two overlapping centres of power (mandala) – the Thai mandala radiating from the Chao Phraya delta and the Malay mandala of the Melaka and Johor empires.

The kolek, still in use among fishing communities in Kelantan and Pattani today, represents these layered relationships: a vessel whose painted Naga speaks not to one tradition but to the intertwined cosmologies of a shared sea.

objects.title: Naga-headed walking stick
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies, Thailand
objects.caption:
Carved from wood, this walking stick has a curved handle topped with the open-mouthed head of a serpent (Naga). The carving runs down the handle and into the shaft of the stick itself; in this manner the serpent’s body becomes the object in its entirety. In southern Thai tradition the Naga is a symbol linking the power of water, the cosmos and human destiny.

Thailand has long drawn on traditions from beyond its borders, including the Chinese lunar calendar and its zodiac, which is used to mark stages of life and key transitions. When this system was adopted into Thai culture, its twelve-year cycle was preserved, but with certain adaptations; notably, the Chinese dragon was reinterpreted through the image of the Naga, an auspicious figure deeply rooted in regional belief. Because of its cultural significance, the Naga was incorporated into the zodiac as the equivalent of the Year of the Dragon (Great Snake), signifying protection and prestige.

This object demonstrates the woodworker's skill and the integration of cyclical time into daily life, where the Naga acts as a guardian of one's fate.

objects.title: Khantruay
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies, Thailand
objects.caption:
Carved wooden corbels (khantruay) such as this one support the eaves of religious buildings and carry profound symbolic weight. The form of the corbels – in the shape of the Naga – reflects the belief in the creature as a guardian of sacred spaces.

Thai artisans historically incorporated the Naga’s form into various structures. They carved the serpent's body with graceful curves, blending detailed scales and flame-like patterns with fluid aesthetics, making them both sturdy and beautiful.

The Naga’s role as protector can be traced to early societies on the Siam Peninsula, in which the serpent was revered as a symbol of fertility, water and nourishment. This association was reinforced in Buddhist tradition through the story of Mucalinda, the Naga king who sheltered the meditating Sakyamuni Buddha from a storm by coiling his body around him and spreading his hood overhead, further establishing the serpent as a guardian figure.

Naga were placed in key positions in temple architecture, appearing on finials, gable boards, arches, balustrades, roof tiers and stairways leading to the main shrine. Naga imagery along the roof tiers evokes the cosmic river of life flowing from this mountain into the human world. This architectural symbolism draws on Hindu-Buddhist cosmology, in which the temple represents Mount Meru, the sacred mountain at the centre of the universe. In this light, the corbel gives physical form to cosmology, situating the building within a sacred geography.

The presence of the Naga in religious architecture is not unique to Thailand. Across Southeast Asia – in Myanmar, Malaysia, Indonesia and beyond – it appears in both vernacular and sacred structures, a shared guardian figure whose recurring form reflects a regional tradition of invoking divine protection in the built environment.

objects.title: Statue of Shiva
objects.place_of_production:
The statue is believed to be a Shiva image mentioned in the Wat Pa Mamuang inscription No. 4, recording that King Thammaracha (Lithai) had the statue enshrined in Mahakaset Temple,
Sukhothai Province.
objects.object_biography: The Shiva image, originally enshrined in the Mahakaset temple in Sukhothai, was moved to the Devasathan (Royal Brahmin Office of the Thai Royal Court), Bangkok, in the early Rattanakosin period. Later, King Rama VI ordered the divine statues, including this one, to be moved and exhibited at the National Museum Bangkok.
objects.caption:
This gilt bronze statue of the Hindu god Shiva is frontal facing, crowned and dressed in full regalia. The broad shoulders and minimal articulation of musculature are characteristic of the Sukhothai style. His third eye appears as a vertical line on the forehead, and both hands are held in the katakahasta mudra, with the index and little fingers pointing upward and the third and fourth fingers clasped over the palm, as the gesture of one holding a flower such as a lotus or lily. The regalia, signifying divine authority, is gilt throughout – including the Yajnopavita, the sacred thread that marks priestly status, slung across his chest over the left shoulder. From behind this thread, the head of a Naga emerges, also gilt.

The serpent, commonly worn by Shiva around his neck or as a Yajnopavita, and sometimes shown encircling his throat, symbolizes the potent venom he consumed during the Samudra Manthana (Churning of the Ocean of Milk). To prevent the venom from devastating the world, Shiva held it in his throat; his consort, Parvati, fearing for his safety, constricted his neck to contain it. This mythic event is reflected in religious painting through the darkened hue of Shiva’s throat (Nilakantha), while in statuary the venom is personified by the serpent. Here, the serpent serves as a testament to divine sacrifice and love.

Commercial links between the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia date from at least the second century BCE, with migrations across the Indian Ocean to Southeast Asia occurring from around 500 BCE into the early centuries CE. By the fifth and sixth centuries CE, epigraphic records across Southeast Asia attest to the enactment of Brahmanical ritual for local rulers, as beliefs from the Indian subcontinent blended with existing animistic traditions to produce a hybrid religious culture.

Though the main religion of the Sukhothai and Ayutthaya kingdoms, like that of Thailand today, was Theravada Buddhism, Hindu gods such as Shiva occupied a position of honour as guardians of the state, regarded as powerful and worthy of homage by kings and communities alike. Shiva statuary in Thailand dates to the sixth century CE.

The Naga coiled at Shiva's neck arrived in Thailand through the current of Hindu transmission, but the serpent was already present in the region's cosmological imagination long before, rooted in traditions predating the arrival of Brahmanical belief, which gave the Naga its meanings across Southeast Asia beyond the sole influence of any one religious system.

objects.title: Gold Swan commemorative fan
objects.caption:
This commemorative fan was designed by His Royal Highness Prince Narisara Nuwattiwong and bestowed upon Mom Chao Ithithepsan Kritdakorn for the funeral of Mom Suphap Kridakorn na Ayutthaya, a wife of Prince Nares Varariddhi, in 1925. It takes the form of a phat na nang (ceremonial fan). Fashioned from pale green and white silk and embroidered with multicoloured threads, it depicts a hamsa (mythical waterbird) standing upon an eight-pointed wooden pedestal, its long tail ending in eye-like motifs resembling the tail feathers of a peacock. The pedestal serves also as the base from which flowering phutthan vines spread and bloom around the hamsa; within a floral panel, the symbol "น." appears enclosed within a heart motif.

The hamsa here is a tribute in animal form. It serves as a symbolic representation of the name "Suphap" and signifies nobility, elegance and purity, qualities reflective of Mom Suphap's character. These qualities become even more emphasized in the image of the hamsa, which embodies precisely those associations in Lanna and Buddhist traditions. The bird also alludes to Suphap’s Mon ancestry, as the hamsa is regarded as a sacred creature in Mon culture and is closely associated with Hongsawadi (Hanthawaddy), the former capital of the Mon kingdom.

Through a single waterbird, the fan preserves three aspects of the deceased’s identity: her name, the virtues attributed to her character and her ancestral heritage. In this process, the hamsa serves as a visual language through which Thai courtly practice, Buddhist ideals and Mon cultural memory are brought together in an act of remembrance.

objects.title: Bangau and okok
objects.place_of_production: Pattani, Narathiwat or Yala, southern Thailand
objects.material: Hardwood (Cengal – Neobalanocarpus heimii; Meranti – Shorea genus; Jelutung – Dyera costulata; or Pulai – Alstonia angustiloba)
objects.caption:
A bangau is a wooden component placed at the bow of a fishing vessel with its ‘neck’ extending gracefully over the port side. An okok, often referred to as the anak bangau (young stork), is positioned on the starboard side as its companion. These carvings serve to support the sails and act as cleats for anchor lines or nets. They are celebrated for their vibrant palettes and intricate, symbolic carvings.

These buatan barat vessels, also known as kolek or kolae, are commissioned by fishermen in Kelantan and Terengganu from master artisans in the provinces of Pattani, Narathiwat and Yala in southern Thailand.

The name bangau is derived from that of the stork, a bird synonymous with patience and precision in the coastal marshes. Okok is believed to stem from the word bongkok (hunched) or ongkok in the local Terengganu dialect.

The  stoic nature of birds makes them a symbol of vigilance, resilience and the successful gathering of sustenance (rezeki). In the lore of east coast fishermen, the bangau is believed to possess a semangat (spirit) that guards the vessel in the open sea. A strict code of conduct (adab) surrounds these objects; for instance, crew members must never turn their backs to the bangau while sailing, nor step over it carelessly. To violate these taboos is to risk the safety of the crew and the bounty of the catch.

The bangau and okok reflect a shared Southeast Asian maritime legacy. The historical trade routes and the mobility of boat builders between peninsular Malaysia and southern Thailand created a corridor for the movement of culture, with the result that maritime communities across the region share a common visual language and a similar cosmology.

In the context of cultural heritage, the bangau and okok are tangible artefacts that carry a vast intangible weight. They encapsulate artisanship, belief systems and shared values. As a cornerstone of Southeast Asian heritage, they demonstrate that art, spirituality and economic life are inextricably intertwined in the region's maritime soul.

objects.title: Blue and white dish with flattened foliate rim
objects.title_raw: Blue and white dish with flattened foliate rim
objects.caption:
This dish depicts a crane standing in a body of water surrounded by plants, and it features a decorative border around the rim. It was recovered from a shipwreck, discovered in 1997, that was 32 nautical miles off the coast of Brunei at a depth of 62 metres. The excavation uncovered more than 13,000 artefacts, the majority of which were ceramics dated to the late fifteenth century and the early sixteenth century CE.

Produced in the kilns of Jingdezhen in Jiangxi Province, China, this blue and white ware is characteristic of the Ming dynasty, a period regarded as a golden age for Chinese ceramics. At this time, a shift from stoneware to porcelain established the cobalt blue underglaze style as the most recognizable form of Chinese export ware. The kilns at Jingdezhen supplied both imperial wares and the vast international markets that carried Chinese ceramics across maritime Southeast Asia and beyond.

The crane on this dish carried its meaning with it. In Chinese culture, the crane represents longevity and good fortune, associations that made it a natural choice for objects intended to impress, as gifts and to circulate as markers of prestige. Recovered from the hold of a ship that never reached its destination, this dish demonstrates one way the crane motif moved through the maritime trade network that connected China to the ports of Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Celadon-glazed kendi in goose form
objects.collection: Brunei Darussalam Maritime Museum, Brunei Museum Department
objects.period: Late fifteenth century to early sixteenth century
objects.caption:
This ceramic ewer (kendi) is modelled in the form of a hamsa bird. It is the only known ewer with this form in the collection of the Maritime Museum of Brunei Darussalam. The Sanskrit word haṃsa (हंस) is often translated as goose or swan but also refers to migratory waterbirds in general. The hamsa is regarded as a symbol of purity and protection across Hindu-Buddhist traditions.

Kendi of this type were used for rituals as well as for everyday functions: used to pour water at table and in ceremony alike. Their zoomorphic forms were a way of investing the act of pouring water with the qualities of the animals they depicted. Water dispensed through this vessel was thus imbued with auspicious meaning.

Likely brought to the region through the Maritime Silk Road in the late fifteenth century to early sixteenth century, this kendi reflects the movement of prestige goods that accompanied long-distance trade and diplomatic missions. The hamsa it depicts expresses sacred meanings, accumulated across the interconnected communities of maritime Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Eurasian Kingfisher
objects.scientific_name: Alcedo atthis bengalensis; Gmelin, 1778; Order: Coraciiformes; Family: Alcedinidae
objects.caption:
The Eurasian Kingfisher (Alcedo atthis bengalensis) is a small bird, only about 16 centimetres long. It is recognizable by its vibrant turquoise blue upper feathers and reddish-brown lower plumage and is often found near water bodies, such as ponds, rivers and mangroves. It is a sub-species of the Common Kingfisher (Alcedo atthis), which has a breeding range that extends across Eurasia and parts of North Africa. Some of its northern-dwelling populations are migratory and move southwards during the northern hemisphere’s winter. In Singapore, this is the most common migratory kingfisher. The kingfisher is renowned for its diving technique, and it hunts for fish and tadpoles underwater. It also eats insects and small aquatic animals. Kingfishers are highly sensitive to the conditions of a freshwater ecosystem. They rely on good water quality and an abundance of fish in order to survive. As such, the presence of kingfishers is a good indicator of a healthy ecosystem.

In Malay, the kingfisher is known as the burung pekaka. The word pekaka is derived from the sound of a bird call, possibly that made by kingfisher species such as the Collared Kingfisher (Todiramphus chloris), whose call is a loud ‘keek-keek’. The Common Kingfisher's call is instead a high, shrill whistle. Given the shyness of kingfishers and the difficulty of seeing them when they are hidden  among tree foliage, it is often easier to find them by following the sound of their calls.

Within indigenous beliefs in the region, kingfishers often have spiritual significance. In Taal in the Philippines, the kingfisher known locally as kasay-kasay, has religious associations; it features in an account of the discovery and apparitions of a statue of the Virgin Mary that became known as Our Lady of Caysasay.

objects.title: Hamsa water container
objects.object_biography: King Rama VII received the object during his royal visit to northern Thailand in 1926 and later bestowed it upon the museum.
objects.caption:
This bronze sculpture of a hamsa shows this sacred bird with its head raised upward. The bird’s neck and wings are decorated with kanok motifs and floral designs. It is believed to have served as a vessel for containing consecrated water used in ritual ceremonies.

Across Thailand, this sacred bird was incorporated into various ritual objects – often ones with close associations to water – including kendi (ewers) in the form of a hamsa and water vessels in which the bird’s mouth serves as a spout.

In Lanna culture, the hamsa is regarded as a symbol of purity and spiritual merit, making it an especially appropriate form for a vessel that holds sacred water during ceremonies. By taking the form of the hamsa, the vessel imbues the water it holds with the qualities attributed to the bird.

The bird also appears in other auspicious motifs, including the Purna-Ghata (Vase of Plenty), where it is associated with abundance and prosperity. Within Buddhist traditions, the hamsa is recognized as an auspicious symbol among the 108 signs of the Buddha and appears in numerous Jataka tales.

The hamsa’s significance extends beyond Buddhism. In Hindu tradition, the hamsa originates from the sacred realm of Mount Meru, the abode of the gods, and it is the mythical vehicle of the deity Brahma. The presence of the hamsa in Sukhothai-Sawankhalok and Lanna traditions reflects a period when Theravada Buddhism, Brahmanical practices and animistic folk belief existed alongside and shaped one another.

The hamsa’s long symbolic history across Lanna, Buddhist and wider Hindu-Buddhist traditions of South and Southeast Asia demonstrates how animal forms were repeatedly adapted into ritual practice in the region. Although its meanings varied across communities, the waterbird consistently occupied a position between the earthly and sacred realms, transformed here into the very vessel through which blessings were transmitted.

objects.title: Keris pekaka
objects.material: Kemuning wood (Murraya paniculata), brass plating and bare cast iron
objects.caption:
This keris (dagger) originates from Kelantan and features a wooden hilt carved in the likeness of a Javanese shadow puppet character. This symbolism embeds the performative traditions of the Malay Peninsula into an object carried as a marker of prestige.

This type of dagger is known as a keris pekaka due to its form, which resembles the beak of a kingfisher (burung pekaka). The upper part of the sheath (sampir) curves gracefully and is made of glossy kemuning (orange jessamine) wood. The long blade reflects the fine work of Kelantanese artisans.

The keris is unique to island communities extending from Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula to Java, Borneo, Sulawesi, Mindanao and Sumbawa, and it is one of the most significant objects of material culture in this part of Southeast Asia. Historically, the value of the keris lay not only in its function, but in the artisanship, materials and meanings accumulated around it. The keris occupied multiple roles in Malay societies: as a weapon, heirloom, ceremonial object and visible expression of status and identity.

Keris of this type are also found in Pattani in southern Thailand. They reflect centuries of movement between Kelantan and Pattani through trade, shared courtly traditions and the circulation of artisans and artistic styles. The presence of the same keris forms across modern borders points to a time when Kelantan and Pattani belonged to a connected cultural sphere. Historically, prestige was expressed through shared forms of artisanship, tradition and symbolic imagery drawn from the natural world.

In the Keris Pekaka, the kingfisher’s distinctive beak is a symbol of refinement, representing the weapon’s connection to the natural world while distinguishing it as an object of artistic and social importance.

objects.title: Offering vessel in the form of a bird
objects.title_raw: Offering vessel in the form of a bird
objects.period: Late nineteenth or early twentieth century
objects.material: Lacquered and gilded wood, inlaid glass and mirrors
objects.dimensions: Length 55 cm, height 53 cm, width 47 cm
objects.object_biography: Accession No. 1999-00795.
objects.caption:
This rare, bird-shaped Buddhist offering vessel (hsun ok) demonstrates the technical mastery of Burmese lacquer makers. Built over a wood substrate, it is decorated with a lacquer putty mixture called thayo that was modelled or moulded, then stuck onto the surface of the vessel and embellished with gold leaf. Inlaid semi-precious stones, glass and mirror pieces add further value. The result is an object that deploys the full vocabulary of Burmese applied lacquer to give form to one of the most sacred birds in Mon culture.

The word hintha derives from the Pali and Sanskrit word haṁsa, which refers both to mythical birds and real waterfowl such as geese and swans. Mythical hamsa are celebrated for their legendary ability to separate milk from water, signifying their capacity for discernment.

In Mon tradition, the hintha developed into a distinctive sacred bird associated with the origins of their homeland. According to Mon legend, when the Buddha travelled and preached in the region he encountered a pair of hintha resting on a small piece of dry land surrounded by water. The Buddha foretold that this place would one day become a prosperous city where his teachings would flourish. In Mon folklore, the city of Hanthawaddy (present-day Bago) was established on this site in the sixth century CE, preserving the memory of the prophecy through its name, which means “city of the hintha”. Another version of the legend recounts that the land was so small that only one bird could stand upon it, causing the female hintha to rest on the back of the male. This image of paired hintha became a recurring motif in Mon religious art, on royal objects such as thrones, and on betel boxes, shoes and other everyday household objects.

Its significance was further reinforced through Buddhist literature, particularly the Javana Hamsa Jataka, in which the Buddha was said to have been a king of the hintha in a previous life. In this tale, the hintha king teaches a human ruler that the passing of time and the inevitability of death are greater than any worldly achievement, encouraging him to practise the virtues expected of a righteous king. Because of this association with wisdom and moral instruction, hintha figures were placed atop prayer posts in temples throughout Myanmar.

As a hsun ok, this object brings these layers of meaning into devotional practice. Food presented via the image of the sacred bird becomes connected to Mon origin traditions, Buddhist teachings and the auspicious qualities attributed to the creature.

The presence of sacred swans in the material cultures of Myanmar, Thailand and neighbouring areas reflects the movement of animal symbolism and Buddhist traditions across mainland Southeast Asia. Yet its meaning remained rooted in local histories. For the Mon, the waterbird became a marker of sacred geography and collective identity and for Buddhist communities it embodied wisdom, generosity and spiritual aspirations.

objects.title: Đông Sơn drum
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.caption:
This bronze drum is a style of drum that was common during the bronze age of Thailand, and is related to the Đông Sơn culture, a metal age culture of Viet Nam dating back approximately 2,700 years. Such drums were often used in ceremonial contexts, including at burials and in ritual spaces. Possessing and using such drums expressed the authority of community leaders who mediated relationships between people, ancestors and the natural world. The sounds of these drums were believed to summon rain, encourage agricultural fertility, protect communities and bring people together for ancestral ceremonies.

Created through the lost-wax casting method, such drums are objects of considerable technical skill The drumhead of the Đông Sơn drum is decorated with a twelve-pointed star, geometric patterns arranged within concentric circles and a counter-clockwise flying bird motif of a kind of egret – a waterbird whose natural domain spans both the sky above and the water below – making it a fitting presence on an instrument believed to call rain from one into the other. A pair of cast-in ears are attached to the sides above the drum body.

The egret and other waterbirds were intimately connected to the seasonal rhythms of rain and were associated with water and agricultural abundance across early Southeast Asian communities. Depicted circling the starburst centre of the drum, the waterbird reflects a worldview in which creatures of the air and water participated in maintaining cosmic balance and agricultural prosperity. The presence of this type of bronze drum in southern Thailand also points to a wider regional connection. Through networks linking communities across mainland Southeast Asia, metalworking techniques and shared understandings of the natural and spiritual worlds travelled together.

objects.title: Saltwater / Estuarine crocodile
objects.collection: Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum, Singapore
objects.caption:
This particular crocodile specimen was donated to the Raffles Museum in September 1887, and it is one of the oldest of its kind in the collection today. A saltwater crocodile (also known as an estuarine crocodile), it was shot on the bank of the Serangoon River in Singapore by George Paddison Owen, a Eurasian resident. The specimen was subsequently preserved by the Raffles Museum's taxidermist of the time, L.A. Fernandis.

Crocodiles are associated with spiritual meanings in the region. They are considered by some as sacred guardians and certain crocodiles are believed to be a manifestation of a keramat spirit. Keramat are sacred shrine sites that are found in Singapore, Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia. A keramat in Butterworth, Malaysia, known as the Floating Cannon Shrine (Meriam Timbul) – due to a miraculously floating cannon found at the site that worshippers make offerings to for good luck – is linked to a crocodile legend. The story suggests that the floating cannon belonged to Panglima (Warrior) Ah Chong, and that he transformed into a crocodile upon his death. It was speculated by believers that this was the very crocodile that was shot and donated to the Raffles Museum in 1887.

A similar story from  Singapore in 1960 involved the fishing community and residents of Sungei Kadut, who believed that a local 6-metre-long crocodile was a sacred guardian and protector. They protected its location, believing that if the crocodile came to any harm or left the area, severe misfortune would befall the fishermen who lived and worked along the river.

A mythical figure that appears in older stories in the region is the ‘white crocodile’, known as buaya putih in Malay. One tale is found in the Hikayat Hang Tuah, which chronicles the life of a Malay warrior Hang Tuah who lived in the Sultanate of Malacca in the fifteenth century CE. In this episode, the Raja of Malacca was sailing through the Singapore Straits when his crown dropped into the sea. Only Hang Tuah had the courage to jump into the water to retrieve it. But just as he was about to succeed, a white crocodile appeared. In a drawn-out duel with the crocodile, Hang Tuah lost his keris, a traditional dagger that also holds important spiritual significance. As such, the white crocodile was regarded as a bad omen – a warning for the raja to return home. Today in Malaysia, a legend states that Hang Tuah's Well, located in Malacca, is the home of a white crocodile – only visible to devout religious scholars – which is believed to be the warrior’s spirit.

Crocodiles also appear in other folktales across Southeast Asia. Most prominently, according to the creation myth of the island of Timor, a giant crocodile gave up his body to form the island to provide a home for a young boy who was his friend. Perhaps the most well-known tale is that of a small animal outwitting crocodiles to cross the river. In some tellings of this story, the trickster animal is a mouse-deer, while other versions involve a monkey or rabbit.

Found in estuaries and rivers and along the coasts of Southeast Asia, Crocodylus porosus, the estuarine crocodile, is the largest living reptile in the world. While these creatures are considered dangerous, their presence as apex predators – occupying the top of the food chain – often indicates that an ecosystem is healthy and stable.

objects.title: Makara palanquin ornament
objects.material: Jackfruit tree wood, zinc, brass and copper plates
objects.dimensions: Length 130.5 cm, width 71.3 cm, height 177.3 cm
objects.object_biography: Acquired with funds from Friends of ACM through Gala Dinner 2003. Accession No. 2004-00906.
objects.caption:
This rare surviving makara ornament once formed part of a palanquin from the Malay Peninsula; it was likely produced in Pattani in the eighteenth or nineteenth century. The makara is a composite mythical creature with features drawn from animals of both land and water, including the crocodile, fish, goat and elephant. Originating from Hindu-Buddhist visual traditions, it is associated with water, fertility and the life-giving forces of nature. It has the ability to move across different realms and serves as the vehicle of the river goddess Ganga.

The makara imagery and meanings were transported across the Indian Ocean to Southeast Asia and over time were embedded in the artistic and ceremonial traditions of societies throughout the region. Within Muslim Malay communities of the northeastern Malay Peninsula, it was understood as a protective water spirit and a symbol of fertility and abundance.

The palanquin that this makara ornament was part of was used in village ceremonies associated with the circumcision of young boys – a rite of passage marking their transition into a new stage of social and religious life that was required by Islamic practice but deeply shaped by local customs. During these celebrations, circumcised boys were paraded in the palanquin and presented to the wider community. The presence of the makara on this ceremonial object demonstrates how regional symbols were reinterpreted within various religious contexts.

Through this object, the makara reveals a broader Southeast Asian tradition of transforming visual languages across varying religious landscapes. A creature born from Hindu-Buddhist cosmology became, in a Malay Muslim setting, part of a ceremony of continuity, maturity and community identity.

objects.title: Antique Chinese porcelain pillow
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies, Thailand
objects.material: High-fired underglaze blue and white stoneware (Din Phao Nuea Kraeng Khluan Khao Khian Lai Khram)
objects.dimensions: Length 13.5 cm, height 11.8 cm, width 6 cm
objects.object_biography: Donated by Mr Pracha and Mrs Namthip Chanthadeeying. Official museum documentation recorded on 22 May 1995. Exhibited in the History and Ethnology Room (Hong Prawattisat lae Chattiphan), Folklore Museum, Institute of Southern Thai Studies.
objects.caption:
This Chinese porcelain pillow is formed from dense high-fired stoneware, coated with a smooth white glaze and decorated with underglaze cobalt blue painting. Its compact rectangular form and cool surface reflect the practical design of ceramic pillows, a tradition of Chinese household objects that travelled through trade and migration to communities across Southeast Asia, including Sino-Thai families in southern Thailand.

The pillow’s cooling quality was central to its use. High-fired glazed ceramic naturally dissipates body heat, helping to keep the sleeper’s head and neck cool in accordance with traditional Chinese medical principles, which emphasised maintaining a cool head and warm feet for bodily balance. Its firm elevation provided support for the neck during rest. Similar ceramic pillows were used by physicians as wrist supports when taking a patient’s pulse.

The pillow’s decorations transformed this practical object into one of protection and blessing. The central panel depicts a pair of mythical guardian lions playing with a sacred ribboned ball, their manes and tails rendered in flowing lines that echo traditional Chinese flame motifs. In Chinese visual traditions, lions were protectors capable of warding off harmful forces and safeguarding the household, while the sacred ball symbolised wisdom, completeness and success. Together, the pair expressed wishes for peace, prosperity and protection, particularly fitting for an object in contact with the body during sleep. The decorative borders feature continuous scrollwork associated with uninterrupted continuity and lasting fortune.

Ceramic pillows were associated with important life transitions. From the Song through Ming periods, they were offered as wedding gifts that conveyed wishes for harmony, longevity and a stable family life. While the ceramic surface supported physical well-being, the animal imagery provided spiritual protection. The guardian lions therefore gave symbolic meaning to an object already connected to bodily care. In this context, the guardian lion on this pillow reinforces the connection between body and belief, in which the ceramic form cared for physical well-being, while the protective animal imagery offered spiritual safeguarding.

By the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, porcelain pillows formed part of the material culture of Chinese communities in southern Thailand, brought by Hokkien, Teochew and Hakka migrants through regional trade networks. Such pillows and the lion motif reflect the movement not only of ceramics, but also of imagery, household practices and healing traditions across maritime Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Balinese Singha Bersayap
objects.caption:
These wooden figures represent the Singa Bersayap (winged lion). Such figures often adorn Balinese temples and palace complexes and were historically placed above entrances and beneath roof structures as guardians, while also serving as sacred mounts for divine images during ritual processions. The fierce expression, open jaws, bulging eyes and extended wings communicate its role as a supernatural guardian against evil forces. The wings, recalling the Garuda, transform the lion from an earthly creature into a celestial being.

In sacred architecture, singa figures such as these reinforced the understanding of the temple as a protected cosmic space, with the temple itself a symbolic reflection of Mount Meru, the sacred mountain at the centre of the universe in Hindu-Buddhist cosmology. Through these guardian figures, architectural spaces were connected to the divine order they represented.

While the lion is not native to Southeast Asia, it has a powerful presence in the region’s religious and artistic traditions. Imported into the region via Hindu-Buddhist traditions, the lion came to represent sovereignty, protection and sacred power in the region. In Bali, this animal developed into the mythical form of the singa, a guardian figure that stands on the threshold between the human and spirit worlds.

Another expression of the Balinese singa is the Barong Ket, the lion-like protector who battles the witch Rangda in ritual performances. Their eternal struggle represents the tension between opposing forces: chaos and order, destruction and protection. Rather than eliminating darkness, the performance renews the balance that allows the world to continue, reaffirming the Balinese belief that harmony depends on maintaining equilibrium between these forces.

The lion was adapted into local traditions across Southeast Asia. In Myanmar, the lion became the chinthe, a guardian figure placed at the entrances of pagodas and important buildings. One legend tells of Sīhabāhu, the son of a lion and a human princess, who killed a lion only to find out that it was his father. To honour his father and atone for the killing, he commissioned lion images for pagodas, giving the chinthe its associations with royal authority, protection and Buddhist devotion.

In the Malay world, the lion entered local memory through the founding legend of Singapore, in which the Sumatran prince Sri Tri Buana (Sang Nila Utama) encountered a powerful animal at Temasek believed to be a lion and named the settlement Singapura, from the Sanskrit singa (lion) and pura (city).

The Balinese singa, Malay singa and Burmese chinthe demonstrate how an animal absent from Southeast Asia’s natural landscape became deeply embedded in the region’s cultural consciousness. Through shared religious traditions that were reshaped via local myths, rituals and political histories, the lion became a guardian figure across Southeast Asia with particular meanings within each community.

objects.title: Gold-sheathed lion-shaped betel nut cutter
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies, Thailand
objects.place_of_production: Mueang Yala District, Yala Province, Thailand
objects.material: Forged steel and repoussé gold sheet (loha thongkham lae lek)
objects.object_biography: Exhibited in the Knives and Traditional Weapons Room (Hong Mit lae Satrawut), Folklore Museum, Institute of Southern Thai Studies.
objects.caption:
The pivot head of this betel nut cutter – the functional joint that opens and closes – is sculpted as a lion (singha) with expressive eyes, sharp fangs and a flowing mane. It is forged from high-grade steel, and the handles are entirely sheathed in gold, with the handle tips intricately decorated with granulated beadwork (lai chut khai pla) shaped like a budding lotus.

The lion and lotus were carefully chosen symbols. Across Hindu-Buddhist traditions, the singha represented strength, courage, protection and authority, while the budding lotus symbolised purity, spiritual virtue and the flourishing of Buddhist teachings. Together, they transformed an everyday implement into an object that communicated both spiritual meaning and social standing.

Across Southeast Asia, betel cutters were used to prepare areca nuts for chewing with betel leaves, lime and aromatic spices. This example belonged to a more ceremonial context. Gold-sheathed betel sets (chian mak) were associated with royalty, high-ranking officials and wealthy merchants. In the Rattanakosin period, specialized sets were presented as gifts to senior monks to recognize their status.

Found in Yala Province of Thailand, this betel cutter reflects the cultural exchanges that shaped the region. This object represents a convergence of Malay Muslim and Theravada Buddhist communities and the Siamese court, and the symbols that passed across religious and cultural boundaries. Through its imagery, materials and artisanship, this object reveals how symbols were transmitted, adapted and reinterpreted by the various communities that used them.

objects.title: Lacquered ceremonial vessel
objects.period: Late nineteenth century and early twentieth century CE
objects.object_biography: Accession No. 2010-00503. Anonymous gift
objects.caption:
This lacquered wood vessel, inlaid with mother-of-pearl, is decorated with animals of the zodiac, including the ox (buffalo), set amidst floral vegetation. The lid bears a large Buddhist lion and the base carries the mark of a crown – details that suggest this ceremonial vessel was intended for a monk of high standing.

Mother-of-pearl, the iridescent inner lining of marine mollusc shells, was widely traded across the region over centuries. In Thailand, opalescent shells were used as early as the Dvaravati period (ninth century) for architectural decoration. Mother-of-pearl became prominent during the Ayutthaya period when laws decreed it to be exclusively used for royal utensils, and a department for the production of mother-of-pearl work was subsequently set up. These associations with the royal court and specialized artisanship gave mother-of-pearl objects a heightened prestige. As a result, the material became especially appropriate for acts of Buddhist merit-making: patrons offered elaborately crafted objects, such as ceremonial vessels, as donations through which devotion and religious virtue could be expressed.

Reportedly found in Thailand and dating to the late nineteenth century or early twentieth century, this bowl reflects the circulation of mother-of-pearl artisanship and Buddhist devotional practices across mainland Southeast Asia. A material formed within the shells of marine creatures was transformed through human skill and religious intention into an object whose value lay not only in its beauty, but in its ability to embody generosity, devotion and the pursuit of merit.

objects.title: Singa Barong cloth
objects.caption:
This cotton cloth from West Java features the Singa Barong, a sacred hybrid creature that emerged within the artistic traditions of the Cirebon Sultanate. The Singa Barong combines the lion’s associations of courage, authority and guardianship with elements drawn from other traditions. It brings together the lion with the Chinese dragon, the elephant and the buraq (a winged horse-like creature) to form a sacred protective figure of Javanese visual culture that represented royal power and the guarding of important thresholds between the human and spiritual worlds.

The Singa Barong motif appeared in palace ceremonies, ritual performances and courtly arts, and was a powerful symbol through which Cirebon communities expressed authority, protection and their place within wider networks of cultural exchange.

Although lions were not native to Java, the Singa Barong reveals how animal imagery was transmitted across Asia over centuries and was transformed through local traditions. With its multiple influences and complex form, the Singa Barong reflects the Southeast Asian region’s history as a meeting point of different cultural influences.

objects.title: Chanap
objects.material: Papaya, camphor wood, carved and gilded with lacquer painting
objects.dimensions: Body: height 23.5 cm, width 14 cm, length 34 cm; Cover: height 17 cm, width 13.5 cm, length 34 cm
objects.caption:
A chanap is a ritual offering used in prayers within Peranakan Chinese households. It is formed by carving preserved half-ripe papaya into intricate shapes such as crabs and flowers. After being carved, chanap are then placed in decorative boxes and are offered at major rituals and life events, including Lunar New Year, prayers to the Jade Emperor (Pai Thi Kong), weddings and funerals. Often the most visually striking object on the altar, it forms the centre of the offering display.

Chanap are traditionally carved into the form of a crab, as the Chinese word for crab (xie) sounds like ‘harmony’, making the creature an auspicious symbol within the offering. Through the form of the crab, the chanap brings together the linguistic symbolism of Chinese tradition with the associations attached to natural resources of the region. It combines wishes for harmony and prosperity into a sacred offering.

The term chanap is used by the Peranakan Chinese of Malacca and Singapore. Similar offerings in Penang, Phuket and Indonesia are known as bit chien or cien nap/hap, names that may derive from the Hokkien term chien hap, meaning ‘sweet-preserves box’. The presence of closely related ritual forms across these port communities reflects the movement of Peranakan Chinese traditions through the maritime networks of Southeast Asia. Here shared practices developed alongside long histories of migration, trade and settlement.

objects.title: Containers with mother-of-pearl inlay
objects.caption:
These two tiab containers, each consisting of a tray supporting a cone-shaped cover, are inlaid with mother-of-pearl against a black lacquer background. Used for presenting food to monks during royal ceremonies, they demonstrate how a material drawn from the sea was transformed into an object of courtly refinement.

The container on the left has a layered four-petalled floral design with sprays of foliage, while that on the right features a motif of a lion set within a ‘rice ball’ shape, surrounded by stylised scrollwork.

Mother-of-pearl inlay, known in Thai as khruang pradab muk, is among the most technically demanding of traditional crafts. The work involves sourcing glossy, iridescent shells from Thailand’s coastal provinces, cutting them into small pieces and then carefully setting them into a black lacquer surface. The precision required in preparing, arranging and polishing each fragment made mother-of-pearl work a highly valued craft associated with royal and religious institutions. During the Ayutthaya period, royal patronage further elevated the status of the craft, with formal regulations governing the ranks and lands of artisans involved in its production.

Mother-of-pearl decoration was applied to objects of distinction including royal furniture, ordination hall doors, Buddhist manuscript cabinets and ceremonial vessels. In these tiab containers, the rarity of the marine material and the skill required to transform it into intricate designs combined to create an object suited to the highest levels of ceremonial use. The shell’s natural brilliance, refined through human artisanship and supported by royal patronage, became a visible expression of prestige in Siamese court culture.

The elevation of the shell from a marine resource to a courtly ornament reflects a wider Southeast Asian tradition in which the natural environment provided not only materials for survival, but also the resources through which societies expressed status and power.

objects.title: Cowrie shells
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies, Thailand
objects.place_of_production: Pak Phanang District, Nakhon Si Thammarat Province
objects.dimensions: Bia Chan Cowrie group: average length 1.5–2.5 cm per shell. Bia Nang Cowrie group: average length 3.5–5.0 cm per shell. Replica metal shell money (bia loha): average length 1.5–2.2 cm, width 1.0–1.4 cm per piece.
objects.object_biography: Exhibited in the Coins and Currency Room (Hong Rian Lae Ngoentra), Folklore Museum, Institute of Southern Thai Studies.
objects.caption:
Cowrie shells are the exoskeletons of small marine gastropods belonging to the family Cypraeidae. They are characterised by their smooth, glossy texture, oval seed-like profiles and varying natural hues, ranging from porcelain white and cream to pale yellow and deep brown.

Historically, cowrie shells (bia) served as a highly efficient medium of exchange. Across markets in Southeast Asia, including the southern Thai Peninsula, varieties such as bia chan, bia nang and bia mu were valued for their consistent size, durability and the difficulty of imitating them. Whenever natural cowrie stocks became scarce, local authorities or merchant guilds produced bia loha – small cast metal replicas shaped specifically to mimic cowrie shells – marking the transition from natural currency to human-made token coinage. This image displays cowrie shells alongside their metal replicas.

Cowries were once used in everyday transactions, from purchasing food and household goods to trading regional commodities and paying taxes. These shells were also used as convenient tokens and betting chips in traditional gambling games such as ka thua. Even during the reigns of King Rama IV and King Rama V, when modern minted coinage was introduced by the central government and widely used, cowries remained a crucial currency for local trade within rural coastal communities. The role of cowrie shells in economic life is recorded in sources including the Law of the Three Seals (Kotmai Tra Sam Duang), royal administrative records and regional literature. The legacy of cowries remains embedded in the Thai language – the word bia continues to serve as the root term for financial concepts, from bia liang (an allowance or stipend) to bia wat (a military pension).

The importance of cowries was closely tied to the environments that produced them. The bia sat (washed-up cowrie) legend from Pak Phanang District recounts historical periods when massive ocean swells deposited vast quantities of cowries onto the shoreline, allowing coastal villagers to gather them freely for use as currency. The story reflects the close relationship between coastal communities and the sea, while also explaining the economic importance of the Pak Phanang estuary.

Beyond their role as a currency of exchange, cowries had social and spiritual meanings. They were associated with good fortune, wealth and fertility, which led them to be incorporated into rituals and protective objects. In southern Thai and Sino-Thai traditions, amulets made from cowrie shells, bia kae, were believed to protect against malevolent spirits, black magic and misfortune, while cowrie shells buried beneath house foundations or sacred structures symbolized enduring prosperity. Ceremonial cowrie strands (phuang hoi bia) were used in votive offerings, the fulfillment of spiritual vows and communal prayers for agricultural and maritime abundance.
