objects.title: Giant Clams
objects.collection:
National Museum Bangkok, Thailand
Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum, Singapore
objects.object_biography: Labrador Nature Reserve on 10 October 2025
objects.caption:
The giant clam is a magnificent marine bivalve whose history is deeply intertwined with both the delicate marine ecosystems of Southeast Asia and the region’s rich cultural beliefs and practices. Southeast Asia is home to many of the world’s twelve giant clam species, which live in the shallow, clear waters of intertidal zones and coral reefs. While sometimes portrayed as ‘killer clams’, they are in fact harmless creatures.

Several species occur in Thai waters, including the iconic fluted giant clam, easily recognized by the prominent, protruding scales on its shell known as scutes. Nestled within the shell is a fleshy, vibrant mantle that displays rich hues of purple, green and yellow. These striking colours are produced by symbiotic algae called zooxanthellae that live inside the tissue and provide the clam with essential nutrients through photosynthesis. Giant clams also obtain nutrients via filter feeding. Their removal of excess nutrients from the water in this way makes them an essential part of keeping marine ecosystems healthy.

Shell forms have long been part of the intangible and material cultures of the Southeast Asian region. Spiral motifs that echo those of sea snail shells appeared on pottery as early as 300 BCE. Giant clams hold particular cultural significance in the region as a consequence of a relationship with human communities that stretches back millennia.

In Thailand, archaeological digs at the Bronze Age site of Ban Nam Daeng in Kanchanaburi Province unearthed prehistoric tools and giant clam shell bracelets dating back some 3,500 to 4,000 years. The presence of these shell objects in areas far beyond the coast is evidence of early trade networks and suggests that these durable marine materials circulated as markers of exchange and social status. In Singapore, archaeological evidence underscores this long-standing presence, with tridacnid shells excavated near St Andrew’s Cathedral dating back to the fourteenth century.

Today, giant clams face enormous pressures that threaten their survival. Their shallow reef habitats make them highly vulnerable to habitat degradation, including through coastal development, land reclamation, pollution and climate change. They are also overharvested, particularly for the international marine aquarium trade. Because giant clams are slow-growing and remain permanently anchored to fixed locations, they are particularly vulnerable marine species, and their recovery from drastic population declines is exceptionally difficult.

Globally, giant clams are strictly protected under CITES regulations, and the true giant clam (Tridacna gigas) is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List. Although international laws prohibit the illegal collection and trade of giant clams, overharvesting continues in parts of the region, leading to the disappearance of some species from certain areas. This is the case in Singapore. Once abundant in Singapore’s coastal waters, several clam species have been driven to local extinction, and the fluted giant clam is listed as Critically Endangered in the Singapore Red Data Book.

Safeguarding reef habitats and water quality remains absolutely essential for the survival of giant clams. In a determined effort to save and propagate these vital creatures, Thailand has pioneered special conservation programmes, breeding and raising all of its native giant clam species as part of a long-term effort to repopulate the region's reefs.

objects.title: Wangpar
objects.caption:
The Tanimbar Islands of Maluku have long been shaped by maritime life, and seashells are an important part of their communities’ material cultures. This traditional necklace, made from strands of cowrie shells attached to a frame, was historically worn together with earrings and a woven headcloth by Tanimbar men, particularly customary elders and warriors.

Cowrie shells were a valuable means of exchange in Maluku. Such necklaces required a large number of matched cowrie shells, so they were expensive to produce and were reserved for village leaders and warriors. Beyond their decorative function, such necklaces therefore signified strength, courage, wealth and social status.

As the shells were derived from the ocean, considered a sacred space inhabited by the souls of ancestors, cowrie shells were perceived as a physical representation of that realm. Wearing this cowrie necklace therefore also signified enduring connections with ancestors.

Through objects such as this, cowrie shells served as visual language through which Tanimbar communities expressed identity, authority and belonging.

objects.title: Mother-of-pearl furniture
objects.material: Wood, carved and inlaid with handcrafted mother-of-pearl
objects.dimensions: Table: diameter 115 cm, height 87 cm; Stool: height 50.5 cm, width 35 cm, length 45 cm
objects.caption:
This table and set of chairs were made in Guangdong Province from dark wood inlaid with handcrafted mother-of-pearl. Designed for Peranakan Chinese (Baba & Nyonya) whose commercial networks extended across maritime Southeast Asia, this set is an example of luxury furniture.

The material that gives this furniture its character is the mother-of-pearl, cut from the iridescent inner lining of marine mollusc shells. The shimmering mother-of-pearl forms motifs of flowers, birds and mythical creatures, blending Chinese artistic symbolism with local influences. The technique shares a common foundation with traditions such as Thai khruang pradab muk – in which shells are gathered, cut, shaped and set against a dark surface to create intricate, contrasting patterns.

The Peranakan Chinese, a culturally hybrid community shaped by interactions between Chinese and Malay worlds, developed domestic styles that reflected their cosmopolitan identities. Wealthy households combined Chinese decorative motifs with Western furniture forms, creating interiors that expressed both ancestral connections and participation in global trade networks.

Exported Cantonese furniture from the late Qing and early Republican periods reflected its own processes of adaptation, incorporating Western Rococo forms and carving techniques while retaining traditional Chinese woodworking practices.

In Peranakan households across Malacca, Singapore, Penang and the wider region, furniture like this marked wealth accumulated through trade. The mother-of-pearl embedded in its surface – the shell of a marine creature, worked by artisans in southern China – was brought to Southeast Asia via the same maritime networks through which the Peranakan communities themselves had moved. They then settled and built the material world of their homes using both imported and local materials.

In the region, furniture such as this became a visible expression of wealth and social position. The mother-of-pearl that illuminates its surface embodies the same process that defined Peranakan material culture: the adaptation of elements from across the maritime world into a distinct regional identity.

objects.title: Neptune cup sponge
objects.collection: Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum, Singapore
objects.caption:
The Neptune cup sponge (Cliona patera) is shaped like a cup or goblet and grows to over a metre in both height and diameter – a scale, by some accounts, large enough for a small child to sit inside its basin. This extraordinary species was described by the naturalist Thomas Hardwicke in 1820, thus making it the first animal species formally described from the island of Singapore. From the time of its first discovery, its unusual shape and immense size captured scientific and public attention.

It lives in marine soft sediment habitats across the Indo-West Pacific, with populations recorded in Singapore, Thailand and the islands of Koh Rong Sanloem and Koh Koun in Cambodia. This specimen in the Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum was collected over a hundred years ago at a time when this species was still a familiar presence in regional waters. Its elegant goblet-like form and unusual size made it a coveted museum specimen, but also fuelled over-collection and its rapid decline.

Once abundant, it had disappeared by the early 1900s. In 2011, two living Neptune cup sponges were discovered in the Singapore Straits. Since then, populations have been found in various other parts of Southeast Asia. In a region where coastal environments are under sustained pressure, the reappearance of the Neptune cup sponge is a reminder that ending the harvesting of threatened marine species can allow them the opportunity to regenerate.

objects.title: Phra Upagutta enshrined in a conch shell
objects.title_raw: Phra Upagutta enshrined in a conch shell
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies, Thailand
objects.dimensions: Length 7.4 cm, width 8.7 cm (Note: source text also states 2.7 cm in the body text elsewhere – both of these figures are preserved as given in the original.)
objects.object_biography: Sourced from Mr Chinwut Samitimetha. Exhibited in the Metalwork and Metallurgy Culture Room, Folklore Museum, Institute of Southern Thai Studies. Data recorded on 12 February 1996.
objects.caption:
Cast entirely from brass, this small amulet depicts the Arhat Upagutta seated in meditation, his hands pressed together in prayer (phanom mue), enclosed within a hollowed conch shell. Its surface has developed a coppery-bronze patina over time. The conch bears the rare right-turning Dakshinavarta (Thaksinawat) spiral, a form regarded in Buddhist and Hindu traditions as an auspicious emblem of cosmic order and balance.

The veneration of Upagutta originated in India and travelled through Mon, Burmese and Lanna regions before reaching southern Thailand and the Malay Peninsula. Within southern Thai folk Buddhism, Upagutta is revered as the supreme guardian of monastic rituals, a subduer of Mara and a protector against forces beyond human control. According to Buddhist legend, he resides in a state of deep meditative absorption (nirodha-samapatti) at the ‘Navel of the Sea’ (sado thale) beneath the mythical ocean. In coastal communities, where livelihoods depended on fishing, maritime trade and journeys across uncertain waters, his role developed particular significance. Once associated with the protection of large public ceremonies and invoked through state ritual, Upagutta’s image was transformed into a personal amulet carried by merchants, sailors and others seeking safety and prosperity. Enclosing his image within a sea conch – a vessel associated with sacred power, water and divine presence – transforms the amulet into a kind of portable shrine. It brings together the protective power of Upagutta and the spiritual potency attributed to the ocean itself.

The representation of a seashell as a dwelling place for a Buddhist guardian reflects a broader Southeast Asian tradition in which spiritual beliefs about protection from multiple belief systems became layered within a single object. The conch’s associations with the power of the sea and the natural world were combined with Buddhist ideas of spiritual guardianship. They merged in an amulet carried by coastal communities as they crossed uncertain waters – both literal and metaphorical.

objects.title: Sacred conch shell
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies, Thailand
objects.place_of_production: Koh Yo Sub-district, Mueang Songkhla District, Songkhla Province
objects.dimensions: Width 19 cm, length 24 cm, circumference 22 cm
objects.object_biography: Contributed by Mr Thaweesak Thongkham. Maintained in the Repository Rooms (Hong Khlang), Folklore Museum, Institute of Southern Thai Studies.
objects.caption:
The conch shell (Turbinella pyrum), known in Thai as hoi sang and in Sanskrit as shankha, has an elegant teardrop silhouette, a thick, highly calcified exterior and a smooth, hollow interior whorl. This geometry made it useful in human societies as a means of holding water and also as a horn, while the spiral gave it cosmological meanings and made it a vessel of religious significance in Southeast Asia for millennia.

In Brahmanical-Hindu cosmology, the conch shell is a foundational symbol for Vishnu, the protector of the universe. He holds the conch shell in one of his four hands, along with the discus, the mace and the lotus. The conch represents the primordial sound of creation. Vedic mythology records that Vishnu descended into the abyssal depths to retrieve sacred texts from a demon concealed inside a conch, thereby infusing the shell with absolute spiritual purity. As such, any water passing through its chamber is transformed into a holy purifying medium.

Among conches, the highest status belongs to the rare mutation known as the right-turning shell. Revered as an exceptional natural form associated with cosmic blessing, such specimens were traditionally reserved for important state and religious ceremonies, including royal coronations.

Along the Maritime Silk Road, conch shells circulated as premium commodities and high-status diplomatic tributes presented to kings. As these associations with conch shells entered Southeast Asia, through centuries of trade and migration, they were reinterpreted. The broader cosmology merged with indigenous beliefs to make the conch the primary vessel for consecrated water (nam mon) across major life-transition ceremonies, including monastic lustration, housewarmings and wedding rituals.

In the folk traditions of southern Thailand, for example, the conch is closely associated with rituals centred on sacred hydrology, where water is regarded as an element of cosmic purity and the source of biological life. To enhance this auspicious quality, many southern Thai households introduce sacred sweet-scented bael leaves (bai matoom) into the conch’s reservoir during domestic lustration ceremonies. The practice of Sang Rot Nam, pouring sacred water from the mouth of a conch shell onto the hands of a bride and groom, remains a foundational matrimonial rite in contemporary Thailand.

As an object originating from the sea, a realm associated with abundance and wealth, the conch serves as a symbol of good fortune and material prosperity, particularly among coastal merchants, shopkeepers and fishermen. Merchants commonly place sacred conches on storefront altars or sales counters to bless daily transactions. Sometimes they place coins, gold leaf or miniature talismans inside the shell’s aperture to enhance its auspicious power.

Today, the conch shell stands as a vital material archive documenting the synthesis of deep Vedic cosmology, local folk traditions and maritime commerce across Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Shell beads and blood cockle shells
objects.title_raw: Shell beads and blood cockle shells
objects.object_biography: Discovered at the Khok Phanom Di archaeological site, Phanat Nikhom District, Chonburi Province.
objects.caption:
Shells have held significance in Southeast Asia from prehistoric times. They have served as  resources and tools, and certain types are used to make ornaments and containers. The use of shells as ornaments reflects an understanding of them as something more than raw material: shells, through their association with the sea, are symbols of life, fertility and the abundance of nature.

In the late twentieth century, shell beads dating to the prehistoric period were discovered at the Khok Phanom Di archaeological site in Chonburi Province, Thailand. The presence of shell ornaments in great quantities indicates that there was trade contact between coastal and inland communities and suggests that the shells functioned as markers of exchange and connection across distances. In the beads from Khok Phanom Di a long relationship is preserved – the sea's materials are used in the cultural life of the region, carried on the body, and are part of a long history of shared meaning.

The blood cockle (Anadara granosa) is found from the eastern coast of South Africa northward and eastward through Southeast Asia, Australia, Polynesia and up to northern Japan. Today, the blood cockle remains in use in Thailand. Its meat is consumed, while its shells are used as ornaments and are processed for lime production.

objects.title: Unglazed stoneware conches
objects.object_biography: Conch shells are religious utensils used in Vajrayana (Tantric) Buddhist rituals. They serve as vessels to hold consecrated water, which is considered sacred.
objects.caption:
These unglazed stoneware vessels, shaped in the form of a conch shell, were utensils used in Vajrayana (Tantric) Buddhist ritual practice. Water held within such vessels was regarded as sacred, and was used in rites of purification, blessing and consecration.

The choice of the conch form was significant. Across Southeast Asia and beyond, the conch shell was associated with water, fertility and life. In Hinduism, the conch is one of the symbols of Vishnu, blown to begin ceremonies or proclaim victories. In Buddhism, it is one of the Eight Auspicious Symbols, representing the sound of the Buddha’s teachings or dharma.

Buriram Province of present-day Thailand, where these vessels were produced, once formed part of the Khmer Empire, whose courts and religious centres fostered a rich tradition of Hindu-Buddhist ritual practice. In Khmer culture, the conch shell (shankha) was associated with sacred sound, divine authority and ceremonial proclamation. Its sound was believed to connect the human world with the divine realm.

Khmer artisans transformed the natural shell into fired clay vessels that could hold consecrated water and also serve as ritual instruments. At sacred sites such as Angkor Wat, water poured from conch vessels was used in ceremonies of purification and consecration, and conches were blown as horns during the worship of deities and the commencement of ceremonies. These associations also made the conch an important element of royal ritual, where it expressed the sacred authority and legitimacy of the king.

This stoneware conch from Buriram reflects how Khmer artisans adapted a natural marine form into a ritual object suited to the shared spiritual beliefs and political worlds of their time. Its use builds upon longstanding associations of the conch across Southeast Asia. Shells from the sea that had long carried meanings of fertility and life later became vessels through which Hindu-Buddhist traditions expressed purification and divine authority.

objects.title: Buffalo-shaped water container
objects.dimensions: Height 21.6 cm, width 33.5 cm, width 10.8 cm
objects.object_biography: This object exists on online inventory, Accession No. 1996-00120.
objects.caption:
This handmade pottery vessel in the form of a buffalo or ox still bears the fingerprints of its maker. Made of low-fired earthenware, using coils of clay to construct the walls, this sturdy vessel has clearly incised features of a water buffalo, with distinctly formed eyes, nose, mouth and ears and nearly symmetrical horns, and an opening to allow it to serve as a container. It was most likely used during important ceremonies or for burial purposes.

Objects and motifs depicting the water buffalo were common among prehistoric communities in Southeast Asia, particularly those associated with wet-rice cultivation. In these farming communities, the buffalo was likely an essential beast of burden, serving as a symbol of a farmer's wealth as well as animistic worship.

objects.title: Calapa with buffalo shape
objects.period: Late eighteenth century and nineteenth century CE
objects.dimensions: Length 36.5 cm, Height 15.5 cm, Width 10 cm
objects.caption:
This copper calapa (betel-nut container) is in the form of a buffalo. Calapa were traditionally used by Bruneians to store betel nuts, and later to store jewellery. Today, such calapa are mainly used as decorative items and are preserved in museums as part of Brunei's cultural heritage.

The buffalo (Bubalus bubalis) was one of the most important animals in the agricultural landscape of inland Brunei, particularly among paddy-farming communities. Farmers relied on buffaloes to clear fields for cultivation and transport heavy loads, including by pulling small boats known as kuntul.

As the animal that enabled wet-rice agriculture, the buffalo came to represent strength, endurance and the productive abundance generated through human and animal cooperation. Shaping a vessel for betel nut in the form of a buffalo brought these associations into the realm of hospitality and social prestige.

Across the Malay world, betel was offered during important encounters as a gesture of respect, welcome and relationship building, and the containers used to hold its ingredients could themselves become objects of display. By representing on a finely crafted copper vessel the animal that sustained the agricultural community, this calapa linked material prosperity with the forces that produced it: the strength of the buffalo, the fertility of the land and the abundance that supported social life.

This familiar working animal became a symbol of prosperity and continuity, and this calapa shows how Southeast Asian communities elevated the creatures that sustained their livelihoods into an auspicious symbol placed on objects of cultural value and prestige.

objects.title: Perminaken
objects.caption:
Known among the Batak peoples of northern Sumatra as a buli-buli, this medicine horn (perminaken, from minak, meaning “medicine”) was carved from the hollow horn of a Sumatran serow (a goat-antelope). It was used by a datu (ritual specialist) to store ritually potent substances prepared from roots, leaves, bark, animal materials and other ingredients. These medicines were believed to protect, heal or, when required, harm. Carried from the shoulder or on a belt, the horn kept these substances close at hand during ritual practice.

The carved figure seated on the stopper may represent a predecessor in a lineage of ritual specialists or a mythical figure found on other Batak ritual objects. Similar carvings also appear on megalithic sculptures from northern Sumatra, linking this vessel to wider artistic and ceremonial traditions.

Across the Batak communities of northern Sumatra, spiritual authority rested with the datu, whose specialized knowledge of ritual and medicine complemented the civic authority of local leaders. A buli-buli was therefore both a practical container and an emblem of ritual expertise.

objects.title: Sumatran Serow
objects.collection: Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum
objects.caption: The Sumatran serow (Capricornis sumatraensis) is a rugged goat-antelope that lives on steep, forested mountains in Sumatra and the Thai-Malay Peninsula. It can be identified by its coarse dark coat, pale patches on the throat and face, a stiff upright mane, and short, slightly curved horns that both males and females have. This skull specimen is on display at the LKCNHM gallery. Serows are found in rugged rainforest between about 200 and 3,000 meters in elevation. They are able to move confidently along cliffs and rocky ledges, often staying near hillsides and caves which give them shelter and safe vantage points. Because they need large, connected areas of wild hillside forest, their presence helps scientists judge how healthy and intact these landscapes are. The serow is well-known across Sumatra. In local languages it is sometimes called the "forest goat," and it appears in stories about their amazing climbing skills. Tales have been told of how serows sleep while hanging by their horns or hook their horns into rock to scale cliffs, highlighting their agility, even if they are not literally true. Historically, serows have been hunted for food and for parts used in traditional medicine. Illegal trade continues to threaten them in Indonesia despite existing laws. The Sumatran serow is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, mainly due to poaching and habitat loss. Protecting steep forest habitats, limiting road-building, and stopping illegal trade are key steps to keep this unique mountain mammal from disappearing.

objects.title: Blue-and-white porcelain plate
objects.period: Ming Dynasty, fifteenth to seventeenth centuries
objects.caption:
Produced using cobalt underglaze painting and high-temperature firing techniques and decorated with two phoenixes surrounded by scrolling foliage, this blue-and-white (qinghua) porcelain plate is an example of the high-quality Chinese ceramics that were dispersed throughout maritime Southeast Asia during the Ming dynasty and is a reminder of the extensive maritime networks that linked China with Southeast Asian ports. It was recovered from the Brunei Shipwreck, a site located 22 nautical miles off the coast of Brunei Darussalam where a ship sank at some time around the turn of the sixteenth century.

During the early sultanate period, Brunei was an important centre of regional trade, connecting merchants, goods and artistic traditions across the South China Sea, and Chinese ceramics such as this plate were prestige objects, used for feasting, ceremonial occasions and display.

The phoenix motif carried powerful associations in Chinese culture. As a symbol of virtue and harmony, it was traditionally linked to the empress and feminine authority. In Brunei, however, the phoenix was also appreciated beyond its original meanings – as an auspicious decorative motif that signified refinement. This plate therefore demonstrates how objects transported along maritime trade networks carried symbols that were interpreted and adapted by communities across Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Covered vessel decorated with phoenixes
objects.dimensions: Length 17 cm, width 17 cm, height 15.5 cm
objects.object_biography: Accession No. 2012-00390.
objects.caption:
This covered stoneware vessel is the only known complete Vietnamese container of this kind decorated with phoenixes. Produced in northern Viet Nam during the fifteenth century, its dark blue glaze and the precisely aligned phoenix design indicate that it was likely a specially commissioned object, possibly intended as a diplomatic gift.

While rooted in Chinese cosmology, the phoenix symbol was adopted and reinterpreted by Vietnamese courts, where it was considered one of the four mythical creatures (Tứ Linh) and became part of local expressions of power, diplomacy and prestige. The phoenix therefore held an elevated position in Chinese and Vietnamese courtly traditions.

The phoenix was associated with attributes such as authority, virtue and refinement and was often used in ceremonial contexts. Its placement on a carefully crafted object identifies this functional vessel as a statement of prestige, signalling the refinement and status of its owner.

Such motifs reflect the movement of shared visual traditions across East and Southeast Asia. Its presence on stoneware produced in Viet Nam shows how symbols originating in China were adopted and reinterpreted within Southeast Asian material culture over centuries of interaction.

objects.title: Kam cheng
objects.dimensions:
Jar – height 20 cm, diameter 30 cm; Lid – height 12 cm,
diameter 32 cm
objects.caption:
A kam cheng is a covered porcelain storage jar traditionally used in Peranakan Chinese communities. Such vessels were valued not only for their usefulness in storing food but also for their decorative presence and as objects that carried wishes for prosperity, harmony and family well-being.

The jar is decorated with phoenixes and peonies, a pairing rich in Chinese symbolic meaning. The phoenix represents grace, virtue and harmony, while the peony symbolizes honour, wealth and flourishing. Together, they express aspirations for a harmonious and prosperous household.

The yellow enamel background further enhances the jar’s auspicious character. Traditionally associated with imperial authority, yellow became widely used in celebratory contexts among Peranakan communities, particularly for occasions such as weddings, birthdays and festivals. Kam cheng were often used to serve ceremonial foods, including nasi kemuli (spiced rice), linking the symbolism of the phoenix directly with acts of hospitality and family celebration.

While once associated with royalty in China, in Peranakan households across maritime Southeast Asia the phoenix became a familiar expression of prosperity, harmony and cultural identity. This jar reveals how symbols once associated with imperial authority in China were incorporated into domestic life in the Southeast Asian region.

objects.title: Offering dish
objects.period: Late nineteenth century or early twentieth century
objects.caption:
This porcelain offering dish was made for ceremonial use. Its thickly potted body, twelve-lobed fluted rim and richly decorated surface reflect the importance placed on vessels used in acts of devotion. The dish is painted with phoenixes among peonies. On ritual vessels such as this, the phoenix carried wishes for harmony between the human and spiritual worlds. The rim features the Eight Auspicious Symbols – Buddhist emblems associated with blessings, protection and spiritual well-being.

In Chinese tradition, the phoenix (fenghuang) is an auspicious creature associated with grace, virtue, harmony and high status. It is a composite being with the features of several animals – the neck of a snake, a swallow's breast, a tortoise's back and a fish's tail – embodying the perfection of many qualities. Its five-coloured plumage and harmonious song reflect cosmic balance, while its association with the empress positions it as a symbol of feminine virtue and authority.

The accompanying peony, a flower associated with honour, prosperity and beauty, reinforces these auspicious meanings. During the late Qing period, altar vessels decorated with such imagery were used in ancestral and religious ceremonies where offerings of food were presented as acts of remembrance and devotion.

When placed on objects used to honour ancestors and the sacred, the phoenix, a creature of cosmological significance, became part of ritual practice through which communities across Southeast Asia express hopes for harmony, continuity and divine blessing.

objects.title: Porcelain plate depicting a phoenix
objects.period: Late nineteenth century to early twentieth century
objects.object_biography: Accession No. 2009-03021. Credit Line: Gift of Sunny Chan Hean Kee.
objects.caption:
This plate is an example of Peranakan Chinese porcelain, or Nyonya ware, made from overglaze polychrome porcelain. The central decorative motif is a phoenix perched on a moss-covered rockery from which blossoming peonies grow. The phoenix is brightly coloured, its neck plumage and feathers painted in blue, red and green strokes.

In Chinese culture, the phoenix represents beauty, grace and high virtue, and also symbolizes the bride or the empress. When depicted perched on a rockery, it connotes stability and permanence. The peony alongside it is a symbol of spring, love, beauty and good fortune. At the edges of the dish are symbols drawn from the Eight Auspicious Symbols of Buddhism, including the unending knot, the lotus flower, the pair of golden fish and the conch shell. The bright yellow background is an auspicious colour among Peranakan Chinese, associated with festive occasions such as Chinese New Year and birthday celebrations.

Produced for Peranakan Chinese households, the plate carries the reign mark “Xuantong nian zhi”, suggesting it was produced during the reign of the Xuantong Emperor, Puyi, a period that coincided with the British Malaya colonial era.

The motifs and symbols on the plate reflect the movement of Chinese artistic traditions through maritime Southeast Asia. The phoenix, a prominent feature of imperial Chinese visual language, became a familiar symbol within domestic life far beyond the court. On this plate, it appears alongside Buddhist imagery and festive decorative traditions, reflecting the layered identities of Peranakan communities shaped by Chinese heritage, local Southeast Asian environments and centuries of cultural exchange.

The presence of the phoenix on a household object produced in colonial Malaya demonstrates how the symbolism associated with animals and mythical creatures travelled with people, goods and ideas across the region. As it moved beyond its origins, the phoenix became part of everyday expressions of family prosperity, social identity and cultural continuity among Peranakan and migrant Chinese communities throughout maritime Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Tiga Negeri cloth
objects.caption:
Tiga Negeri batik is a celebrated textile tradition that was developed on the north coast of Java. Its name, meaning three regions, refers to the dyeing process for this cloth, which combines the finest natural pigments from three renowned batik centres: the deep red (merah getih pithik) of Lasem, the indigo blue of Pekalongan and the soga brown of Solo. The resulting cloth brings together the colours, techniques and artistic traditions of these centres in a single textile, creating hybrid designs that blend inland (pedalaman) and coastal (pesisiran) batik aesthetics.

Classified as a form of Peranakan batik, Tiga Negeri textiles often feature the phoenix (burung hong), alongside floral and botanical motifs and the intricate isen-isen (decorative filler patterns) characteristic of inland Javanese batik.

The phoenix was brought to Java through interaction over centuries between Chinese and Southeast Asian communities. In Chinese tradition, the phoenix symbolizes attributes such as virtue, beauty and harmony, and within Peranakan communities it came to also represent domestic prosperity and refinement and was incorporated into decorative imagery for textiles, ceramics and household objects.

The presence of the phoenix on this cloth reflects the movement of ideas with trade in materials between China and Southeast Asia over centuries. Reinterpreted through Javanese artisanship and Peranakan artistic traditions, the phoenix became part of the multicultural visual language of coastal Java, demonstrating how communities of the region adopted symbols through cultural exchange and adapted them through local creativity.

objects.title: Batik Hokokai long cloth
objects.caption:
Hokokai batik emerged in Java during the Japanese occupation of Indonesia (1942–1945) and reflects the synthesis of Javanese batik traditions and Japanese aesthetics. Its name derives from Java Hokokai, an organization established by the Japanese administration during the occupation.

Hokokai textiles are distinguished by their finely detailed designs and elaborate motifs, which include flowers, butterflies and peacocks. The peacock is commonly associated with beauty and elegance, while the butterfly symbolizes love and harmony.

The cloth features the distinctive pagi sore (morning–evening) design, which combines two contrasting compositions on a single textile. Developed during a period of material shortages, this ingenious format allowed the cloth to be worn in two different ways, allowing a single textile to serve as multiple garments. The susomoyo border motif, adapted from the decorative hems of Japanese furisode and tomesode kimonos, illustrates how Javanese artisans incorporated and interpreted new artistic influences within the batik tradition.

objects.title: Betel box set of Sultan Abdul Samad
objects.title_raw: Betel box set of Sultan Abdul Samad
objects.period: Reign of the Sultan Abdul Samad (1859–1880)
objects.caption:
This betel box set is believed to have belonged to Sultan Abdul Samad Ibni Almarhum Raja Abdullah, the fourth Sultan of Selangor. It is thought to have been used during palace ceremonies, including the reception of distinguished guests at royal weddings and coronations.

Across maritime Southeast Asia, the offering and receiving of betel was an important social practice. The choice of vessel and the manner of presentation communicated status and respect. In ceremonial settings, a finely crafted betel set expressed both the refinement of its owners and the social standing of those who used it.

The box features moth carvings at the corners of the lid, a floral bouquet in the central medallion and scalloped floral motifs around the edges. Its elaborate details and imagery indicate that the set was used for ceremonial purposes and display. Resting inside the set is a functional betel nut cutter (kacip sireh, also known as a kalakati) in the form of a bird. By combining the symbolism of the bird with the artisanship of the betel set, it brings the associations with birds into the shared ritual of offering betel and transforms a functional implement into an expression of abundance and prestige.

This was also the case with cutters shaped as a horse's head. Within Malay court traditions, the horse was associated with nobility, military ability and social status. Introduced through networks linking the Malay world with India, China and mainland Southeast Asia, horses were valued animals that denoted prestige. In Java, they are recorded as symbols of status from as early as the seventh century, and in the nineteenth century they remained important markers of status as well as valued diplomatic gifts.

objects.title: Cloth for Buddhist prostration, featuring Garuda and peacock motifs
objects.title_raw:
Cloth for Buddhist prostration, featuring
Garuda and peacock motifs
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.material: Supplementary weft patterned cotton (Pha fai tho yok dok)
objects.object_biography: Woven by Mrs Plek Nuiphol. Exhibited in the Local Textile Exhibition Room (Hong Pha Tho Phuen Mueang), Folklore Museum, Institute of Southern Thai Studies. Condition: Excellent / complete pristine condition (Saphap Sombun).
objects.caption:
This ceremonial textile from Na Muen Si in Trang Province, Thailand, is a Buddhist prostration cloth woven with Garuda and peacock motifs using the intricate supplementary weft (yok dok) technique. During Buddhist ceremonies, such textiles are placed on the floor where devotees kneel to prostrate before Buddha images and statues or senior monks.

Created by master weaver Mrs Plek Nuiphol, this cloth features raised golden-yellow patterns against a deep red background, a colour combination traditionally reserved for important ritual textiles in southern Thailand.

The textile’s significance lies not only in its artisanship but also in the animals woven into its surface. In Hindu-Buddhist traditions in Southeast Asia, the Garuda (khrut), a mythical creature that is half human and half bird, represents divine protection, strength and the defence of Buddhist teachings. In Buddhist stories, the peacock (nok yung) is associated with overcoming desire, spiritual discipline and cultivating wisdom and symbolises beauty and purity. Its ability to remain radiant despite consuming poisonous plants made it a symbol for transforming worldly difficulties into spiritual strength.

Together, the Garuda and peacock create a powerful ritual pairing. The Garuda offers protection, while the peacock embodies inner purity and moral cultivation. Their presence on a prostration cloth reflects the devotee’s spiritual journey: approaching the sacred space under protection while seeking purification and enlightenment.

The Na Muen Si weaving tradition evolved as a communal art form centred on life rituals. Textiles featuring Garuda and peacock motifs were woven as ceremonial fabric for weddings, ordinations and funerals. In funerals they served to cover coffins. In this context, the Garuda and peacock were understood as celestial beings capable of guiding the deceased towards the afterlife and served as spiritual companions whose qualities helped connect human life with the divine realm.

objects.title: Green Peafowl
objects.collection: Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum, Singapore
objects.caption:
The Green Peafowl (Pavo muticus) is a large bird belonging to the pheasant family. Native to mainland Southeast Asia, it can be found in Cambodia, Indonesia, Lao PDR, Myanmar, Thailand, and Viet Nam. Distinguished by its iridescent green plumage, long train and striking crest, it is one of the most spectacular bird species in the region.

Both male and female Green Peafowl possess green neck plumage, but the males are larger and have longer ornamental trains. During the breeding season, males perform elaborate displays, fanning their trains and making loud calls to attract females.

Green Peafowl occupy a variety of habitats, including forests, grasslands and riverbanks. They are omnivorous and forage on the ground for such things as seeds, fruit, shoots, insects and reptiles.

In Southeast Asia, the Green Peafowl has long been associated with royalty. In Java, for example, peafowl feathers were once symbols of nobility and prestige. The Green Peafowl is also a recurring motif in traditional textiles, carvings, temple art and folklore in the region, particularly those associated with royalty.

Historically widespread across Southeast Asia, the population of the Green Peafowl declined dramatically over the twentieth century as a result of habitat loss, agricultural expansion and hunting. It has been classified as Endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List since 2009 and today only survives in fragmented populations within protected areas. Conservation efforts in the region include protection and restoration of habitats and community-led initiatives to prevent poaching.

The Green Peafowl is part of the rich avian heritage of Southeast Asia and serves as a powerful reminder of the importance of conserving the region's remaining natural forest, grassland and riverine ecosystems.

objects.title: Kalakati
objects.caption:
This copper kalakati (betel cutter) from Brunei Darussalam is in the shape of a bird. Traditionally used to cut betel nut (pinang) and local fruits, such tools were once an important part of the material culture of hospitality and daily social exchange in the region. Today, this example is valued primarily as a decorative object and for its traditional artisanship.

The bird represented in this betel cutter carries meanings beyond decoration. In traditional Bruneian Malay society, the behaviour of birds such as egrets, herons, mynas, fantails, swallows and tailorbirds around paddy fields and waterways was observed as part of agricultural life, as it helped communities interpret seasonal changes, including when to begin or delay farming activities. Birds were familiar companions within these landscapes, their movements forming part of local ecological knowledge.

The species of bird represented in this artefact would have been immediately recognizable to the users of this cutter as a familiar presence from Brunei’s fields and waterways. The bird connects the object to the attributes associated with birds and the natural world from which communities drew their understanding of time, season and place.

Here, the bird that guided agricultural rhythms became the bird that adorned a prestigious possession, showing how animals in Southeast Asian societies were valued for their contributions to everyday life and the symbolic language of prestige and identity.

Incorporating the bird motif as a crafted element for an object associated with hospitality, refinement and social interaction elevates this functional tool into a marker of culture and identity. The bird shape of the kalakati also reflects the movement and exchange of ideas and artistic traditions across the communities of maritime Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Noken
objects.caption:
A noken is a traditional bag from Papua, Indonesia, that is woven from natural fibres. Across Papuan communities, noken are used to carry everyday goods and are traditionally worn by suspending the bag from the head.

The cassowary feet adorning this bag distinguish this example from everyday noken, marking it as an object associated with leadership and social status. The cassowary is a powerful flightless bird native to Papua, the Moluccas, Papua New Guinea and northeastern Australia. Known for its strong legs, sharp claws and ability to move rapidly through dense rainforest, it has long been respected by Papuan communities as a creature of exceptional strength and spiritual potency. Its body parts carry meanings beyond their physical form, embodying the qualities associated with the animal itself. By incorporating cassowary feet into a noken, these qualities become part of the object's social meaning. Worn close to the body and carried in a prominent position, the bag expresses the strength, protection and vitality associated with the cassowary.

This relationship between people, animals and material culture can be found in many parts of the Southeast Asian region. Communities of the region traditionally incorporated feathers, hair, claws, horns, teeth and other animal parts into objects associated with leadership, status, ancestry and spiritual power.

objects.title: Pending (Traditional Belt Buckle)
objects.caption:
A pending (belt buckle) is a functional fastening for a samping (sarong). Worn in Malay and Baba & Nyonya (Peranakan) communities, its design, ornamentation and symbolism traditionally communicated the wearer’s social standing, wealth and identity. Historically, the pending also carried protective functions: it could shield the body from a keris (dagger) and, when inscribed with auspicious motifs or Quranic verses, or combined with amulets, was believed to guard the wearer from harm.

Among Malay communities, the characteristic ogival (eye-shaped) form of the pending was associated with power and prestige. Among Baba & Nyonya communities, pending developed into highly decorative heirloom objects, often incorporating intricate motifs drawn from both Malay and Chinese visual traditions.

Bird imagery featured prominently in Baba & Nyonya ornaments, where birds symbolized prosperity, beauty, harmony and auspicious fortune. Rendered on a prestige object worn close to the body, these birds also symbolized refinement. As a wearable marker of status, the pending shows how animals that carried meanings of prosperity, protection and belonging could elevate everyday objects into the realm of prestige.

The bird motifs on the Baba & Nyonya pending reveal the layered cultural exchanges that shaped the Malay Archipelago. Combining Malay traditions of personal adornment with Chinese-inspired decorative symbolism, these objects demonstrate how communities across maritime Southeast Asia adapted shared visual languages to express their identities.

objects.caption:
This small silver casket, produced by silversmiths in Thailand’s Nakhon Si Thammarat Province, is in the shape of a quail, with a plump, rounded body and an upturned head. The casket has two parts: a lower base and an upper lid, and the parts fit flush together.

It was produced using metal casting on sheet silver combined with detailed repoussé and chasing techniques (salak dun). The silversmith hammered the sheet from the reverse to create three-dimensional depth, then chased fine details onto the outer surface to delineate the wings, anatomical posture and plumage of the bird.

In southern Thai folklore, the quail (nok khum) is an auspicious symbol of protection, particularly against fires. This belief links directly to the Vattaka Jataka, a tale from the canonical Buddhist Jataka literature well known to the local population that recounts a past life of the Buddha, reborn as a baby quail in a forest. One day, a wildfire swept toward the quail’s nest. While the bird’s parents were able to fly away to save themselves, the fledgling was still unable to fly, so faced the flames alone. He recited a formal declaration of truth, grounded in the purity of his virtues, which caused the fire to pass over his nesting ground. Owing to this tale, the quail became a symbol of safekeeping, protective grace, misfortune evasion and loving kindness.

Functionally, this casket was designed to hold the ingredients for betel-quid chewing: areca nuts, betel leaves, slaked lime paste and shredded tobacco. In traditional Thai and Malay societies, this practice was associated with formal social etiquette, the reception of guests and diplomatic hospitality. Receptacles to hold these ingredients were crafted with the same artistic care as fine jewellery and scabbards.

That this casket takes the form of the fire-extinguishing quail of the Jataka is not incidental: the protective bird was brought into the domestic space as a spiritual choice, not just a decorative one.

In southern Thai manuscript culture, the Quail Yantra (Yant Nok Khum) was historically recorded in accordion-folded bark books. They featured geometric interpretations of the quail, surrounded by sacred protective incantations (katha) written in a specialized Khmer script (Khom), and were kept as talismans to protect households from fire and disaster.

objects.title: Garuda sculpture
objects.caption:
This wooden sculpture depicts Vishnu seated upon his mount, Garuda. Both figures are adorned with crowns and jewellery that signify divine and royal authority.

Garuda, a hybrid being with the body of a human and the features of a bird, is one of Southeast Asia’s most enduring legendary figures. In Hindu mythology, Garuda embodies strength, knowledge, courage, loyalty and discipline, while his role as the vehicle of the Hindu god Vishnu — the preserver of the universe — connects him with the protection of cosmic order.

In Bali and the wider Java region, rulers were often associated with Vishnu and his incarnations, linking kingship with the deity’s role in maintaining harmony and order.

One of the most famous accounts of Garuda appears in the Indian epic Ramayana. During Rama’s battle against the demon king Ravana, the latter’s son Indrajit uses the magical serpent weapon known as the nagapasha to bind Rama and his brother Lakshmana, leaving them powerless. Suddenly, a great storm descends upon the battlefield and from the sky emerges Garuda, whose very presence terrifies the serpents that form the weapon’s bindings. As Garuda approaches, the serpent arrows release their hold. Garuda then restores Rama and Lakshmana’s strength by touching their wounds.

Although this story belongs to a world of divine beings and mythical creatures, it reflects close observations of the natural world. The ancient association between Garuda and serpents echoes the real relationship between large birds of prey and snakes, and how communities saw birds as protectors against creatures sometimes associated with danger. As Hindu epics travelled to Southeast Asia, where such natural dynamics apply too, this tale was preserved, including in local versions of the Ramayana such as the Thai Ramakien, in which Garuda represented attributes such as protection, power and victory over harmful forces.

Garuda figures are a common feature of Hindu-Buddhist sacred spaces, including as architectural elements, ritual objects and standalone sculptures. Their presence reflects the Hindu-Buddhist cosmology in which temples represent a connection between the earthly and divine realms, while sacred beings such as Garuda serve as protectors of that boundary. The sculpture therefore represents not only a religious image, but also the process through which Southeast Asian communities transformed shared mythological traditions into expressions of their own identities, beliefs and histories.

objects.caption:
In this sandstone relief, which in its original setting would have been positioned high on a wall, Garuda strides in triumph over the Naga.

In the Mahabharata, an epic poem from ancient India known throughout Southeast Asia, the king of birds, Garuda, battles the gods for divine nectar (amrita), which Naga (mythical creatures that can take the form of serpents and humans) have demanded in exchange for his mother’s freedom. Vishnu, impressed by Garuda’s courage, grants him immortality and accepts his service as a faithful mount (vahana).

Rulers of Champa built temples (located mostly in what is today central and southern Viet Nam) dedicated to Buddhist deities and to local incarnations of Shiva and Vishnu. Today, the Cham people are mostly Muslim, with communities in Cambodia and Viet Nam.

figma_2026_11.title_raw: Bas-relief of a procession, illustrating the life of the Buddha
figma_2026_11.caption:
This relief forms part of the narrative cycle illustrating the life of the historical Buddha (Lalitavistara) carved along the first gallery of Borobudur. It depicts a royal or aristocratic procession, reflecting both Buddhist narrative traditions and the courtly life of eighth- and ninth-century Java. Inspired by Buddhist texts, the artists represented architecture, clothing, vehicles, ornaments, and ceremonial practices familiar to the Javanese world, making the relief an invaluable record of early Southeast Asian society as well as Buddhist visual culture. The panel remains in its original location within Borobudur, one of the world's largest Buddhist monuments, commissioned under the Sailendra dynasty in the late eighth and early ninth centuries.

Throughout history, elephants have been deeply intertwined with the lives of Southeast Asian communities, both symbolically and practically. They served as transport in warfare, where elephant duelling (Yuttahatthi) between opposing kings was regarded as the highest form of martial honour, and facilitated the movement of goods along trade routes through forests and mountainous terrain. This relief bears witness to the enduring presence of elephants in the region from an early period. While it depicts a Bodhisattva riding an elephant in eighth-century Java, by the nineteenth century elephants had also become the primary workforce of the logging industry in northern Thailand.

objects.caption:
A brown-glazed stoneware pouring vessel, shaped as an elephant with its rider, was recovered from a shipwreck off the coast of Brunei Darussalam in 1998. Crafted in the 15th–16th century at the Si Satchanalai kilns in Central Thailand, this striking object offers a vivid glimpse into Southeast Asia’s interconnected maritime world.
Elephants, symbols of wisdom, strength, and loyalty in Hindu-Buddhist traditions, were powerful cultural icons carried across the region by trade, ritual, and storytelling. As this elephant-shaped kendi travelled across seas, it became part of the vibrant networks that once linked Brunei, Thailand, and communities far beyond.
Today, this remarkable vessel stands as a reminder of our shared heritage, shaped by the movement of goods, ideas, beliefs, and the ocean itself. Through birds, animals, and objects carried by maritime exchange, Southeast Asian museums continue to illuminate stories of creativity, connection, and cultural dialogue across the region.

figma_2026_11.title: Elephant and Mahout Kendi
figma_2026_11.caption:
This brown-glazed stoneware vessel (kendi), shaped as an elephant with its rider (mahout), was crafted at the Si Satchanalai kilns in central Thailand. Historically, kendi were used across South-East Asia as pouring and drinking vessels, including in rituals and ceremonies such as weddings. Recovered in 1998 from a shipwreck off the coast of Brunei Darussalam, this striking object reflects the interconnections between communities across maritime South-East Asia.

The form of the kendi mirrors the elephant’s own act of drawing and pouring water through its trunk, creating a direct connection between the vessel’s function and its imagery. In this way, the kendi does not merely depict the elephant but evokes its presence through both form and use.

Elephants are powerful cultural symbols associated with wisdom, strength and loyalty in Hindu-Buddhist traditions. By shaping this vessel in the form of an elephant, the makers of the kendi drew upon these associations, connecting the act of pouring with the auspicious qualities attributed to the animal.

These associations were spread across the region through storytelling, rituals and trade. As the elephant symbol was transferred across the seas, it became part of the cultural networks that linked communities in Brunei and Thailand with communities across South-East Asia. Its journey reveals how heritage was shared not only through religious sites and royal courts, but also through everyday objects that moved with people, beliefs and ideas across the maritime world.

objects.title: Elephant Leg Bone (Elephas maximus indicus)
objects.caption:
This bone originates from the Asian elephant (Elephas maximus). Identified as a femur (posterior thigh bone), it was received by the National Museum Bangkok from the Ministry of Finance. Elephant bones such as this one served a critical industrial function in the production of Pod Duang (Bullet Money), a silver currency used from the 14th to 20th century: artisans shaped the silver by hammering it on an elephant thigh bone, preferred for its toughness and elasticity that allowed it to absorb repeated impact without deforming the metal. An example of Pod Duang (Bullet Money) appears later in this trail.

The specimen displayed here belongs to the Indian subspecies (Elephas maximus indicus), which inhabits natural forests across the Asian mainland — from Nepal, Bhutan and India through Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Vietnam, Cambodia, Malaysia, and Yunnan, China. Two further subspecies occur in the region: the Sumatran Elephant (Elephas maximus sumatranus), found only in Sumatra and generally smaller; and the Borneo Elephant (Elephas maximus borneacus), which shares a similar appearance to the Indian subspecies but carries a distinct genetic code.

Elephants are native to Southeast Asia, with elephant bones dating back to prehistoric times discovered in the region. A fossilised jaw identified as Stegodon insignis, believed to be related to modern Asian elephants and living approximately 2,000,000 to 10,000 years ago, was discovered at the headwaters of the Chao Phraya River in Thailand. Similar fossils have also been found in a limestone cave in Perak, Malaysia, and fossilised tusks in the Patiayam Mountains of Central Java, Indonesia.

Throughout history, elephants have been deeply intertwined with the way of life of Southeast Asian peoples, both symbolically and practically. They served as transport in warfare, where elephant dueling (Yuttahatthi) between opposing kings was regarded as the highest form of martial honour, and facilitated the movement of goods along trade routes through forests and mountainous terrain. A relief on the 8th-century Candi Borobudur in Indonesia depicts a Bodhisattva riding an elephant, while in the 19th century, elephants became the primary workforce in the northern Thai logging industry, especially after its expansion following Britain and France obtaining permission to open forest sawmills in Myanmar.

Elephant body parts served practical ends too. Across Maritime Southeast Asia, ivory was used for kris handles, ornaments, and furnishings, while in Thailand, elephant bone was turned on a lathe to produce walking stick handles, betel nut grinders, and boxes.The flexible and impact resistant properties of elephant bone also lent it well to forms of delicate handicrafts, such as the manufacture of the reeds of the Khaen, a traditional woodwind instrument from Northeastern Thailand and Laos.

This femur (thigh bone) belonged to an Asian elephant (Elephas maximus indicus), a subspecies native to the mainland forests of South-East Asia and the Indian subcontinent. It was discovered in a prehistoric site. Such sites also contain ancient fossil remains of related species, such as Stegodon insignis.

Elephants have long played an important role in South-East Asian societies, serving as transport, as war mounts and as draft animals in the logging industry. Elephant bone has also played a role. Possessing specific mechanical qualities, including toughness and high impact resistance, elephant bone was historically used to make various craft objects. These included walking stick handles, betel nut grinders and boxes.

In some cases, elephant bones served as tools. A notable example is the use of elephant thigh bones in the production of pod duang (“bullet money”), the primary silver currency used in Thailand between the fourteenth and twentieth centuries. Mint artisans used the elephant femur as an anvil surface; its unique combination of strength and elasticity allowed it to absorb repeated heavy hammer strikes without deforming or marring the silver coins. Similarly, the reeds of the khaen, a traditional woodwind instrument from northeastern Thailand and Lao PDR, were historically made using elephant bone as a cutting surface.

objects.title: Elephant Molar Coconut Grater (Dwarf Elephant Bone)
objects.title_raw: Elephant Molar Coconut Grater (Dwarf Elephant Bone)
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies, Thailand
objects.dimensions: Length 58 cm, width 33 cm, height 18 cm
objects.object_biography: Contributed by Mrs. Sriya Kongyen, House No. 21, Ranot Sub-district, Ranot District, Songkhla Province. Data recorded on 28 January 1997. Exhibited in the Coconut Grater Room (Kratai Khud Maphrao Room), Folklore Museum, Institute of Southern Thai Studies.
objects.caption:
This coconut grater, known in Southern Thai as a lek khud maphrao, is distinguished by its base, which is fashioned from the large molar of a megafaunal animal. Attached to the front is a serrated iron blade used to shred coconut meat into fine flakes for pressing coconut milk. Elephant molars are among the densest and hardest skeletal structures in the animal kingdom, making them well suited to withstand repeated pressure and impact. The use of this material reflects local knowledge in repurposing durable natural resources for everyday life.

Elders around the Songkhla Lake Basin believe this molar belonged to the “dwarf elephant” (chang khrae or chang khom), which is said to have once inhabited the peat swamps and wetlands of Southern Thailand. Folk memory places these elephants across Songkhla Province, Nakhon Si Thammarat, and Phatthalung Province, before they vanished roughly eight decades ago. Some accounts tell of villagers spotting elephants foraging in the twilight hours or slipping into paddy fields to feed. These sightings prompted the community to band together in a regional herding cry to drive them back into the wilderness. Certain locals also compare these creatures to the pygmy elephants of Sabah, Malaysia. Though scientific evidence remains inconclusive, these oral histories and folklore preserve a community’s memory of its landscape and its long relationship with elephants.

The idea of miniature elephants also appears in classical Thai treatises on elephant lore (Kotchasat) and ancient Southern palm-leaf manuscripts (Nangshue Bod), which document unusual elephant phenotypes under names such as chang klaeb(husk-sized elephants) and chang khom (stunted elephants). Beyond folklore, elephant molars have long been regarded in Thai society as auspicious protective amulets, believed to bestow Metta Mahaniyom (loving-kindness and popularity) and ward off misfortune.

These beliefs were not confined to ritual or spiritual practice, but were also embedded in everyday life. Coconut is central to Southern Thai cuisine, and the coconut grater was an essential household tool as well as a focus of communal life during merit-making ceremonies, festivals, and weddings. Villagers often gathered to share labour in the tradition known as ok pak khud phrao (“asking for mouths to grate coconuts”). By transforming a molar attributed to the dwarf elephants of local folk memory into a tool of daily use, this coconut grater demonstrates how material culture preserves human relationships with elephants and the landscapes they once shared.

objects.caption:
These miniature relic containers, fashioned from quartz and semi-precious stones, were discovered in 1960 at Wat Chedi Sung in Chiang Mai province, Thailand. They date to the Lanna period of the 16th century.
Relic containers of this type served as receptacles for Buddha’s relics, i.e., bodily fragments attributed to the historical Buddha. These relics were enshrined within a stupa or other sacred structures as objects of veneration. The animal forms chosen for such containers were not arbitrary. In fact creatures regarded as auspicious within Hindu-Buddhist traditions typically shaped these vessels to hold sacred material. Thus, the animal forms reinforced the sanctity and spiritual significance of what was held within.
The elephant form also evokes the Buddha’s previous lives as recounted in the Jataka tales, which are narratives of the Bodhisattva’s many births across human and animal forms. These tales are central to Buddhist traditions across mainland Southeast Asia. In one story, the Bodhisattva appears as an elephant king who willingly offers his tusks to a forester, thus embodying ideals of generosity and selflessness. In another, he is reborn as the king of the six-tusked elephants. Hunted because of a past grievance, the elephant king chooses not to harm the hunter upon seeing him dressed in the saffron robes of a monk, thus demonstrating compassion and restraint even in the face of suffering.
The elephant form connected these relic containers to the Buddha’s sacred presence by recalling narratives of compassion, sacrifice, and moral virtue. These narratives continued to be shared widely in Southeast Asian Buddhist traditions.

objects.title: Ganesha
objects.object_biography: The Dutch government in Java presented this to King Chulalongkorn (Rama V) of Thailand during his visit in 1896.
objects.caption:
Carved from volcanic stone, this monumental statue depicts Ganesha, the elephant-headed deity associated with wisdom, learning, and the removal of obstacles. According to Hindu tradition, Ganesha acquired his elephant head after Shiva restored him to life using the head of the first living creature encountered by his attendants. As the deity invoked at the beginning of new undertakings, he came to embody knowledge, good fortune, and successful beginnings.

The elephant's form draws on meanings that extend beyond Ganesha himself. Across South and Southeast Asia, elephants were admired for their strength, intelligence, and close relationship with water and agricultural fertility. In Hindu tradition, these qualities were also expressed through Airavata, the celestial elephant of Indra, whose association with rain and abundance reflects the importance of elephants within agrarian societies. Ganesha's rounded body likewise came to symbolise the fullness of the harvest and prosperity.

Beneath Ganesha appears his companion, the mouse. Although small, it represents the obstacles, desires, and disruptions that can hinder human life. By placing the mouse beneath him, Ganesha demonstrates his mastery over these forces, reinforcing his role as the remover of obstacles.

This sculpture reflects how communities across Southeast Asia continually reinterpreted the elephant through religious imagination and artistic practice. In the figure of Ganesha, one of the region's most familiar animals became a powerful expression of wisdom, protection, prosperity, and renewal.

objects.title: Gringsing
objects.collection: Department of Museums Malaysia (Jabatan Muzium Malaysia)
objects.caption:
Did you know that Bali’s sacred gringsing cloth and India’s exquisite patola share one of the rarest textile techniques in the world? Both are created using double ikat, a mastery practiced in only three places globally: Gujarat (India), Bali (Indonesia), and Okinawa (Japan).
From the 11th to the 19th century, Gujarati patola travelled widely across the Indian Ocean through Gujarati Muslim merchants, reaching ports in Sumatra, Malay courts, Java, Bali, and the Spice Islands Across Southeast Asia, patola became a symbol of prestige and spiritual protection.
Evidence shows that it directly influenced local weaving traditions. This shared heritage traces back to centuries of maritime trade. Gujarati patola, like the stunning piece housed at the National Museum of Malaysia, circulated among royal courts and coastal communities.
These luxurious cloths inspired new local traditions, including in Tenganan Pegringsingan in Bali, where weavers transformed the imported technique into their own spiritually potent Geringsing. Tenganan’s oral histories even recount that their ancestors once received a sacred patola from India, which became the foundation for developing their distinct patterns and ritual meanings.
Together, patola and gringsing remind us how craftsmanship, ideas, and symbols moved across the sea, weaving a shared heritage between India and Southeast Asia that continues to inspire today

objects.title: Hand-Carved Ivory and Metal Opium Pipe
objects.title_raw: Hand-Carved Ivory and Metal Opium Pipe
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies, Thailand
objects.caption:
This hand-carved ivory opium pipe (in Thai: Klong Sup Fin Nga Chang Kae Sa-lak) reflects the intersection of Chinese decorative traditions, maritime trade, and elite consumption in the Southern Thai Peninsula during the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Beyond its function as a smoking implement, its use of rare animal material and intricate craftsmanship transformed it into a prestige object associated with wealth, refinement, and social status.

The pipe’s long stem, measuring 50.5 centimetres, was designed for reclining while smoking, a practice widespread across China and Southeast Asia during this period. Its length was both functional and technical, allowing the smoke to cool before reaching the smoker and demonstrating a refined understanding of material properties and smoking practices developed over generations.

The main stem is constructed from carefully joined segments of ivory or dense bone, reinforced with blackened metal fittings.Its surface is carved in low relief with Taoist immortals and deities dressed in ceremonial robes, surrounded by auspicious clouds (xiangyun) symbolising the celestial realm and spiritual transcendence.

Ivory was a highly valued material across Southeast Asia, prized not only for its durability and smooth surface but also for its associations with rarity, power, and prestige. The choice of material connected the owner to wider cultural traditions in which elephants represented wealth, authority, and auspiciousness.

In Southern Thailand, opium pipes such as this one became closely linked to the growth of tin mining, maritime trade, and Chinese migration during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Following the expansion of coastal commerce, Chinese communities brought their smoking customs to port cities such as Songkhla and Phuket, where opium became both a commodity and a social practice. Under the Siamese state’s tax farming system and opium monopolies, finely crafted pipes made from ivory or other valuable materials became markers of elite status, owned by wealthy merchants, mine owners, and community leaders.

At the same time, opium occupied an ambivalent position within society. While opium dens served as spaces for social interaction, business exchange, and leisure, they were also criticised for their social and health consequences. With the later suppression of opium use and the destruction of smoking equipment, surviving pipes such as this became rare records of a period shaped by migration, trade, and cultural exchange.

This ivory opium pipe reveals how elephant-derived materials carried meanings beyond their physical properties. Ivory became a medium through which wealth, prestige,artistic skill, and social identity were expressed in a landscape of constant cultural exchange.

Over the past century, Southeast Asia’s elephant populations have declined significantly, owing to habitat loss and illegal hunting for ivory. Despite the international ban on ivory trade under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) in 1989, illegal trade remains a serious threat. Climate-driven droughts further affect the distribution of water sources critical for elephant survival. As a result,the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) classified the Asian elephant as an Endangered species on The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species in 2019.

objects.title: Ivory Fire Piston / Ivory Fire Syringe
objects.title_raw: Ivory Fire Piston / Ivory Fire Syringe
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies, Thailand
objects.caption:
This ivory fire piston (in Thai: lek fai tob nga chang / taban fai nga chang) is a traditional indigenous fire-making tool widely used in Southern Thailand before the introduction of matches and modern lighting devices. In parts of Central Thailand, it is known as a taban fai. The device operates through the principle of rapid air compression: when air inside the cylinder is compressed, heat is generated rapidly enough to ignite tinder. It reflects the practical experimentation and technological knowledge of past generations, who developed tools closely adapted to their environment and natural resources.

The fire piston consists of two primary components: a hollow cylinder (tua mia) and a piston rod (tua phu) inserted into it. The tip of the piston contains a small cavity for holding dry tinder, such as fibre from the tao rang palm (fishtail palm), kapok fluff, or other flammable materials. A thread or natural gasket lubricated with animal fat or resin creates an airtight seal, allowing efficient compression. Through a swift downward strike, the compressed air produces a sharp rise in temperature, igniting the tinder into an ember that can then be transferred to other fuels to create a flame.

Beyond its mechanical function, the fire piston reflects how communities incorporated animal-derived materials and knowledge of the natural world into everyday technologies. While commonly crafted from hardwood, bamboo, or animal horn, some fire pistons were made from ivory, a rare and valuable material associated with prosperity and protection. In regional folklore and animist traditions, ivory was believed to possess protective qualities, allowing an ivory fire piston to serve also as a talisman when travelling through forests or remote areas.

The fire piston is documented in Nangshue Bod, ancient Southern Thai manuscripts that preserve knowledge of traditional medicine, magical practices, and folklore. Within medical traditions, the fire piston was used to kindle fires for boiling herbal decoctions and preparing medicinal ingredients, reflecting its role in the practices of traditional healers.

Its significance was especially evident in postpartum care, known in Southern Thailand as kao kam (entering the ritual restriction period) or non fai (lying near fire). According to traditional midwives and folk healers, the fire used during maternal confinement had to be newly created within the home, to prevent the bad luck and spiritual pollution that external flames may carry. The fire piston was therefore used to produce the first flame for the firewood beneath the postpartum bamboo bed. Specific medicinal woods, such as kaen nom sao (Anaxagorea luzonensis) and mai phlong (Memecylon species), were selected to support the mother’s recovery.

objects.title: Patola cloth
objects.collection: Department of Museums Malaysia (Jabatan Muzium Malaysia)
objects.caption:
This silk cloth, known as patola in India and cendai in Malaysia, was imported from India by traders in the nineteenth century. With a ruby-red ground, it is woven with elephants, birds and stylised lozenge blossoms with two leaves on a stem, arranged in a diamond-shaped (potong wajik) pattern. Its rectangular form suggests that it was likely worn as a shawl or cummerbund (bengkung). The elephant motif woven into the textile represents associations with the elephant such as strength, power and protection, transforming the cloth into a symbolic safeguard.

In maritime South-East Asia, patola textiles such as this one were treasured possessions believed to carry spiritual protection and were given as gifts and used as coverings in ceremonies marking important life transitions, including birth, marriage and death. Patola also held protective meanings beyond ceremonial settings. Malay warriors were said to wrap the cloth around their waists before battle; along with the spiritual protection of the cloth, its many folds offered some physical protection against weapons. 

The cloth was made using double ikat, one of the world’s rarest textile techniques, historically practised in only three regions: Gujarat in India, Bali in Indonesia and Okinawa in Japan. From the eleventh to the nineteenth centuries, patola were transported across the Indian Ocean by Gujarati Muslim merchants, reaching ports and courts in Sumatra, the Malay Peninsula, Java, Bali and the Spice Islands (the Moluccas). As these textiles circulated, they influenced weaving traditions in the region. In Bali, for example, the weavers of Tenganan Pegringsingan adopted elements of the patola into their own spiritually significant geringsing cloth. Accordingly, oral histories recount the arrival of a sacred patola from India that inspired their distinctive patterns.

The elephant reflects the visual and symbolic language of strength and auspiciousness. When woven into a textile, this language became part of India and South-East Asia’s shared beliefs and practices.

The cloth was made using double ikat, one of the world’s rarest textile techniques, historically practised in only three regions: Gujarat in India, Bali in Indonesia and Okinawa in Japan. From the eleventh to the nineteenth centuries, patola were transported across the Indian Ocean by Gujarati Muslim merchants, reaching ports and courts in Sumatra, the Malay Peninsula, Java, Bali and the Spice Islands (the Moluccas). As these textiles circulated, they influenced weaving traditions in the region. In Bali, for example, the weavers of Tenganan Pegringsingan adopted elements of the patola into their own spiritually significant geringsing cloth. Accordingly, oral histories recount the arrival of a sacred patola from India that inspired their distinctive patterns.

The elephant reflects the visual and symbolic language of strength and auspiciousness. When woven into a textile, this language became part of India and South-East Asia’s shared beliefs and practices.
