objects.caption:
Pod Duang (Bullet Money) is a form of silver currency produced by hammering a piece of silver into a compact, rounded shape resembling a bullet. Markings stamped onto Pod Duang are categorised into two types: the State Symbol, stamped on top to represent the kingdom, and the Royal Cypher, stamped on the front to represent the specific reign of the monarch. The specimen displayed here bears the Chakra and Great Crown marks of the reign of King Rama IV.

The production of Pod Duang was a form of traditional craftsmanship in which artisans shaped the silver by hammering it on an elephant thigh bone — preferred for its toughness and elasticity, allowing it to absorb repeated impact without deforming the metal. The elephant femur displayed in this trail was employed for precisely this purpose.

Pod Duang served as the primary currency for trade and exchange in Thai marketplaces from the Sukhothai and Ayutthaya dynasties through the 19th century. In 1904, King Chulalongkorn (Rama V) ordered the Royal Treasury Department to announce the end of Pod Duang. Growing trade with other countries made the traditional currency too slow to produce and too susceptible to forgery. From 1904, Thailand switched to banknotes and flat coins, which remain in use today.

The use of an elephant bone anvil in the production of the kingdom’s silver currency reveals how the elephant’s physical presence extended beyond symbolism into the material workings of the state. While absent from the finished coin, the elephant’s body supported the craftsmanship behind the currency that represented royal authority and economic exchange.

objects.title: Singhasari Ganesha
objects.place_of_production: Singasari Hindu-Buddhist temple complex, East Java, Indonesia
objects.dimensions: Height 154 cm, length 105 cm, width 72 cm
objects.object_biography: This statue was formerly held by the Wereldmuseum Leiden (National Museum of World Cultures) in the Netherlands. It was returned to Indonesia in September 2023 as part of the Dutch government's repatriation programme.
objects.caption:
Carved from volcanic andesite, this thirteenth-century statue depicts Ganesha, the elephant-headed deity associated with wisdom, learning, and the removal of obstacles. This Ganesha comes from the Singhasari temple complex in East Java, one of the last great centres of religious and artistic patronage in Java before the rise of Majapahit. Singhasari developed a distinctive artistic tradition that drew on Hindu-Buddhist cosmology crafted through local forms of kingship, devotion, and craftsmanship.

In Java, Ganesha became deeply rooted in religious life as a protector of sacred places and a patron of knowledge, appearing in temples and other sacred spaces where communities sought wisdom, good fortune, and successful beginnings. The elephant's form also carried meanings beyond Ganesha himself. Across Southeast Asia, elephants were admired for their strength, intelligence, and ability to work alongside people in forests, warfare, transport, and ceremony.

Removed from the Singhasari temple complex during the Dutch colonial period, the statue remained in the Netherlands for more than two centuries before being returned to Indonesia in September 2023. Provenance research established that it had been removed in 1802 by Dutch colonial administrator Nicolaus Engelhard. Ganesha, together with the statues of Bhairava and Nandi, was shipped to the Netherlands in 1819 and installed in the gardens of the Koninklijk-Nederlandsche Instituut in Amsterdam. Three companion sculptures that had remained in Buitenzorg were sent to the Netherlands in 1827–1828 and entered the collection of the National Museum of Antiquities in Leiden, where they were reunited with the first three statues in 1841. In 1904, all six sculptures were transferred to Museum Volkenkunde, now Wereldmuseum.

objects.title: Siwaih
objects.caption:
The siwaih is a curved dagger derived from the Indian sewar, traditionally worn through the belt. Its royal form, distinguished by a bulbous hilt and luxurious embellishments, was reserved for the sultan. Across much of Islamic Southeast Asia, gold-adorned daggers were reserved for royals or as gifts from royals.

The dagger’s construction reflects Aceh’s cosmopolitan networks of trade and craftsmanship: a crossguard of ivory, a chiselled blade, a collar of gold-copper alloy, a black coral pommel topped with high-carat gold filigree, and a wooden scabbard. In particular, the placement of ivory at the crossguard—where a warrior's hand meets the blade—situates this protective material at the most physically and symbolically vulnerable juncture of combat. As a result, the crossguard protects the hand while reinforcing the dagger’s associations with power and authority. Meanwhile, the use of enamelwork on precious metal and gold filigree reflects close engagements with Ottoman Turkey and Safavid Persia. Ottoman craftsmen were sent to Aceh in the 16th century to support weapons production against the Portuguese.

Aceh, located at the northern tip of Sumatra—commanding access to the Indian Ocean and the Malacca Strait—was at its height a major centre of Islamic learning and a gathering point for pilgrims travelling to Mecca. Renowned for its exceptional wealth and ceremonial processions, the court of Aceh sustained hundreds of specialist artisans, ranging from goldsmiths and silversmiths to weavers and wood-carvers. An object like this siwaih was the concentrated expression of that accumulated cultural exchange, crafting technology, and sovereign authority.

This Acehnese siwaih thus embodies the interconnected histories of the Islamic world in Southeast Asia. It brings together the form of an Indian dagger, the techniques of Ottoman metalworking, the opulence of the Acehnese court, and materials drawn from the natural world. Its ivory crossguard, in particular, reveals how elephants and their materials were woven into expressions of protection and prestige shared within and beyond the region.

objects.title_raw: Tin ingot in the shape of an elephant

objects.caption:
The use of animal-shaped tin ingots was not confined to the Malay Peninsula. Archaeological findings and historical records reveal that ingots in the likeness of fish, crocodiles, and roosters served as currency in Sumatra, Southern Thailand, and 
the 
Philippines. This serves as testament to the active maritime trade networks connecting Southeast Asian kingdoms. The state of Perak was the primary producer of these 
zoomorphic ingots, crafting forms such as elephants, tortoises, crocodiles, goats, roosters, grasshoppers, fish, and crabs since the 16th century. In commerce, they were utilized as standard weights to ensure the accuracy of other tin blocks and goods. 
Periodically, they functioned as a direct medium of exchange. The shared motifs of these animals across borders highlight a cultural continuity and economic interaction that transcends modern political boundaries, proving that traditional Southeast Asian economies were rooted in a system of values and symbols understood by the entire regional community.

objects.title: Swan-shaped holy water pot
objects.caption:
This swan-shaped water vessel is carved from wood and consists of two parts: the body of the vessel, and a fitted lid. The exterior is decorated with gilding and inlaid with red, green and white glass, while the interior is coated with red lacquer. The vessel's gilded exterior and inlaid glass place it within the tradition of high-status ceremonial objects in Thailand.

It is presumed to have been used for consecrated holy water in religious ceremonies, as the swan is regarded as a symbol of purity and elevated status. This association made the swan a fitting form for a vessel whose contents carried the same qualities. Like the hamsa, with which the swan shares deep kinship across Hindu-Buddhist traditions of the region, the swan’s plumage and graceful bearing made it a natural embodiment of the sacred. In this object, the material prestige and the symbolic weight of the animal form reinforce each other.

objects.title: Krutor trut
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies, Thailand
objects.place_of_production: Tha Khae Sub-district, Tha Chang District, Surat Thani Province
objects.material: Hardwood (mai nuea khaeng) and forged iron (lo-ha lek)
objects.dimensions: Blade (forged carbon steel) – Length 16.5 cm, Width 1.9 cm. Handle (hardwood) – Length 64 cm. Handle Apex – carved to resemble a rooster's comb (hngon kai).
objects.object_biography: Donated by Mrs Krip. Exhibited in the Knife and Weaponry Room (Hong Mit Lae Satthrawut), Folklore Museum, Institute of Southern Thai Studies
objects.caption:
A trut (known also as a krut) – the eel-tail finger sickle – is a rice-harvesting implement for single-stalk harvesting that is unique to the agricultural landscape of southern Thailand. It features a small, curved carbon-steel blade mounted on an elongated wooden handle. The handle apex is carved to resemble a rooster's comb (hngon kai), while the sweeping rear tail mimics the form of a freshwater eel, giving the tool a distinctive dual zoomorphic identity. Its form is in stark contrast to the hand-sickles used to cut large bundles.

The design of the trut lends itself to the rice harvesting approach used in southern Thailand, where local rice varieties typically ripen at uneven rates across the same field. To use the tool, the harvester slides the elongated tail behind a cluster of mature rice stalks, then rotates their wrist to bring them against the blade and shear them cleanly – a motion that prevents grains from spilling into the mud and allows selective harvesting of only fully ripened stalks, leaving younger ones to mature.

Within the spiritual framework of southern Thai farming communities, this tool carries a sacred dimension. The trut is intimately linked to Phra Mae Phosop, the Rice Mother – the goddess of grain who is believed to reside as a living spirit within each stalk and is revered across mainland Southeast Asia. Oral traditions describe using the trut not as cutting but as formally inviting (anchoen) the Rice Mother from the paddies into the protection of the family granary – an act of welcome rather than severance.

The two animals on the handle were chosen to carry that intention. The rooster, a folkloric symbol of early rising, tireless diligence, fertility and the awakening of new life at dawn, greets the Rice Mother at the moment of harvest. The eel, deeply tied to paddy field moisture and endurance through drought, embodies the patience that makes the harvest possible. This tool, featuring both the rooster's comb and the eel's tail, is the vehicle through which a community's cosmological understanding of the harvest is transferred via the hand that holds it.

The trut embodies a shared Southeast Asian understanding of agriculture as a relationship between humans, nature and the spirit world. While the use of the rooster and eel in this tool relates to the specific plants and beliefs of southern Thailand, they also reflect a broader regional tradition in which animals carry cosmological meanings and mediate interactions between the earthly and sacred realms.

objects.title: Turtle-shaped gold plaque
objects.object_biography: Discovered during the excavation of Prasat Phako, Chok Chai District, Thailand.
objects.caption:
This plaque was fashioned from thinly hammered gold and incised in the form of a turtle. It was discovered at Prasat Phako alongside other valuable objects, such as silver sheets, quartz and gemstones carved with auspicious designs including elephants, the Garuda and lotus flowers.

In Hindu belief, Vishnu, honoured as the preserver of cosmic order, descends to the mortal world in various avatars (incarnations). One of these is Kurma, the turtle, who supported Mount Mandara during the Churning of the Ocean of Milk, using his body as a pivot to provide the stability that allowed the gods to obtain the elixir of immortality. This avatar was venerated in Khmer belief, and the turtle's qualities – stillness, weight and endurance – made it the natural embodiment of divine foundation and cosmic stability.

It is within this context that the plaque's function becomes fully legible. It is believed to have been a votive offering placed within a foundation shrine as part of the Shilanyas ceremony to sanctify a temple structure, which involved laying the first brick. Prasat Phako, like other Khmer temple-towers of its period, was built as an image of Mount Meru, the cosmic axis at the centre of the Hindu-Buddhist universe. Placing the depiction of a turtle beneath a temple-mountain served to complete the cosmological picture: the turtle in the foundation, the mountain rising above and the temple re-enacting the very act through which cosmic order was first established.

The turtle's significance extends beyond Hindu traditions, however. As a familiar creature of the riverine ecosystems of the Mekong Delta and the broader Southeast Asian environment, its depiction equally reflects indigenous beliefs venerating animals associated with water and abundance – layers of meaning that would have coexisted with, and deepened, its Brahmanical significance.

Similar gold plaques bearing turtle forms, worked in both incision and repoussé, have been found across Southeast Asia – among them at the Óc Eo, Gò Tháp and Đá Nổi sites in southern Viet Nam, associated with the ancient Funan kingdom (first to seventh centuries CE) which produced some of the earliest known Hindu iconographic images in Southeast Asia.

objects.title: The red barking deer
objects.collection: Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum, National University of Singapore, Singapore
objects.caption:
The red barking deer (Muntiacus muntjak), also known as the southern red muntjac, is among the smallest deer species in the world, with the adults weighing between 13 kilograms and 35 kilograms. This specimen is a juvenile. Adult male red barking deer have antlers and tusks, while adult females have small bony knobs on their heads, covered with tufts of fur.

Red barking deer can be found in low-density forest habitats and in forest environments near plantations in the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Java, Bali and Borneo. Once found in Singapore, the species is now locally extinct due to overhunting and habitat loss. Unlike most deer species, this one is omnivorous, with a diet that, while mainly consisting of vegetation and fruit, also includes bird eggs and small animals such as lizards and rodents.

In Malay, the red barking deer is known as kijang. There are several stories and symbolic meanings associated with the kijang: in Bornean Iban mythology, Telanjing Kijang is known to be a powerful female spirit; and in the Malaysian state of Kelantan, the kijang served as the royal symbol of Che Siti Wan Kembang, a warrior queen who ruled between 1610 and 1667.

The kijang is also associated with names of islands, such as Pulau Sekijang Bendera (Saint John's Island) and Pulau Sekijang Pelapah (Lazarus Island) in Singapore. According to a former headman of the islands, two barking deer lived on Sekijang Bendera. Eventually they separated, with one staying on the island and the other moving to Sekijang Pelapah, thus giving these two islands their names.

objects.title: Gold Naga earrings
objects.caption: This style of earrings originated in Indonesia. Such earrings are traditionally worn by Balinese and Javanese women for ceremonies and other important occasions. Their design draws inspiration from the Naga, the mythical serpent, whose associations with protection, wisdom and prosperity have long been expressed through Southeast Asia's artistic traditions. Finely crafted in gold, the earrings reflect the enduring place of the Naga in Indonesian culture, as expressed through ceremonial jewellery and dress.

objects.title: Saltwater crocodile skull
objects.collection: Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum, Singapore
objects.caption:
The saltwater crocodile, with a broad, armoured body, a powerful tail and conical teeth, is the world's largest living reptile. Adult males commonly reach between 4 and 5 metres in length, with exceptional individuals exceeding 6 metres. Females are smaller. The crocodile is a patient predator that relies on stealth – a "sit-and-wait" strategy for ambush predation – and explosive power. Its diet includes fish, crustaceans, birds and mammals. Adult crocodiles are strong enough to take large prey at the water's edge.

Within Southeast Asia, the saltwater crocodile historically ranged from Myanmar through Thailand, Cambodia, Viet Nam, Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei, Indonesia and the Philippines. The species inhabits coastal and estuarine environments, including tidal rivers, mangroves, mudflats, lagoons and nearshore marine waters, and can also be found further upriver. Mangrove forests and deltas are especially important, providing sheltered nesting sites, nursery habitat for hatchlings and places to bask.

The crocodile (buaya) occupies an emotional space in the regional imagination. It inspires awe for its power and antiquity but also evokes fear from the real danger it can pose. Folklore across Southeast Asian communities features crocodiles as gatekeepers of rivers, as embodiments of taboo and as moral arbiters in traditional tales. In everyday speech in Malay and Indonesian languages, buaya can signify cunning or predation; in some vernaculars, it metaphorically labels a playboy suitor.

In Singapore, crocodiles straddle the boundary between physical ecosystems and mythic narratives, stirring human imagination while merging respect, fear and cautious coexistence. These conflicting views of the creature – reverence and revulsion – help explain the enduring presence of buaya in local art, media and memory.

Crocodile populations in Southeast Asia have contracted over the past two centuries and are today highly fragmented. Intensive hunting in some parts of the region, including Singapore, led to local extinction by the mid-twentieth century. A key threat to crocodiles today is coastal development, particularly when it involves mangrove destruction and river modification as this results in habitat loss. Another threat is human-wildlife conflict in fishing areas, which often leads to the illegal killing of crocodiles.

Today, saltwater crocodiles are legally protected in Singapore, in recognition of their important role in maintaining ecosystem health. Conservation tools range from habitat restoration to species protection and community education. Management focuses on safeguarding mangrove and estuarine habitats while also emphasizing public safety. The challenge – and opportunity – lies in balancing human use of coasts and rivers with ensuring the continued ecological role of an apex predator that has shaped Southeast Asian waters for millennia.

objects.dimensions: Height 90 cm, width 29 cm, length 120 cm
objects.object_biography: This example was discovered at the archaeological site of Sungai Mas (Gold River) in Kedah.
objects.caption:
Across Southeast Asia, makara, mythical creatures that are a combination of various animals, were commonly placed in pairs at the entrances of temples (candi) and other sacred buildings, where they served as guardians of thresholds between the everyday and the sacred to ward off evil forces or spiritual danger before a person stepped inside.

This makara combines the features of an elephant and a fish, bringing together the qualities of powerful animals of both land and water. It was discovered at Sungai Mas (Gold River) in Kedah, one of the earliest centres of maritime trade and religious exchange on the Malay Peninsula. Dating to the seventh century CE, this granite sculpture of a makara reflects the ways communities drew on the symbolism of animals associated with protection so as to harness that power.
